profileDesc.creation:
Initially created: 2025-12-06T13:37:49.399+09:00 by chris Translate the following text from Classical Chinese into English.
Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.
5. The target language is English.

p.seg: Sīmǎ Guāng
Fèngchì Biānjí
Hòu Xué Tiān Tái
Jìn Wáng Lǐ Kèyòng shǐ fēng yú Jìn,
Cúnxù sì fēng,
jí jí dà wèi,
zì yǐ jì Táng yǒu tiānxià,
guó suì hào yuē Táng.
Tōngjiàn yuē Hòu Táng,
yǐ bié Cháng'ān zhī Táng.
Zhuāngzōng Guāngshèng Shénmǐn Xiào Huángdì Shàng
Huì Cúnxù,
Jìn Wáng Kèyòng zhǎngzǐ yě.
Qí xiān běn hào Zhūyé,
chū yú Xī Tūjué Chùyuè bié bù,
jū Shātuó qì,
zì hào Shātuó,
ér yǐ Zhūyé wéi xìng.
Zhì Zhíyí guī Táng.
Zhíyí zǐ Chìxīn yǒu gōng yú Táng,
cì xìngmíng Lǐ Guóchāng,
biān yú shǔ jí.
Kèyòng,
Chìxīn zhī zǐ yě.
Wǔdài Huìyào Yuē: Zhíyí,
Shātuó fǔ dūdū Báyěgǔ zhī liù dài sūn.
Ōuyáng Shǐ Yuē: Báyěgǔ,
Zhūyé tóngshí rén,
fēi qí shǐzǔ.
Tóngguāng Yuánnián
(Guǐwèi 、 jiǔ èr sān)
Shì nián sì yuè shǐ jí wèi gǎi yuán.
1 Chūn,
èr yuè,
Jìn Wáng xià jiào zhì bǎiguān,
yú sì zhèn pànguān zhōng xuǎn qián cháo shìzú,
yù yǐ wéi xiàng.
Sì zhèn,
Hédōng、Wèibó、Yìdìng、Zhènjì.
Cháo,
zhí yáo fān.
Xiàng,
xī liàng fān;
xià tóng.
Zhì gù cí,
Lú Zhì màn mà Jìn Wáng zhū dì,
yòu néng cí xiàngwèi yú wéixīn zhī cháo,
shì bì yǒu jiàn yě.
Wáng jí zhào Gé、Chéng bài xíngtái zuǒ、yòu chéngxiàng,
Kǎoyì Yuē: Xuē Shǐ Táng Jì zuò
「Lú Chéng」.
Jīn cóng Shílù、Zhuāngzōng Lièzhuàn.
Liáng Zhǔ qiǎn bīngbù shìláng Cuī Xié děng cè mìng Wúyuè Wáng Liú wéi Wúyuè Guówáng.
Dīngmǎo ,
Liú shǐ jiàn guó,
yíwèi míngchēng duō rú tiānzǐ zhī zhì,
wèi suǒ jū yuē gōngdiàn,
fǔshǔ yuē cháotíng,
jiàolìng xià tǒng nèi yuē zhìchì,
jiànglì jiē chēng chén,
wéi bù gǎi yuán,
biǎoshū chēng Wúyuè Guó ér bù yán jūn.
Yǐ jiàn guó,
bù kěn fù chēng Zhènhǎi、Zhèndōng jūn jiédù.
Zǒng jūnfǔ shì.
Zhì bǎiguān,
yǒu chéngxiàng、shìláng、lángzhōng、yuánwàiláng、kèshěng děng shǐ.
2 Lǐ Jìtāo suī shòu Jìn Wáng mìng wéi Ānyì liúhòu,
shì jiàn shàng juàn shàng nián.
Mùliáo Wèi Zhuó、yájiàng Shēn Méng fù cóng ér jiàn zhī
yuē:
「Jìn cháo wú rén,
zhōng wéi Liáng suǒ bìng ěr.」
Huì Jìn Wáng zhì bǎiguān,
sān yuè,
zhào jiānjūn Zhāng Jūhàn、
Zhāng Jūhàn,
Táng Zhāozōng shí wéi Fànyáng jiānjūn,
Tiānfù zhōng dà zhū huànzhě,
jiédù shǐ Liú Réngōng nì Jūhàn yú Dà'ān Shān zhī běi xī yǐ miǎn.
Qí hòu Liáng bīng gōng Réngōng,
qiǎn Jūhàn cóng Jìn Wáng gōng Liáng Lùzhōu yǐ qiān qí bīng,
Jìn suì qǔ Lùzhōu,
yīn yǐ Jūhàn wéi Zhāoyì jiānjūn.
Zhuó、Méng fù shuō Jìtāo yuē:
「Wáng jí zhào èr rén,
qíng kě zhī yǐ.」
Jìtāo dì Jìyuǎn yì quàn Jìtāo zì tuō yú Liáng,
Jìtāo nǎi shǐ Jìyuǎn yì Dàliáng,
qǐng yǐ Zélù wéi Liáng chén.
Liáng Zhǔ dà xǐ,
gèng mìng Ānyì Jūn yuē Kuāngyì,
yǐ Jìtāo wéi jiédù shǐ、tóng píngzhāngshì.
Jìtāo yǐ èr zǐ wéi zhì.
Ānyì jiù jiàng Péi Yuē shù Zézhōu,
qì yù qí zhòng yuē:
「Yú shì gù shǐ yú èr jì,
gù shǐ,
wèi Jìtāo fù Sìzhāo yě.
Shí'èr nián wéi yī jì.
Shǐ,
shū lì fān.
Zhì miè chóuchóu.
Bùxìng juān guǎn,
sǐ wèi zhī juān guǎn,
yán qì juān guǎnshè ér shì yě.
Ér lángjūn jù bèi jūnqīn,
qì jūn shì chóu,
bù wéi bèi jūn,
yì bèi qīn zhī jiàomìng.
Bèi,
pú mèi fān.
Suì jù zhōu zì shǒu.
Liáng Zhǔ yǐ qí xiāo jiàng Dǒng Zhāng wéi Zézhōu cìshǐ,
jiàng bīng gōng zhī.
Jìtāo sàn cái mù shì,
Yáoshān rén Guō Wēi wǎng yìng mù.
Wēi shǐ qì shā rén,
xì yù,
Jìtāo xī qí cáiyǒng ér yì zhī.
Guō Wēi shì shǐ cǐ.
Ōu Shǐ yún: Wēi cháng yóu yú shì,
shì yǒu túzhě,
yǐ yǒng fú qí shì rén.
Wēi zuì hū túzhě shǐ jìn jǐ gē ròu.
Gē bù rú fǎ,
Wēi chì zhī,
túzhě pī qí fù shì zhī yuē:
「Ěr yǒng zhě,
néng shā wǒ hū?」
Wēi jí qián qǔ dāo cìshā zhī,
yī shì jiē jīng,
ér Wēi zìrú.
Wéi lì suǒ zhí,
Jìtāo zòng shǐ wáng qù.
3 Qìdān kòu Yōuzhōu,
Jìn Wáng wèn shuài yú Guō Chóngtāo,
Chóngtāo jiàn Hénghǎi jiédù shǐ Lǐ Cúnshěn.
Shí Cúnshěn wò bìng,
Jǐmǎo ,
xǐ Cúnshěn wéi Lúlóng jiédù shǐ,
yú jí fù zhèn.
Yǐ fānhàn mǎbù fù zǒngguǎn Lǐ Sìyuán lǐng Hénghǎi jiédù shǐ.
Lǐ Sìyuán shí cóng Jìn Wáng zǒng bīng,
shǐ lǐng Hénghǎi jié.
4 Jìn Wáng zhù tán yú Wèizhōu yáchéng zhī nán,
xià,
sì yuè,
Jǐsì ,
shēng tán,
jìgào Shàngdì,
suì jí huángdì wèi,
yuē suì zhě,
xiān yǒu jí wèi zhī xīn,
ér jīn suì qí shì yě.
Dà shè,
gǎi yuán.
Yīn Táng guóhào,
gǎi Tiānyòu niánhào wéi Tóngguāng.
Dímǔ Qínguó Fūrén Liú shì wéi huáng tài.
Jūnzǐ yǐ shì zhī dì zhī bù zhōng.
Lú Chéng wéi zhōngshū shìláng,
bìng tóng píngzhāngshì;
Guō Chóngtāo、Zhāng Jūhàn wéi shūmì shǐ,
Xú Wúdǎng Yuē: Shūmì shǐ,
Táng gùshì huànzhě wéi zhī,
qí zhí shèn wēi,
zhì cǐ shǐ cānyòng shìrén,
ér yǔ zǎixiàng quánrèn jūn yǐ.
Yú àn Táng mò liǎng shūmì yǔ liǎng shéncè zhōngwèi,
hào wéi sì guì,
qí zhí fēi shèn wēi yě,
tè zhuānyòng huànzhě wéi zhī ěr.
Xiàng Ānshì Yuē: Táng yú zhèngshì táng hòu liè wǔ fáng,
yǒu shūmì fáng yǐ zhǔ cáo wù,
zé shūmì zhī yào,
zǎixiàng zhǔ zhī,
wèi shǐ tā fù;
qí hòu chǒng rèn huàn rén,
shǐ yǐ shūmì guī zhī nèishì.
Zhāng Xiàn wéi gōngbù shìláng、zūyōng shǐ,
Sòng Bái Yuē: Zūyōng shǐ zì Tiānbǎo sān nián Wéi Jiān shǐ.
Déxiū,
Jiàng zhī sūn yě.
Lǐ Jiàng xiàng Táng Xiànzōng,
yǒu zhí shēng.
An edict was issued for Lú Chéng to go to Jìnyáng to confer the titles of Empress Dowager and Empress.
Initially,
the Empress had no sons,
was virtuous by nature,
and not jealous or envious;
the Empress Dowager was a serving maid of Emperor Wǔ,
and the Empress often urged Emperor Wǔ to treat her well,
(Jìn Prince Lǐ Kèyòng was posthumously honored as Emperor Wǔ).
Thus, they got along very happily.
When the conferment took place,
the Empress went to the Empress Dowager’s palace to offer congratulations,
showing a joyful expression,
while the Empress Dowager appeared bashful and uneasy.
The Empress said:
“I hope our son enjoys a long reign over the country,
and that we may pass away peacefully underground,
with the imperial tombs having a master—
what more is there to say!”
Thereupon, they faced each other and sighed tearfully.
Dòulú Gé and Lú Chéng were both shallow and lacking in ability.
The Emperor, because of their distinguished family backgrounds,
and as senior officials of the ruling establishment,
employed them.
According to the Ouyáng History,
the Dòulú family was a renowned clan for generations,
Gé’s father, Zàn, served as the Prefect of Shūzhōu under the Táng.
During the turmoil at the end of the Táng,
Gé took refuge in Zhōngshān,
serving as a Judge under Wáng Chùzhí.
Lú Chéng’s family background is unknown.
During the reign of Emperor Zhāozōng of Táng, he passed the imperial examination,
and served as an Inspectorate Officer in the Salt and Iron Commission.
At the end of the Táng, to avoid the chaos,
he changed into Daoist robes,
and wandered between Yān and Zhào.
Dòulú Gé served as a Judge under the Yìwǔ Military Commissioner,
Lú Rǔbì served as Deputy Military Commissioner of Hédōng,
both were from famous Táng families,
and their status was equal to Chéng’s,
so they jointly recommended him as an Assistant Judge of the Hédōng Military Commissioner.
The Emperor discussed selecting a Chancellor,
but the old families of Táng nobles had nearly all perished in the turmoil,
Lú Rǔbì and Sū Xún were already dead,
and Lú Zhì declined,
so Gé and Chéng were appointed.
For a ruler establishing a new dynasty,
to appoint chancellors like these,
the state of the realm can be imagined.
Initially,
Lǐ Shàohóng served as the Palace Gate Commissioner,
with Guō Chóngtāo as his deputy.
By this time,
he was recalled from Yōuzhōu,
(in the fifth year of Liáng Zhēnmíng,
Lǐ Shàohóng’s assignment to Yōuzhōu is recorded in the previous volume).
He recommended Zhāng Jūhàn as the Bureau of Military Affairs Commissioner,
and appointed Shàohóng as the Palace Affairs Commissioner,
which made Shàohóng resentful.
Under the Táng system,
the Palace Affairs Commissioner ranked below the Bureau of Military Affairs Commissioner,
and his authority was far less.
Military and state affairs were all managed by Chóngtāo.
The Financial Commissioner Kǒng Qiān considered himself capable and diligent,
and should have been appointed as the Tax Commissioner;
but the consensus was that Qiān was of lowly origin and humble status,
and should not hastily assume such an important position.
(Kǒng Qiān
was a clerk in Wèizhōu.
When the Jìn Prince gained Wèizhōu,
he appointed him as Financial Commissioner.)
Qiān was made deputy,
and he was also displeased.
Wèizhōu was designated as Xìngtáng Prefecture,
establishing the Eastern Capital;
(Xué Jūzhèng’s History of the Five Dynasties: When the Jìn Prince ascended the throne,
he elevated Wèizhōu to the Eastern Capital, Xìngtáng Prefecture,
changed Yuánchéng County to Xìngtáng County,
and Guìxiāng County to Guǎngjìn County.)
Also, Zhènzhōu was designated as Zhēndìng Prefecture,
establishing the Northern Capital.
Wáng Zhèngyán, Judge of the Wèibó Military Commissioner, was appointed as Minister of Rites,
and concurrently Prefect of Xìngtáng;
Mèng Zhīxiáng, Commander of the Tàiyuán Infantry and Cavalry, was appointed as Prefect of Tàiyuán,
and concurrently Deputy Garrison Commander of the Western Capital;
Rèn Huán, Observation Judge of Lùzhōu, was appointed as Minister of Works,
concurrently Prefect of Zhēndìng,
and Deputy Garrison Commander of the Northern Capital;
(“Capital”
should be
“Capital.”)
He was also put in charge of the Six Armies and various guards.
(According to records, Later Táng’s Luòyáng had the Western Palace, Xìngshèng Palace.
At this time, Luòyáng had not yet been captured,
so the government buildings in Wèizhōu were used as Xìngshèng Palace.
Sòng Bái said: When Emperor Zhuāngzōng of Táng ascended the throne in Wèizhōu,
Chancellor Dòulú Gé proposed establishing Xìngshèng Palace,
with the imperial son Jìjí as the Commissioner of Xìngshèng Palace.)
Thirteen military districts:
Tiānxióng, Chéngdé, Yìwǔ, Hénghǎi, Lúlóng, Dàtóng, Zhènwǔ, Yànmén, Hédōng, Hùguó, Jìnjiàng, Ānguó, and Zhāoyì.
Fifty prefectures:

Wèi, Bó, Bèi, Chán, Xiāng, Yùn, Míng, Cí, Zhèn, Jì, Shēn, Zhào, Yì, Qí, Dìng, Cāng, Jǐng, Dé, Yíng, Mò, Yōu, Zhuō, Tán, Jì, Shùn, Yíng, Píng, Yù, Shuò, Yún, Yìng, Xīn, Guī, Rú, Wǔ, Xīn, Dài, Lán, Shí, Xiàn, Lín, Fǔ, Bìng, Fén, Cí, Xí, Zé, Lù, Qìn, and Liáo,
totaling fifty prefectures.
However, the Zhāoyì district governed Zé and Lù prefectures,
which had already submitted to Liáng,
leaving only twelve military districts and forty-eight prefectures.
In the intercalary month,
the Emperor’s great-grandfather Zhíyí was posthumously honored as Emperor Zhāoliè of the Yì lineage;
his grandfather Guóchāng as Emperor Wén of the Xiàn lineage;
and his father, the Jìn Prince, as Emperor Wǔ of the Tàizǔ lineage.
An ancestral temple was established in Jìnyáng,
with Gāozǔ, Tàizōng, Yìzōng, Zhāozōng, and the Yì lineage and below as the seven shrines.
(Four Táng emperors’ shrines,
and three of his own lineage’s shrines.)
On the day Jiǎwǔ,
the Qìdān invaded Yōuzhōu,
reaching Yìdìng before retreating.
At that time, the Qìdān frequently invaded,
plundering supplies,
and Yōuzhōu had less than half a year’s food reserves.
Wèizhōu had been captured by Liáng,
Lùzhōu had rebelled internally,
and people were anxious,
thinking Liáng could not be taken,
which troubled the Emperor.
Then, Liáng’s general Lú Shùnmì from Yùnzhōu defected.
Previously, Liáng’s Tiānpíng Military Commissioner Dài Sīyuǎn was stationed at Yáng Village,
(Dài Sīyuǎn’s stationing at Yáng Village began in the fifth year of Liáng Zhēnmíng, recorded in the previous volume).
(First,
all recommended promotions.)
Shùnmì said to the Emperor:
“Yùnzhōu’s garrison has fewer than a thousand soldiers,
and Liú Suíyán and Yàn Yǒng have both lost the people’s support—
it can be captured by surprise.”
Guō Chóngtāo and others all believed
“sending troops on a distant surprise attack,
if it fails,
would waste several thousand men in vain—
Shùnmì’s suggestion should not be followed.”
The Emperor secretly summoned Lǐ Sìyuán to his tent to discuss, saying:
“The Liáng forces aim to swallow Zélù,
and are unprepared in the east.
If we capture Dōngpíng,
it will strike at their heart.”
Can Dōngpíng really be taken?”
(Yùnzhōu was originally Dōngpíng Commandery.
The matter is recorded in volume 270, fourth year of Liáng Zhēnmíng.)
Sìyuán replied:
“Now, after years of war,
the people are exhausted,
if we do not achieve victory through surprise,
how can great success be achieved!
I am willing to undertake this campaign alone,
and will surely report success.”
The Emperor was pleased.
On the day Rényín,
Sìyuán was sent with five thousand elite troops from Déshèng to Yùnzhōu.
When they reached Yángliú,
it was already dusk,
dark and rainy,
and the officers and soldiers were reluctant to advance.
Gāo Xíngzhōu said:
“Heaven is aiding us—
they will surely be unprepared.”
At night,
they crossed the river and reached the city walls,
unknown to the people of Yùnzhōu.
(This route from Yángliú to Yùnzhōu city walls
did not pass through Dōng’ē County seat.)
They killed the guards,
opened the gates to admit the outside troops,
attacked the inner city,
causing great chaos within.
At dawn on the day Guǐmǎo,
Sìyuán’s troops all entered,
and captured the inner city.
Liú Suíyán and Yàn Yǒng fled to Dàliáng.
Sìyuán forbade burning and looting,
pacified the officials and people,
and arrested the acting prefect Deputy Military Commissioner Cuī Dāng and Judge Zhào Fèng, sending them to Xìngtáng.
The Emperor was overjoyed, saying:
“The Commander is truly a man of extraordinary talent—
my affairs are accomplished!”
He immediately appointed Sìyuán as the Tiānpíng Military Commissioner.
The Lord of Liáng, upon hearing of the loss of Yùnzhōu,
was greatly alarmed.
He had Liú Suìyán and Yān Yóng executed in the marketplace,
dismissed Dài Sīyuǎn from his post as Pacification Commissioner,
demoted him to the position of Deputy Military Commissioner of Xuānhuà,
(according to the "Geographical Treatise" in the *History of the Five Dynasties*,
Liáng established the Xuānhuà Army in Dèngzhōu.)
and urged him to advance and engage in battle.
Jìng Xiáng, aware that the Liáng court was in peril,
placed a rope inside his boot,
entered to see the Lord of Liáng and said:
"When the late emperor conquered the realm,
he did not consider me unworthy,
and none of my strategies went unused.
Now the enemy's power grows stronger,
yet Your Majesty disregards my words.
Since I am of no use,
it would be better to die."
He then drew out the rope, intending to hang himself.
The Lord of Liáng stopped him,
asking what he wished to say.
Xiáng replied:
"The situation is critical.
Unless Wáng Yànzhāng is appointed as the chief general,
there is no hope of salvation."
(Jìng Xiáng chose Wáng Yànzhāng merely for his momentary prowess in battle.
Observing his military strategy, which lacked long-term vision,
how could he possibly save Liáng from destruction!)
Yànzhāng was appointed to replace Sīyuǎn as the Northern Pacification Commissioner,
with Duàn Níng as his deputy.
The Emperor, upon hearing this,
personally led his imperial troops to station at Chánzhōu,
ordering Zhū Shǒuyīn, the Commander of the Cavalry and Infantry of the Fan and Han forces, to defend Déshèng,
cautioning him:
"Wáng the Iron Spear is brave and decisive.
Riding on his fervent spirit,
he is sure to launch a sudden attack.
You must prepare carefully!"
(According to the *Guǎngyùn*,
"tángtū"
is written as
"tángtū" [with variant characters],
also written as
"dàngtū,"
where "táng" and "dàng" share the same meaning.)
The history notes that the Jìn Prince was adept at predicting Wáng Yànzhāng's actions,
but not at selecting the right person to defend Déshèng.
(Zhū Shǒuyīn was a servant who attended the Emperor in his youth.
The *History of the Five Dynasties* states: Zhū Shǒuyīn served the Emperor as a slave in his youth,
and was named Huì'ér.
When the Emperor studied,
Huì'ér often attended him.)
He also sent an envoy with a letter to the King of Wú,
informing him that he had captured Yùnzhōu,
and requesting a joint military campaign against Liáng.
In the fifth month,
the envoy arrived in Wú.
Xú Wēn wished to remain neutral,
planning to lead his fleet north along the coast,
to aid whichever side was victorious.
Yán Kěqiú said:
"If the Liáng forces request our landing to provide support,
how could we refuse?"
Wēn then abandoned the plan.
Yànzhāng replied:
"Three days."
Those around him all laughed in disbelief.
(From Dàliáng, it would take more than three days just to reach the river,
hence they laughed at his words.)
Two days later,
he galloped to Huázhōu.
(According to the *Jiǔyùzhì*: Dàliáng is 210 lǐ north of Huázhōu.)
On the day Xīnyǒu,
he held a grand banquet,
while secretly sending men to prepare boats at Yángcūn.
At night,
he ordered six hundred armored soldiers,
all wielding large axes,
along with smiths,
equipped with bellows and charcoal,
to sail downstream.
(From Yángcūn to Déshèng downstream is a water journey of only eighteen lǐ.
"Bèi"
is pronounced pú bài fān,
meaning a leather bag
used to blow air into a fire.)
Yànzhāng pretended to rise to relieve himself,
then led several thousand elite troops along the southern bank of the river toward Déshèng.
A light rain was falling,
and Zhū Shǒuyīn was unprepared.
The soldiers in the boats raised the iron chains and burned them until they broke,
then used giant axes to cut the pontoon bridge,
while Yànzhāng led his troops in a swift assault on the southern city.
With the pontoon bridge severed,
the southern city was captured,
exactly three days after he had received his orders.
Shǒuyīn ferried armored soldiers across the river in small boats to rescue the city,
but it was too late.
Yànzhāng advanced to attack the forts at Pānzhāng, Májiākǒu, and Jǐngdiàn,
capturing them all.
(The surnames Pān and Zhāng shared a village,
hence the name.
"Diàn"

Over fifty military commissioners appointed by Liáng all submitted memorials and offered tribute.
The King of Chǔ, Mǎ Yīn, sent his son Xīfàn, the commander of the Yánèi Cavalry and Infantry, to have an audience,
and presented the seal of the overall commander of the Hóng and È campaign headquarters.
Liáng had appointed Yīn as the overall commander of the Hóng and È campaign headquarters.
Gāo Jìchāng, the military commissioner of Jīngnán, heard that the Emperor had destroyed Liáng.
To avoid the temple taboo of Táng,
he changed his name to Jìxīng,
because the taboo name of the honored ancestor (of Táng) was Guóchāng.
Change:
gōng héng fān.
Liáng Zhèn said:
"Táng has the ambition to swallow the world.
If we strictly guard the strategic points with troops,
we still fear we cannot protect ourselves;
how much less by going to court several thousand *li* away!
Moreover, you are an old general of the Zhū family."
The beginning of Gāo Jìxīng's service as a general for Liáng is recorded in the 263rd scroll, in the second year of the Tiānfù era of Táng Zhāozōng.
Jìxīng did not listen.
22 The Emperor sent envoys to inform Wú and Shǔ of the destruction of Liáng.
Both states were afraid.
Xú Wēn especially reproached Yán Kěqiú, saying:
"You previously thwarted my plan,"
referring to sending envoys from Yùnzhōu to join forces.
This was when Xú Wēn wanted to advance north by sea with a fleet.
The event is recorded in the fifth month.
Kěqiú laughed and said:
"I hear that the ruler of Táng, having just gained the Central Plains,
is arrogant and complacent in spirit,
and governs his subordinates without proper methods.
Within a few years,
there will be internal turmoil.
We should use humble
words and generous gifts,
protect our borders and pacify our people, and wait for it."
Excellent observation!
The men of Wú did not accept (the initial communication).
The Emperor changed his letter,
using the protocol between equal states,
saying:
"The Great Táng Emperor sends this letter to the Ruler of the State of Wú."
The men of Wú replied, calling themselves
"The Great Wú State's Ruler to the Great Táng Emperor,"
with wording and protocol like a memorial.
23 Someone from Wú reported that Zhōng Tàizhāng, the training commissioner of Shòuzhōu, had encroached upon and traded official horses.
Xú Zhīgào, by order of the King of Wú,
sent Wáng Rěn, the prefect of Chúzhōu, to patrol Huòqiū,
and thereby replaced him as training commissioner of Shòuzhōu.
Huòqiū
was a border town of Wú.
Xú Zhīgào ordered Wáng Rěn to use patrolling the border as a pretext,
thereby replacing Tàizhāng.
Xú Wēn summoned (Tàizhāng) to Jīnlíng,
and had Chén Yànqiān interrogate him three times,
but he did not answer.
Someone asked Tàizhāng:
"Why don't you defend yourself?"
Tàizhāng said:
"When I was in Yángzhōu,
I was known as a mighty warrior among a hundred thousand troops.
Shòuzhōu is only a few *li* from the Huái River.
The infantry and cavalry there number no less than five thousand.
If I had other intentions,
how could Wáng Rěn replace me with just a single horse?
My sense of duty will not betray the state.
Even if I were demoted to a county magistrate, I would go;
how much more so as a prefect!
Why should I defend myself and thereby expose the court's fault?"
Xú Zhīgào wanted to use the law to restrain the various generals,
and requested to arrest Tàizhāng and punish him.
Xú Wēn said:
"If not for Tàizhāng,
I would have already died at the hands of Zhāng Hào."
The event is recorded in the 266th scroll, in the second year of the Kāipíng era of Liáng Tàizǔ.
How can I betray him!"
He ordered Zhīgào to have his son Jǐngtōng marry Tàizhāng's daughter to resolve the matter.
24 A comet appeared in Yǔguǐ,
over a *zhàng* long.
Yǔguǐ consists of five stars,
corresponding to the divisions of Qín and Yōngzhōu.
Comet:
xiáng suì fān,
also xú zuì fān.
Appear:
xián biàn fān.
Length:
zhí liàng fān.
The ruler of Shǔ issued an edict to set up a Daoist altar at the Yùjú Huà.
The Yùjú Huà is in Chéngdū.
Péng Chéng's records say: In the first year of the Yǒngshòu era of the Later Hàn,
Lǎo Jūn and Zhāng Dàolíng arrived here.
A jade table with curved legs emerged from the ground.
Lǎo Jūn ascended and sat,
expounding the Northern and Southern Dipper Scriptures to Dàolíng.
After he left, the seat vanished,
and a cave formed in the ground.
Therefore, it was named
"Yùjú"
(Jade Table).
Daoist scriptures correlate twenty-four *huà* with the twenty-four solar terms.
Yùjú is one of them,
and it has been passed down and believed by the common people.
(The ruler of Shǔ) thought:
"The resentment of the common people has reached up to Heaven,
hence the comet appears.
This is an omen of a state's destruction,
not something that can be dispelled by prayers and sacrifices."
The ruler of Shǔ was angry,
and exiled (the official who said this) to Yúnlízhōu,
where he died on the journey.
25 Guō Chóngtǎo submitted a memorial saying:
"The military commissioners and prefects of Hé'nán who submitted memorials only gave their names,
as they have not yet been appointed to new offices.
I fear they harbor worries and suspicions."
In the eleventh month,
an imperial decree was finally issued appointing them to their new offices.
26 Lǐ Shàoqīn, the acting military commissioner of Huázhōu, through the actor Jǐng Jìn, bribed the inner palace,
and was appointed military commissioner of Tàiníng.
The Emperor was skilled in music from a young age,
so many actors were favored,
and often attended him.
The Emperor sometimes applied powder and ink himself,
and performed together with actors in the courtyard,
to please Lady Liú.
His stage name was called
"Lǐ Tiānxià" (Lǐ All-under-Heaven).
Once, while performing,
he called out himself,
"Lǐ Tiānxià,
Lǐ Tiānxià."
The actor Jìng Xīnmó hurried forward and slapped his face.
The Emperor changed countenance,
and the other actors were also shocked and frightened.
Xīnmó slowly said:
"The one who rules All-under-Heaven is only one person.
Who else are you calling?"
The Emperor was pleased,
and richly rewarded him.
The Emperor once hunted in Zhōngmóu,
trampling the people's crops.
*Jiǔyù Zhì*: Zhōngmóu County is seventy *li* west of Dàliáng.
Trample:
cí yǎn fān.
"Your Majesty is the parent of the people.
Why destroy their food,
causing them to die in ditches and ravines?"
The Emperor was angry,
shouted at him to leave,
and intended to kill him.
Jìng Xīnmó chased and caught him in front of the Emperor's horse,
and reprimanded him, saying:
"You are the county magistrate.
Do you alone not know that our Son of Heaven likes to hunt?
Why do you allow the people to farm,
obstructing our Son of Heaven's galloping?
Your crime deserves death!"
He then requested to carry out the execution.
The Emperor laughed and released him.
The various musicians came and went from the palace,
insulting and mocking the officials.
The ministers were filled with indignation and resentment,
yet none dared to voice their anger.
The Book of Documents says: "To treat gentlemen with familiarity and disrespect
is to prevent them from giving their full loyalty."
How much worse, then, to allow musicians to insult and mock them!
The regional military governors from all directions competed in offering bribes to win their favor.
How countless were those without talent who sought profit and official salary!
Jǐng Jìn was the leader among them.
Jìn was fond of gathering trivial and vulgar matters from the streets and alleys to report to the Emperor,
and the Emperor also wished to know about affairs outside the palace,
so he entrusted Jìn to be his eyes and ears.
Whenever Jìn presented a report,
the Emperor would often dismiss his attendants to question him,
and thus Jìn was able to carry out his slander and wickedness,
interfering in government affairs.
From generals and ministers on down, all feared him,
and Kǒng Yán often served him as an elder brother.
"Kǒng Yán"
should be
"Kǒng Qiān".
On the 27th, Rényín,
the Prince of Qí sent an envoy with a letter,
congratulating the Emperor on destroying Liáng,
but he styled himself as the Emperor's uncle,
and his language and etiquette were extremely arrogant.
The Prince of Qí, Lǐ Màozhēn, considered that he and the Prince of Jìn, Lǐ Kèyòng, had both been regional military governors under the Táng,
and moreover, each had been granted the imperial surname and entered into the Táng imperial lineage for their merits,
so in terms of righteousness, they were like brothers.
Therefore, he styled himself as the Emperor's uncle.
On the 28th, Guǐmǎo,
the military governor of Hézhōng, Zhū Yǒuqiān, came to court.
The Emperor feasted with him,
bestowing favors and gifts beyond measure.
On the 29th, Zhāng Quányì requested that the Emperor move the capital to Luòyáng;
this was approved.
Textual analysis states: According to the Veritable Records:
"On Jiǎchén,
it was discussed to repair the Imperial Ancestral Temple in Luòyáng."
Note: Liáng took Biànzhōu as its Eastern Capital,
and Luòjīng as its Western Capital.
Zhuāngzōng took Wèizhōu as the Eastern Capital,
Tàiyuán as the Western Capital,
and Zhēndìng as the Northern Capital.
After destroying Liáng,
he abolished the Eastern Capital, making it Biànzhōu,
and took the Yǒngpíng Army as the Western Capital,
but it is not stated what capital Luòyáng was made.
If it was considered the Eastern Capital,
then it would be no different from Wèizhōu.
Various texts only refer to it as Luòjīng,
and there was also no edict changing Liáng's Western Capital to Luòjīng.
It was not until the third year of Tóngguāng that an edict was issued to restore Luòjīng as the Eastern Capital, as before.
Perhaps when Yǒngpíng was made the Western Capital, Liáng's Western Capital was simultaneously changed to Luòjīng, but the historical record omitted this?
Now there is no way to verify,
so it is simply called Luòyáng.
On the 30th, Yǐsì,
Zhū Yǒuqiān was granted the surname Lǐ and the personal name Jìlín,
and Lǐ Jìjí was ordered to serve him as an elder brother.
On the 31st, Kāng Yánxiào was appointed as the defense commissioner of Zhèngzhōu,
and granted the surname Lǐ and the personal name Shàochēn.
On the 32nd, the Northern Capital was abolished,
and it was restored as the Chéngdé Army.
In the fourth month of this year,
the Northern Capital had been established in Zhènzhōu.
On the 33rd, the military governor of Xuānwǔ, Yuán Xiàngxiān, was granted the surname Lǐ and the personal name Shào'ān.
The military governor of Kuāngguó, Wēn Tāo, came to court,
and was granted the surname Lǐ and the personal name Shàochōng.
Shàochōng brought much gold and silk to bribe Lady Liú and the powerful musicians and eunuchs.
After ten days,
he was sent back to his garrison.
Guō Chóngtāo said:
"Our state has avenged the shame of the Táng,
yet Wēn Tāo excavated nearly all the Táng imperial tombs.
This matter is recorded in the 267th scroll, in the second year of Liáng Tàizǔ's Kāipíng era.
How can he be allowed to remain as a regional military governor?
What will the righteous men of the world think of us!"
The Emperor said:
"At the beginning of our entry into Biàn,
we had already pardoned his crimes."
In the end, he was sent away.
On the 34th, Wùshēn,
the Secretariat memorialized, stating:
"As the state's finances are not yet sufficient,
we request to retain a limited number of officials from the Three Departments, the Nine Courts, and the Directorates,
and dismiss the rest.
When those currently in office have served for twenty-five months,
they may be replaced in turn;
'currently in office'
refers to those presently holding official positions.
'Xiàn'
is pronounced xiàn.
We order the Bureau of Military Affairs to follow this model."
In the order of court assemblies,
the military officials were ranked on the west side,
hence called the Western Rank.
Many people sighed with resentment.
Earlier,
when the Prince of Jūn of Liáng was about to perform the southern suburban sacrifice in Luòyáng,
he stopped upon hearing that Yángliú had fallen.
This matter is recorded in the 270th scroll, in the third year of the Zhēnmíng era.
Zhāng Quányì requested that the Emperor promptly proceed to Luòyáng,
and after paying respects at the Imperial Ancestral Temple—
the Táng Eastern Capital also had a Grand Ancestral Temple.
In the late period, when the capital moved east, it was strictly maintained,
hence Zhāng Quányì requested the Emperor to repair and pay respects.
This was approved.
On the 36th, Bǐngchén,
Liáng's Eastern Capital, Kāifēng Prefecture, was again made the Xuānwǔ Army's Biànzhōu.
Liáng had made Sòngzhōu the Xuānwǔ Army;
an edict was issued to change its name to the Guīdé Army.
Liáng's capital was at Biàn,
and the designation of the Xuānwǔ Army was transferred to Sòngzhōu.
'Gēng'
is pronounced gēng.
On the 37th, an edict was issued ordering civil and military officials to proceed first to Luòyáng.
On the 38th, commentators held that Guō Chóngtāo, though a meritorious minister serving as chancellor,
was not knowledgeable about the precedents and regulations of the court,
and that a famous scholar from the previous dynasty should be employed to assist him.
Some recommended the Minister of Rites, Xuē Tíngguī,
and the Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent, Lǐ Qí,
who had once served as the ceremonial envoy for Tàizǔ's investiture.
Both were elderly and accomplished men of letters,
and were fit to be chancellors.
Chóngtāo memorialized that Tíngguī was frivolous and showy, lacking the substance for the chancellorship,
and that Qí was devious and treacherous, lacking the integrity of a scholar.
The Vice Director of the Left of the Department of State Affairs, Zhào Guāngyǐn, was honest, incorruptible, and upright.
Even before Liáng's fall,
northerners all said he had the capacity to be a chancellor.
All three had served under Liáng.
Tíngguī and Qí served as ceremonial envoys for Tàizǔ's investiture;
they must have once received court orders during the Táng to invest the Prince of Jìn.
On Dīngsì,
Guāngyǐn was appointed as Vice Director of the Secretariat,
and together with Dòu Lú Gé, they were made Tongpingzhangshi.
Guāngyǐn
was the younger brother of Guāngféng;
Zhào Guāngféng appears in the 266th scroll, in the first year of Liáng Tàizǔ's Kāipíng era.
He was the son of Zhào Xiù;
Tíngguī
was the son of Xuē Féng.
Xuē Féng
was renowned for his literary talent during the Huìcháng era of the Táng.
He was fond of self-aggrandizement;
Gé was merely cautious, steady, and conservative.
After Zhào Guāngféng retired from the chancellorship under the Liáng court—
In the first year of the Zhēnmíng era of Liáng's Prince of Jūn,
Zhào Guāngféng retired from the chancellorship.
Guāngyǐn went to visit him from time to time,
and they spoke of government affairs.
One day,
Guāngféng wrote on his door:
"Please do not speak of matters of the Secretariat."
On the 39th, the Vice Commissioner of Finance, Kǒng Qiān, feared Zhāng Xiàn's impartiality and integrity,
and wished to monopolize the affairs of the commission—
meaning he wished to monopolize the affairs of the Finance Commission alone.
'Shǐ'
is pronounced shǐ.
He said, "The Eastern Capital is a place of great importance,
and must be garrisoned by a high minister.
No one but Lord Zhāng is suitable."
Chóngtāo immediately memorialized to appoint Xiàn as Vice Garrison Commander of the Eastern Capital,
in charge of garrison affairs.
Thus, Zhāng Xiàn was sent out to garrison Wèizhōu.
On Wùwǔ,
Dòu Lú Gé was appointed to administer the Finance Commission,
concurrently serving as Commissioner of Salt, Iron, and Transport for all circuits.
Qiān was even more disappointed.
On the 40th, Jǐwèi,
Zhāng Quányì was additionally appointed as Acting Minister of Works,
and Gāo Jìxīng as Acting Director of the Secretariat.
At that time, Jìxīng had come to court,
and the Emperor treated him with great favor.
Casually, he asked:
"We wish to use military force against Wú and Shǔ.
Which of the two states should be dealt with first?"
Jìxīng, considering the Shǔ roads perilous and difficult to capture,
replied:
"The land of Wú is poor and its people impoverished.
Conquering it would bring no benefit.
It would be better to attack Shǔ first.
The land of Shǔ is rich and abundant,
and moreover, its ruler is dissolute and its people resentful.
Attacking it would surely lead to victory.
After conquering Shǔ,
following the current downstream,
taking Wú would be as easy as turning over one's hand."
The Emperor said:
"Excellent!"
On the 41st, Xīnyǒu,
the Yǒngpíng Army's Dà'ān Prefecture was again made the Western Capital's Jīngzhào Prefecture.
Liáng changed Cháng'ān to the Yǒngpíng Army,
as seen in the 267th scroll, in the third year of Tàizǔ's Kāipíng era;
it changed Jīngzhào Prefecture to Dà'ān Prefecture,
as seen in the 266th scroll, in the first year of Kāipíng.
On the 42nd day of the sexagenary cycle (Jiǎzǐ),
the Emperor departed from Dàliáng;
in the twelfth month,
on the day Gēngwǔ,
he arrived in Luòyáng.
43. Wúyuè King Qián Liú appointed the Army Marshal Dù Jiànhuī as Left Chancellor.
44. On the day Rénshēn,
an edict was issued designating the palaces and gardens of Biànzhōu as the imperial traveling palace.
45. Yàozhōu was renamed the Shùnyì Army,
Yánzhōu the Zhāngwǔ Army,
Dèngzhōu the Wēishèng Army,
Jìnzhōu the Jiànxióng Army,
and Ānzhōu the Ānyuǎn Army.
After the Emperor had destroyed Liáng,
he specifically changed the army names established by Liáng,
but did not alter any of the regional commanders.
Liáng had changed Yàozhōu to Chóngzhōu,
and renamed the Yìshèng Army as the Jìngshèng Army,
which had been established by Qí.
Yánzhōu,
under the Táng, was the Bǎosài Army,
and under Qí, it was the Zhōngyì Army.
Dèngzhōu,
under Liáng, was the Xuānhuà Army.
Jìnzhōu,
under Liáng, was initially the Dìngchāng Army,
and later renamed the Jiànníng Army.
Ānzhōu,
under Liáng, was the Xuānwēi Army.
All were restored to their former Táng names.
46. On the day Gēngchén,
the Censorate memorialized:
"Zhū Wēn usurped the throne,
altering the statutes, ordinances, regulations, and precedents of our dynasty.
The revision of statutes, ordinances, regulations, and precedents by Liáng is recorded in the 267th volume, in the fourth year of the Kāipíng era.
'Our dynasty'
refers to the former Táng.
Now, the Censorate, the Ministry of Justice, and the Dàlǐ Temple all use the laws of the false court.
We have heard that the archives in Dìngzhōu alone still possess the complete statutes, ordinances, regulations, and precedents of our dynasty.
We request that the local authorities be ordered to copy and submit them."
This was approved.
47. Lǐ Jìtāo, upon hearing that the Emperor had destroyed Liáng,
grew anxious and fearful,
unsure of what to do.
He considered fleeing north to the Qìdān,
when an edict arrived summoning him to the capital.
As Jìtāo prepared to depart,
his younger brother Jìyuǎn said:
"Elder brother, you have been branded a rebel;
where can you find refuge?
Whether you go or not, the outcome is the same.
It would be better to deepen the moats and heighten the ramparts,
sit and consume the stored grain,
and perhaps prolong your days.
If you go to court,
you will surely die."
Someone advised Jìtāo:
"Your late father rendered great service to the state.
'Late father'
refers to Jìtāo's father, Sìzhāo.
Sìzhāo held the title of Zhōngshū Lìng,
hence the reference.
He was the Emperor's uncle.
Lǐ Sìzhāo, as an adopted son of the Jìn King,
was like an elder brother to the Emperor,
so the Emperor was Jìtāo's uncle.
Jìtāo's mother, Lady Yáng,
was skilled at accumulating wealth,
and the family assets amounted to a million.
So, he traveled together with Lady Yáng,
bringing four hundred thousand taels of silver,
and other goods of equivalent value,
distributing large bribes.
Actors and eunuchs vied to speak on his behalf:
"Jìtāo initially had no treacherous intentions;
he was merely misled by wicked men.
Sìzhāo was a close and worthy man;
his line should not be extinguished."
Lady Yáng also entered the palace to see the Emperor,
weeping and pleading for her son's life,
invoking his ancestors;
she also begged for mercy from Lady Liú,
and Lady Liú also spoke on his behalf.
When Jìtāo entered the court to await punishment,
the Emperor pardoned him,
kept him for over a month,
and often took him along on hunts,
treating him with the same favor as before.
The Emperor's younger brother, Yìchéng Military Commissioner and Tóngpíngzhāngshì Cún Wò, harshly criticized him.
The incident where Jìtāo and his brothers plotted to kill Cún Wò is recorded in the previous volume, in the second year of the Liáng Emperor Jūn's Lóngdé era.
Liáng had changed the Yìchéng Army of Huázhōu to the Xuānyì Army,
and the Emperor restored the Táng's former name.
Jìtāo again bribed those around him, seeking to return to his garrison,
but the Emperor refused.
Jìtāo secretly sent someone to deliver a letter to Jìyuǎn,
instructing the soldiers to set fires,
hoping the Son of Heaven would again send him to pacify them.
The plot was exposed,
and on the day Xīnsì,
he was demoted to Vice Prefect of Dēngzhōu,
and soon executed south of the Tiānjīn Bridge,
along with his two sons.
An envoy was sent to execute Lǐ Jìyuǎn in Shàngdǎng,
and Lǐ Jìdá was appointed as Military City Patrol Inspector.
Acting Military Governor Lǐ Jìchóu was summoned to the capital.
Jìchóu had taken possession of Jìtāo's household,
selecting concubines and entertainers,
and searching for valuables,
delaying his departure.
'Depart'
means to set out.
Jìdá said angrily:
"Our family—brothers and father and sons—have been executed together, four in total.
Jìtāo and his two sons,
along with Jìyuǎn, make four.
Jìtāo had seven brothers,
and Jìchóu, as the eldest,
is called 'Eldest Brother.'
I am truly ashamed,
unable to face others;
better to die than live!"
On the day Jiǎshēn,
Jìdá, dressed in mourning clothes,
led a hundred cavalry under his command and sat at the gate, shouting:
Shǐ Zhào said: Halberds are displayed at the gate,
hence it is called the halberd gate.
'Led'
is read as 'shuài.'
'Mourning'
is pronounced 'cuī.'
'Shouting'
is pronounced 'hū.'
"Who will rebel with me?"
He then attacked the official residence.
'Official residence'
refers to the governor's residence.
Deputy Military Commissioner Lǐ Jìkē heard of the disturbance,
recruited townspeople,
gathering over a thousand,
and attacked the inner city.
Jìdá, realizing the situation was hopeless,
opened the east gate,
and returned to his private residence.
The east gate
refers to the east gate of Lùzhōu's inner city.
He intended to flee to the Qìdān,
but after traveling several li out of the city,
his followers all scattered,
and he took his own life.
48. On the day Jiǎshēn,
the King of Wú again sent the Minister of Agriculture, Luóyáng native Lú Píng, as an envoy.
Yán Kěqiú anticipated the questions the Emperor might ask,
and instructed Píng on how to respond.
When he arrived,
everything proceeded as Kěqiú had predicted.
Upon returning,
Píng reported that the Táng ruler was indulging in hunting and excursions,
hoarding wealth and rejecting advice,
causing resentment both inside and outside the court.
49 Gāo Jìxīng was in Luòyáng.
The emperor's attendants, entertainers and officials
sought goods without satiation.
(Entertainer officials
[eunuchs]
refers to entertainers and eunuchs.)
Satiation,
yān.
Gāo Jìxīng was resentful of them.
The emperor wanted to detain Gāo Jìxīng.
Guō Chóngtǎo admonished:
"Your Majesty has newly obtained the empire.
The various lords have merely sent their sons, younger brothers, generals, and aides to present tribute.
Only Gāo Jìxīng came to court in person.
He should be praised and rewarded to encourage those who will come;
to detain him and not send him back,
abandoning trust and harming righteousness,
would dampen the hearts of all within the four seas.
This is not a good plan."
So he was sent away.
Gāo Jìxīng traveled day and night to depart.
He reached Xǔzhōu.
(Jiǔyù Zhì: Luòyáng is 310 lǐ east to Xǔzhōu.)
"This journey had two errors: my coming to court was one error,
and letting me go was one error."
(Meaning both sides erred.)
Military Commissioner Kǒng Qíng detained him for a feast.
In the middle of the night,
he broke through the gate and left.
On Dīngyǒu,
he reached Jiānglíng.
Grasping Liáng Zhèn's hand, he said:
"Had I not followed your words,
I would have nearly not escaped the tiger's mouth."
(What Liáng Zhèn said is seen above.)
Nearly,
jī.
"The new court fought a hundred battles to obtain Hénán.
(Because Zhuāngzōng had newly obtained the empire, it is called the new court.)
Court,
cháo.
'I obtained the empire on my ten fingers.'
Boasting like this,
then all others have no merit.
Who would not become disheartened!
Moreover, he is lost in hunting and women.
How can it last long!
I have no worries."
So he repaired the walls and stored up grain,
recruited and accepted former Liáng soldiers,
and prepared for offense and defense.
(The history states that the emperor was dissolute, arrogant, and boastful,
being spied upon by neighboring enemies and treacherous, ambitious men.)
Diàn Guǎngmíng punctuated, Niè Chóngqí proofread.
Sīmǎ Guāng
respectfully compiled by imperial order.
Later student from Tiāntāi.
Second year of Tóngguāng
(Jiǎshēn, 924)
1 Spring,
first month,
Jiǎchén,
Yōuzhōu reported that the Qìdān had invaded,
reaching Wǎqiáo.
(Report by Lǐ Cúnshěn.)
Shǎnzhōu Deputy Commander Huò Yànwēi assisted him.
Palace Commissioner Lǐ Shàohóng served as Army Supervisor,
leading troops to rescue Yōuzhōu.
2 Kǒng Qiān again said to Guō Chóngtǎo:
"The Chief Minister is overwhelmed with myriad affairs,
and his residence is rather distant.
Tax and labor registers and documents are often delayed.
A different plan should be considered."
(He requested changing the person serving as Tax and Labor Commissioner; Kǒng Qiān wished to obtain it himself.)
Change,
gēng.
Nowadays, common people call borrowing money 'convenient money,'
meaning borrowing to facilitate use.
At that time, tax and labor money all went into the treasury.
Chóngtǎo subtly hinted at Gé.
Gé was afraid.
He memorialized requesting Chóngtǎo exclusively manage tax and labor.
Chóngtǎo firmly declined.
The emperor said:
"Then who is suitable?"
Chóngtǎo said:
"Although Kǒng Qiān has long managed finances,
since the emperor obtained Wèibó,
Kǒng Qiān served as the Expenditure Commissioner.
I fear he does not meet public expectations.
I request reappointing Zhāng Xiàn."
The emperor immediately ordered his summons.
Qiān was even more disappointed.
(Qiān had hoped to become Tax and Labor Commissioner since the emperor's accession in the fourth month last year; the matter is seen in the previous volume.)
3 The Prince of Qí, hearing the emperor had entered Luòyáng,
was inwardly uneasy.
(Hearing the emperor entered Luòyáng from Dàliáng, he feared troops would be shifted west to attack him.)
Lǐ Jìyǎn served as Fèngxiáng Campaign Military Commander and concurrently Jīngzhōu Military Commissioner.
The emperor, considering him a senior official of the former dynasty,
who stood shoulder to shoulder with the Grand Ancestor—
(Former dynasty refers to the reigns of Táng Emperor Xīzōng and Zhāozōng.
The emperor, upon accession, posthumously honored his father, Prince of Jìn Lǐ Kèyòng, as Emperor Wǔ,
temple name Grand Ancestor.)
Up,
shàng.
Court,
cháo;
same below.
—in each bestowed edict addressed him only as Prince of Qí and not by name.
On Gēngxū,
he added to Jìyǎn the title of
Secretariat Director,
and sent him back.
4 An edict:
"Palace officials should not reside outside.
All former dynasty palace officials and the various circuits' Army Supervisors, as well as those previously kept in private households,
regardless of rank,
are to be sent to the court."
(At the end of the Táng, eunuchs were executed. Those who escaped scattered, joining external military governors or being kept by private households.)
Keep,
xù.
By now, there were nearly a thousand.
All were given generous provisions,
entrusted with duties and responsibilities,
and made confidants.
The various internal commissioners,
since the Tiānyòu era, had been replaced by scholars.
(In the third year of Táng Emperor Zhāozōng's Tiānfù reign, eunuchs were executed, and scholars were made internal commissioners; at that time, only nine commissioners remained.)
By Liáng, there were the Reception Commissioner,
changed the Small Stables Commissioner to Celestial Steed Commissioner,
Flying Dragon Commissioner,
Manors Commissioner,
Ceremonial Regalia Commissioner,
Literary Thought Commissioner,
Five Wards Commissioner,
Rujing Commissioner,
Palace Food Commissioner,
changed the Imperial Food Commissioner to Palace Provisions Commissioner,
Luò Garden Commissioner,
Music Academy Commissioner,
Eastern Upper Gate Commissioner,
Western Upper Gate Commissioner,
Inner Garden Planting Commissioner,
Archery Storehouse Commissioner,
Great Inner Palace Wall Commissioner,
Armory Commissioner,
Introduction Commissioner,
Left Treasury Commissioner,
Leisure Stable Commissioner,
Palace Gardens Commissioner,
Hanlin Commissioner,
Great Harmony Treasury Commissioner,
Abundant Virtue Treasury Commissioner,
Qianwen Academy Commissioner.
Later Táng, although not using the Liáng system,
restored the Táng old system,
and the various internal commissioners were also numerous.)
Gradually, they interfered in government affairs.
Then again, the various circuits' Army Supervisors were established.
When military governors went on campaign or remained at court,
the military government's affairs were all decided by the Army Supervisor.
They bullied and scorned the commanding generals,
relying on power to contend for authority.
Consequently, the military governors were all angry.
(This sets the stage for the later military governors taking advantage of changes to kill the Army Supervisors.)
5 The Qìdān exited the frontier.
Lǐ Sìyuán's army was recalled.
Tàiníng Military Commissioner Lǐ Shàoqīn and Zézhōu Prefect Dǒng Zhāng were ordered to garrison Wǎqiáo.
6 Lǐ Jìyǎn, seeing the Táng's abundant armor and troops,
returned
and spoke to the Prince of Qí.
The Prince of Qí became even more fearful.
On Guǐchǒu,
he submitted a memorial requesting to perform the proper rites of a vassal.
A gracious edict did not permit it.
7 Kǒng Qiān disliked the arrival of Zhāng Xiàn.
At that time, Zhāng Xiàn was summoned from Wèi to serve again as the Commissioner of Taxes and Tributes.
Zhāng Xiàn was upright and principled,
so Kǒng Qiān disliked his arrival.
Disliked,
pronounced wù.
"Matters of money and grain are trivial affairs,
which a capable official can handle.
Wèidū is the fundamental base,
is it not more important?
The Governor of Xìngtáng, Wáng Zhèngyán, has integrity and restraint to spare,
but lacks intelligence and capability.
If absolutely necessary,
place him in the imperial court,
with many others assisting him,
which would still be better than entrusting him solely with regional authority."
Gé spoke on his behalf to Guō Chóngtāo,
and Guō Chóngtāo then petitioned to retain Zhāng Xiàn in the Eastern Capital.
On the jiǎyǐn day,
Wáng Zhèngyán was appointed as Commissioner of Taxes and Tributes.
Wáng Zhèngyán was muddle-headed and weak,
which suited Kǒng Qiān as he was easy to control.
8 Lǐ Cúnshěn reported that the Khitan had withdrawn,
and Xīnzhōu was recaptured.
The fall of Xīnzhōu is recorded in scroll 269, in the third year of the Zhēnmíng era of Liáng Emperor Jūnwáng.
9 On the wùwǔ day,
an edict was issued placing the three offices of Salt and Iron, Revenue, and Population all under the jurisdiction of the Commissioner of Taxes and Tributes.
The authority of the Commissioner of Taxes and Tributes grew even heavier.
10 The Emperor sent his younger brother Cúnwò and his son Jìjí to welcome the Empress Dowager and the Grand Empress Dowager from Jìnyáng.
The Grand Empress Dowager said:
"The imperial tombs and ancestral temple are here.
If we all leave together,
who will perform the seasonal sacrifices!"
She thus remained and did not come.
After the Emperor ascended the throne,
he honored his great-grandfather Zhíyí with the temple name Yìzǔ,
and his mausoleum was named Yǒngxīng;
Guóchāng received the temple name Xiànzǔ,
and his mausoleum was named Chángníng;
Kèyòng received the temple name Tàizǔ,
and his mausoleum was named Jiànjí.
All three mausoleums were located in Yànmén County, Dàizhōu,
while the ancestral temple was in Jìnyáng.
The Grand Empress Dowager's refusal to come
was surely not solely because of the tombs and temple;
her mind was firmly set on a certain perspective,
and moreover, her reasoning was very proper.
This sets the background for both the Empress Dowager and the Grand Empress Dowager falling ill from worry and melancholy.
On the gēngshēn day,
the Emperor went out to welcome them at Héyáng;
on the xīnyǒu day,
he accompanied the Empress Dowager into Luòyáng.
11 In the second month,
on the jǐsì day, the first day of the month,
the Emperor performed the suburban sacrifice to Heaven,
and issued a general amnesty.
Kǒng Qiān sought to amass wealth through exactions to curry favor,
and he reimposed all taxes that had been exempted by the amnesty decree.
Kǒng Qiān re-collected them.
From then on, whenever an imperial edict or order was issued,
people no longer trusted it,
and the common people were filled with sorrow and resentment.
When Guō Chóngtāo first arrived in Biàn and Luò,
he quite accepted gifts from the military governors,
and some close to him admonished him.
Guō Chóngtāo said:
"I hold both military and civil offices of the highest rank,
Guō Chóngtāo was Commissioner of Military Affairs,
additionally appointed as Zhōngshū Lìng,
and commanded the Chéngdé military district.
The Commissioner of Military Affairs
is involved in all affairs of the realm.
Zhōngshū Lìng is the head of one of the Three Departments,
and he also commanded a military district,
hence he said he held both military and civil offices.
How could I rely on external resources!
But in the final years of the false Liáng,
bribery became a widespread practice.
Now, the military governors in Hénán are all former officials of Liáng,
enemies of our Sovereign.
If I refuse their gifts,
would they not feel fearful!
I am merely storing them for the state in my private residence."
When the suburban sacrifice was about to be held,
Guō Chóngtāo was the first to contribute one hundred thousand strings of cash for rewarding the army.
Previously,
eunuchs had advised the Emperor to divide the empire's financial resources into internal and external treasuries.
Taxes submitted by the prefectures and counties went to the external treasury,
to cover administrative expenses,
while tributes from the military governors went to the internal treasury,
to fund banquets, entertainment, and rewards for the attendants.
Consequently, the external treasury was often empty and exhausted, while the internal treasury piled up like mountains.
When the officials were preparing for the suburban sacrifice,
they lacked funds to reward the army.
Guō Chóngtāo said to the Emperor:
"I have already exhausted all my family's wealth to assist the grand ceremony.
I hope Your Majesty will also contribute from the internal treasury to assist the officials."
The Emperor remained silent for a long time,
then said:
"I have reserves in Jìnyáng.
Order the Commissioner of Taxes and Tributes to transport them here for assistance."
Thus, they took several hundred thousand in gold and silk from Lǐ Jìtāo's private residence to supplement the funds.
Lǐ Jìtāo's father, Sìzhāo, rose with the Prince of Jìn, Kèyòng, from Jìnyáng,
hence his private residence was there.
Jìtāo was executed for rebellion,
and his family's assets were confiscated by the state.
The Emperor began to harbor resentment,
and his heart grew alienated.
This sets the background for the later mutiny of the various armies.
12 The military governor of Hézhōng, Lǐ Jìlín, requested the state monopoly on salt from Ānyì and Xiè Counties,
submitting the tax revenue to the central government each season.
That is, submitting the salt tax to the central government every three months.
Monopoly,
pronounced jué.
Xiè,
pronounced xiè.
On the jǐmǎo day,
Lǐ Jìlín was appointed as Commissioner for the Salt Monopoly of the Two Ponds.
13 On the xīnsì day,
the Prince of Qí was elevated in rank to Prince of Qín.
Examination of discrepancies: Regarding Màozhēn's change of title to Prince of Qín,
the Old History of the Five Dynasties does not record the exact month and year.
According to the Veritable Records,
on the rényín day of the eleventh month in the first year of Tóngguāng,
it already mentions
"the Prince of Qín, Màozhēn, sent an envoy to congratulate the recovery,"
and thereafter he is consistently referred to as the Prince of Qín.
By the edict on the xīnsì day of the second year,
"the Prince of Qín, Lǐ Màozhēn, may be enfeoffed as the Prince of Qín,"
how could a Prince of Qín be enfeoffed as Prince of Qín!
It must be that it was at this time he first changed from Prince of Qí to Prince of Qín.

The original placement of this examination of discrepancies in the Comprehensive Mirror was under the entry for the Prince of Qí submitting a memorial acknowledging vassalage in the first month of the second year;
it is now moved here.
14 Guō Chóngtāo knew that Lǐ Shàohóng was discontented,
so he established the post of Internal Auditing Commissioner,
in charge of auditing the finances of the three offices,
and appointed Shàohóng to it,
hoping to appease him.
However, Shàohóng remained unhappy.
Lǐ Shàohóng resented Guō Chóngtāo,
as seen in scroll one of the first year.
Audit,
pronounced gōu.
According to the Old History of the Five Dynasties: In the eleventh month of the first year of Tóngguāng,
Lǐ Shàohóng was appointed concurrently as Internal Auditor,
and all financial records and books of the empire were entrusted to him for decision.
From then on, the accounts supplied by the prefectures and counties became excessively burdensome and costly,
drawing criticism from commentators.
This differs in chronology from the account here.
Guō Chóngtāo held both military and civil offices,
and also commanded a military district.
He took the affairs of the empire as his personal responsibility,
and his power rivaled that of the sovereign.
Carriages and horses crowded his gate day and night.
He was by nature stern and impatient,
and would erupt when encountering issues.
The favorites and those seeking favors through luck
were often suppressed and thwarted by him.
The eunuchs hated him for this,
and slandered him to the Emperor day and night.
Guō Chóngtāo clenched his wrists in frustration,
wanting to curb them but unable to do so.
Dòulú Gé and Wéi Shuō once asked him:
"The Prince of Fényáng was originally from Tàiyuán but moved to Huáyīn.
Your family has been for generations in Yànmén.
Could you be a branch of his lineage?"
Chóngtāo then said:
"We were lost due to the turmoil of war,
and the genealogy was lost.
But I have heard my ancestors say
that we are only four generations removed from the Prince of Fényáng."
Gé said:
"Then he is certainly your ancestral relative."
From then on, Chóngtāo considered himself a member of the elite aristocracy,
often distinguishing and classifying people by social status,
promoting those who were flashy and superficial,
while despising and neglecting the veteran meritorious officials.
When someone sought an official position,
Chóngtāo would say:
"I am well aware of your merits and capabilities,
but your family background is humble and plain.
I dare not employ you,
for fear of being ridiculed by the renowned elite."
Consequently, the favorites hated him within the palace,
and the veteran meritorious officials resented him outside.
Chóngtāo repeatedly requested to yield the position of Commissioner of Military Affairs to Lǐ Shàohóng,
but the Emperor refused.
He also requested to divide the duties of the Bureau of Military Affairs and assign them to the various internal offices to reduce its power,
but the eunuchs slandered him incessantly.
Chóngtāo was depressed and discontented.
He discussed with a close associate the idea of going to his own military district to avoid the situation.
That person said:
"That won't do.
If a dragon loses the water,
even ants can control it."
Previously,
the emperor wished to make Lady Liú empress,
but the principal wife, Lady Hán, was still present.
The Ouyáng History states: The principal wife of Zhuāngzōng was Lady Hán, titled Duchess of Wèiguó;
the next was Lady Yī, titled Duchess of Yānguó;
and then Lady Liú, titled Duchess of Wèiguó.
According to the Ouyáng History,
Lady Liú was obtained by Yuán Jiànfēng,
who placed her in the Empress Dowager's palace,
where she was taught to play the shēng, sing, and dance.
Zhuāngzōng was pleased with her,
and the Empress Dowager bestowed her upon Zhuāngzōng.
However, those who disliked her
did so because of her lowly origins and her jealous, fierce nature.
For this reason, the emperor did not succeed in his wish.
Thereupon, someone close to Guō Chóngtāo advised him, saying:
"If you, sir, request the establishment of Lady Liú as empress,
the emperor will certainly be pleased.
With the empress's assistance from within the palace,
then the actors and eunuchs and their ilk will be unable to cause trouble."
Chóngtāo followed this advice,
and together with the chief ministers, led the officials in a joint memorial stating that Lady Liú should be properly installed in the central palace.
On the guǐwèi day,
Lady Liú, Duchess of Wèiguó, was established as empress.
Guō Chóngtāo sought to preserve himself through this,
but it was precisely what brought disaster upon himself.
This sets the stage for the killing of Guō Cóngtāo.
The character "shuài"
is read as "lǜ";
the same applies below.
Once she became noble,
she devoted herself solely to amassing wealth.
While in Wèizhōu,
she even sold firewood, kindling, fruits, and vegetables.
Cutting wood for firewood,
gathering grass for kindling.
"Guǒ"
refers to fruits with pits.
"Rú"
refers to vegetables.
Tributes from all quarters were divided into two portions,
one presented to the Son of Heaven,
and one presented to the central palace.
Thus, treasures and goods piled up like mountains,
used only for copying Buddhist scriptures
and giving alms to Buddhist nuns.
At this time, the decrees of the Empress Dowager,
the instructions of the Empress,
and the imperial edicts circulated together among the military governors,
who obeyed them all equally.
The words of women and the words of the king were implemented side by side;
since ancient times, there has never been such extreme disorder in governance as during the Tóngguāng era.
15 An edict ordered Zhū Qíng, the prefect of Càizhōu, to dredge the Suǒ River,
to facilitate water transport.
The Commentary on the Water Classic states: The Chēguān River originates from the Sōngzhǔ Mountains,
emerging from layered hills.
It has one source but two branches,
which flow separately and pour down,
commonly called the Shíquán River.
The eastern flow is the Suǒ River,
and the western flow is the Chēguān River.
The Suǒ River is north of Chénggāo.
Qíng
is pronounced "qú jīng fān."
Suǒ
is pronounced "shān kè fān."
16 In the third month,
on the first day, jǐhài,
the ruler of Shǔ held a banquet for his close ministers at the Yíshén Pavilion.
When the wine was flowing freely,
the ruler, his ministers, and the palace ladies all removed their caps, exposing their hair knots,
and became boisterous and unrestrained.
Lǐ Guīzhēn of Jīngzhào, who was in charge of drafting edicts, admonished:
"If the ruler and his ministers indulge in dissipation,
and do not concern themselves with the governance of the state,
I fear it may invite schemes from the northern enemy."
The northern enemy
refers to Táng.
17 On the yǐsì day,
Zhènzhōu reported that the Qìdān were about to invade the frontier.
This was reported based on intelligence.
Lǐ Sìyuán, the military commissioner of Tiānpíng, stationed troops at Xíngzhōu.
Shàobīn's original surname was Zhào,
and his given name was Xíngshí.
He was from Yōuzhōu.
18 On the bǐngwǔ day,
Gāo Jìxīng was additionally appointed as Shàngshū Lìng,
and was advanced to the title of Prince of Nánpíng.
19 Lǐ Cúnshěn, considering himself the foremost among the generals,
Lǐ Cúnshěn was at that time the overall commander of the Fan and Han cavalry and infantry.
felt indignant and resentful,
and his illness grew worse.
Lǐ Cúnshěn had moved from Cāng to Yōu
when he was already bedridden with illness.
Guō Chóngtāo suppressed him and did not permit it.
When Cúnshěn's illness became critical,
he submitted a memorial begging to see the emperor's face while still alive,
and only then was he permitted.
Earlier,
the emperor once wrestled with Lǐ Cúnxián, the General of the Right Martial Guard,
and Cúnxián did not use his full skill.
Cúnxián was originally Wáng Xián of Xǔzhōu.
In his youth, he was a soldier
skilled in wrestling.
Jìn Prince Lǐ Kèyòng obtained him,
bestowed upon him a surname and given name,
and raised him as a son.
"Jì"
is pronounced "qú qǐ fān."
"If you can defeat me,
I will grant you a military governorship."
Cúnxián then complied with the imperial command,
merely throwing the emperor down and stopping there.
When Cúnshěn was allowed to have an audience,
the emperor appointed Cúnxián as the marching secretary of Lúlóng.
Within ten days, he was appointed military commissioner,
and the emperor said:
"The promise from the wrestling match,
I have not broken my word."
To obtain a major military governorship through wrestling
shows that military governorships could be obtained through jest.
20 On the gēngxū day,
Yōuzhōu reported that the Qìdān were raiding Xīnchéng.
Xīnchéng County belonged to Zhuōzhōu.
It was established in the sixth year of the Tàihé era of Táng on the former site of Dūgāng.
The Xiongnu Essentials states: Xīnchéng County is sixty lǐ north of Zhuōzhōu.
21 Meritorious ministers feared the slander of the actor-officials,
and all felt insecure.
Lǐ Sìyuán, the deputy overall commander of the Fan and Han inner and outer cavalry and infantry, requested to be relieved of his military authority;
the emperor did not permit it.
22 Since the turmoil at the end of the Táng,
some families of officials sold their official appointment documents to clansmen or relatives by marriage.
"Chì"
should be
"chì."
Selling them to clansmen or relatives was already wrong;
who could have known that later generations would sell them to those not of their own kind!
There were even cases of uncles or elder uncles bowing to nephews or grandnephews,
meaning an uncle bowing to his nephew,
or an elder uncle bowing to his grandnephew.
Guō Chóngtāo wished to reform this malpractice,
and requested that the Bureau of Appointments conduct rigorous examinations.
The Bureau of Appointments
refers to the Ministry of Personnel.
"Xuǎn"
is pronounced "xù juǎn fān."
"Hé"
is pronounced "xià gé fān."
For all suburban sacrifices,
those who participated in the duties were called "officials performing duties."
Nine out of ten had their letters of appointment defaced and destroyed.
Some candidates wailed on the roads,
while others starved to death in inns.
23 The various tombs of the Táng imperial house had previously been excavated by Wēn Tāo.
The emperor could not punish Wēn Tāo's crime,
see the previous year in the previous scroll.
On the gēngshēn day,
Lǐ Tú, a vice-director of the Ministry of Works, was appointed as commissioner to inspect the various tombs in Cháng'ān.
24 The imperial prince Jìjí replaced Zhāng Quányì in overseeing the affairs of the Six Armies and various guards.
25 In summer,
the fourth month,
on the first day, jǐsì,
the ministers presented the emperor with the honorific title "Emperor of Illustrious Culture, Profound Military Prowess, Ultimate Virtue, and Luminous Filial Piety."
The honorific titles of the various Táng emperors all contained
the character "filial"
following the Hàn system,
and now this again followed the Táng system.
26 The emperor sent Lǐ Yán, the commissioner of guest reception, as an envoy to Shǔ.
Yán greatly praised the emperor's majesty and virtue,
and his ambition to unify the realm.
Moreover, he said that when the Zhū clan usurped power,
the various lords had not even made any effort to rescue the king.
Wáng Zōngchóu felt his words encroached upon Shǔ,
and requested to have him executed,
but the ruler of Shǔ did not consent.
Sòng Guāngbǎo, commissioner of the northern bureau of the palace administration, submitted a memorial stating:
"The Prince of Jìn has the ambition to encroach upon our state.
We should select generals, train troops,
station garrisons at the border regions,
accumulate dry provisions,
and build warships in preparation."
The ruler of Shǔ then appointed Guāngbǎo as observation commissioner of Zǐzhōu,
acting as deputy military commissioner of Wǔdé.
Shǔ established the Wǔdé Army in Zǐzhōu.
27 On the yǐhài day,
Chǔ Prince Mǎ Yīn was additionally appointed as Shàngshū Lìng.
28 On the gēngchén day,
the former deputy military commissioner of Bǎoyì, Huò Yànwēi, was bestowed the surname Lǐ and the given name Shàozhēn.
After Táng destroyed Liáng,
it changed the Zhènguó Army of Shǎnzhōu to the Bǎoyì Army.
29 The Prince of Qín, Lǐ Màozhēn, who was posthumously titled Zhōngjìng, died.
His final memorial requested that his son Jìyǎn temporarily administer the affairs of the military government of Fèngxiáng.
In the early days of the 30th year,
Yáng Lì, a subordinate general of Ānyì, was favored by Lǐ Jìtāo.
When Lǐ Jìtāo sought hereditary succession,
he changed the Zhāoyì Army to the Ānyì Army.
See the previous year in the previous volume.
At that time, three thousand soldiers from the Ānyì Army were dispatched to garrison Zhuōzhōu.
Yáng Lì said to his troops:
"Previously, soldiers from Lùzhōu have never garrisoned the border.
When Jìn and Liáng armies fought,
Lùzhōu soldiers were never sent north to garrison,
as they were kept to defend against Liáng.
It was because they did not want to station them in Lùzhōu.
Rather than leaving our bones exposed on the battlefield,
it would be better to occupy the city and defend ourselves.
Zhuōzhōu is south of Yōuzhōu,
and is not an isolated frontier fortress.
People of the Táng dynasty called desert lands 'shāchǎng' (battlefield),
but how could Zhuōzhōu be such a place?
Yáng Lì used these words to incite the anger of the Lùzhōu soldiers.
If we do not garrison, we will become bandits."
Thereupon, they gathered in an uproar and attacked the east gate of the inner city,
burning and looting the markets and shops.
The deputy military governor Lǐ Jìkē and the supervising army officer Zhāng Hóngzuò abandoned the city and fled.
Yáng Lì proclaimed himself acting military governor,
and sent generals and soldiers to submit a memorial requesting an official appointment.
An edict appointed Lǐ Sìyuán, the military governor of Tiānpíng, as the campaign commander,
and Lǐ Shàoróng, the military governor of Wǔníng, as the deployment officer.
The position of deployment officer first appears in the *Zīzhì Tōngjiàn*.
Originally, it was below the campaign commander.
Later, there was the chief deployment officer,
who then became the specially appointed commander-in-chief.
31. Kǒng Qiān lent money to the people,
requiring them to repay with silk at a low valuation,
and repeatedly issued orders to the prefectures and counties to enforce this.
Lú Zhì, the academician recipient of edicts and acting administrator of Biànzhōu, submitted a memorial stating:
"When Liáng's Zhào Yán was the commissioner of revenues,
he imposed loans and levies,
incurring resentment among the people.
Your Majesty has reformed the old and established the new,
eliminating harm for the people.
The *Miscellaneous Hexagrams* of the *Book of Changes* says: 'Gé' (Revolution)
means removing the old.
'Dǐng' (The Cauldron)
means taking up the new.
'Wèi' (for)
is pronounced 'yú wèi fān'.
Now this is like Zhào Yán being reborn.
This spring, frost damaged the crops,
and silk production is very low.
Even paying the regular taxes alone,
people fear they will have to flee.
How much more so with the added burden of loans?
'Chēng' (称)
means to raise.
'Dài' (贷)
means to borrow.
I serve only the Son of Heaven,
not the commissioner of revenues.
Imperial decrees have not been issued,
yet directives from the department frequently come down.
'Shěng dié' (省牒)
refers to documents issued by the commissioner of revenues.
'Xià' (下)
is pronounced 'hù jià fān'.
The emperor did not respond.
32. The ruler of Hàn led troops to invade Mǐn,
camping on the border between Tīngzhōu and Zhāngzhōu.
The two prefectures of Tīngzhōu and Zhāngzhōu in Mǐn
both bordered Cháozhōu of Hàn.
The ruler of Hàn was defeated and fled.
33. Earlier, during the battle of Húliǔ,
see the 270th volume, the fourth year of Zhēnmíng of Liáng Emperor Mò.
the emperor often thought of it.
The emperor thought of Zhōu Zā but not of Zhōu Déwēi,
which is why he perished.
Zhōu Zā paid his respects before the emperor's horse,
having entered Biàn. See the previous year in the previous volume.
'Jiàn' (见)
is pronounced 'xián biàn fān'.
Zhōu Zā tearfully said:
"The reason I survived
is entirely due to the efforts of Liáng's music bureau director Chén Jùn and the palace garden cultivation director Chǔ Déyuán."
The Liáng palace garden cultivation director
was similar to the Táng palace garden director.
Sòng Bái said: The cultivation director
existed as early as the Zhēnyuán era.
According to the *Fenji of Official Posts*: During the Five Dynasties, there was a palace garden cultivation director;
in our dynasty, it is simply called the palace garden director.
The emperor agreed.
Guō Chóngtǎo remonstrated:
"Those with whom Your Majesty took the empire
are all heroic, loyal, and brave men.
Now that the great achievement has just been accomplished,
not a single one has been rewarded or enfeoffed,
yet you first make entertainers prefects.
I fear this will lose the hearts of the empire."
Because of this, it was not carried out.
After a year,
the entertainers repeatedly brought up the matter.
The emperor said to Chóngtǎo:
"I have already promised Zhōu Zā.
It makes me ashamed to face these three men.
The three men
refer to Zhōu Zā, Chén Jùn, and Chǔ Déyuán.
In the matters of Zhōu Zā and Lǐ Cúnxián,
the emperor thought he had fulfilled his word.
Can this be considered governance?
You should
reluctantly carry this out for me."
In the fifth month,
on the Rényín day,
Chén Jùn was appointed prefect of Jǐngzhōu,
and Déyuán was appointed prefect of Xiànzhōu.
Xiànzhōu was originally the Lóufán horse pasture.
In the first year of Lóngjì of Táng Emperor Zhāozōng, the Prince of Jìn, Lǐ Kèyòng, submitted a memorial to establish Xiànzhōu.
There was no one who was not indignant and sighing.
It is fitting that they rebelled.
34. On the Yǐsì day,
the right admonisher and grand master Xuē Zhāowén submitted a memorial,
stating:
"There are still many who usurp and steal authority in the various circuits.
At this time,
some of the circuits that offered tribute are not considered,
such as Shǔ, Wú, and Hàn,
which were all circuits of the Táng.
They cannot be quickly pacified.
Also,
soldiers have long been engaged in campaigns,
and rewards have not been generous.
Many are impoverished,
which is a current malady.
They should be further bestowed with rewards.
Also,
the various armies in Hénán are all elite troops of Liáng.
I fear that usurping states may secretly lure them with substantial profits.
They should be won over and pacified.
Also,
for households that have fled,
corvée labor should be lightened and taxes reduced to settle and gather them.
Also,
non-urgent construction projects
should be curtailed and reduced.
He also requested selecting vacant land for horse pastures,
so as not to let them trample the farmland in the capital region."
None of these were heeded.
On the day Wùshēn (the 35th day of the cycle),
the ruler of Shǔ sent Lǐ Yán back.
Lǐ Yán had entered Shǔ in the fourth month,
and by now was returning.
Huán (return),
is read with the pronunciation of xuān,
and also with its usual reading.
Textual analysis notes: The Veritable Records state:
"In the seventh month,
on Wùwǔ,
Shǔ sent Ōuyáng Bīn to present tribute.
In the tenth month,
on Guǐsì,
they sent the Guest Reception Commissioner Lǐ Yán to serve as the envoy returning a message to Shǔchuān.
In the third year,
in the eighth month,
on Wùchén,
Yán returned from Xīchuān."
The History of Shǔ states:
"In the fourth month,
on Jǐsì, the first day,
the Táng envoy Lǐ Yán came on a diplomatic mission.
In the fifth month,
on Wùshēn,
they sent Yán back to his own country.
In the eleventh month,
on Jǐwèi, the first day,
they sent Bīn as the envoy for establishing friendly relations with the Táng state."
According to the Jǐnlǐ Qíjiù Zhuàn:
"In this year, they sent Ōuyáng Bīn on a diplomatic mission to Luòjīng,
and Zhuāngzōng sent Lǐ Yán to restore friendly relations."
The Hùjì states:
"How could it be that the Great Shǔ Emperor,
specially dispatched men like Sū Qín and Zhāng Yí,
to revive the friendship between Táng and Shǔ!
Our Emperor, moved by the Shǔ Emperor's gesture,
reciprocated the generous courtesy from afar with proper rites."
Thus, Yán was the envoy returning a message.
Perhaps before Ōuyáng Bīn,
Shǔ had already sent an envoy to Luò?
If following the year and month in the Veritable Records,
then Lǐ Yán received his mission in the tenth month of the second year,
and did not return until the eighth month of the third year.
Why was he detained for so long!
The Shǔ History in the Shíguó Jìnián also states:
"In the ninth month,
on Jǐhài,
the Táng Emperor sent Lǐ Yànchóu as an envoy.
In the eleventh month,
on Xīnchǒu,
they sent Yànchóu back east."
Furthermore,
after the eighth month, they dispatched Wáng Zōng'è and others to garrison Yáng and Lì to prepare for eastern forces,
seemingly acting on Sòng Guāngbǎo's advice;
after the eleventh month, due to the establishment of friendly relations with the Táng state,
they recalled the various armies,
seemingly disbanding them because Yànchóu came.
Now, the year and month from the History of Shǔ are followed for all.
The Emperor, because Yán entered Shǔ,
ordered him to trade horses for rare treasures from the palace,
but Shǔ law prohibited brocades, damasks, and rare curios from entering the Central Plains.
Only coarse and inferior goods were permitted to enter the Central Plains,
called
"goods for the grasslands."
When Yán returned,
he reported this,
and the Emperor angrily said:
"Can Wáng Yǎn avoid becoming a man for the grasslands!"
Yán then said to the Emperor:
"Yǎn is childish, foolish, dissolute, and unrestrained,
not personally attending to government affairs,
alienating the old and experienced,
and befriending petty men.
His ministers in power, Wáng Zōngbì and Sòng Guāngsì,
are sycophantic, flattering, arbitrary, and willful,
corrupt and insatiably greedy,
confusing the worthy and the foolish,
throwing punishments and rewards into disorder,
and the ruler and ministers, high and low, exclusively compete in extravagance and licentiousness.
In my observation,
once a great army approaches,
they will collapse like tiles and crumble like earth,
which can be expected while waiting on tiptoe."
The Emperor deeply agreed.
This laid the groundwork for attacking Shǔ.
36 Because of the rebellion in Lù Prefecture,
on Gēngxū,
the Emperor issued an edict that the prefectures and towns of the realm must not repair city walls or dredge moats,
and must completely destroy defensive city equipment.
Destroying defensive city equipment
was due to fear that commanders and soldiers across the realm might rely on cities to defy orders.
However, Zhào Zàilǐ attacked Wèi and Wèi could not hold it,
Zhào Zàilǐ occupied Wèi and the attackers could not capture it,
and the Emperor consequently also died under mutinous soldiers.
The way to guard against calamity certainly does not lie in this.
37 On Rénzǐ,
the new Xuānwǔ military commissioner and concurrently Secretariat Director, Fan-Han Cavalry and Infantry Commander-in-Chief Lǐ Cúnshěn died in Yōuzhōu.
Lǐ Cúnshěn had received the appointment to Xuānwǔ but had not yet left Yōuzhōu.
He often admonished his sons:
"Your father left his hometown carrying a single sword in his youth,
and within forty years,
reached the highest positions of general and minister.
This refers to being a military commissioner and concurrently participating in determining government matters.
The arrows extracted from broken bones numbered over a hundred."
He then gave them the extracted arrowheads,
ordering them to be kept,
saying:
"You were born into wealth and comfort,
you should know your father started his family like this."
38 Yōuzhōu reported that the Qìdān were about to invade.
On Jiǎyín,
they appointed Héng Hǎi military commissioner Lǐ Shàobīn as commander of the Northeastern Front Field Headquarters,
leading a large army across the river northward.
The Qìdān encamped outside the southeastern city gates of Yōuzhōu,
enemy cavalry were everywhere,
and much of the supply transport was plundered.
39 On Rénxū,
they appointed Lǐ Jìyǎn as Fèngxiáng military commissioner.
He succeeded Lǐ Màozhēn in commanding Qí.
40 On Yǐchǒu,
they appointed acting Guīyì interim military governor Cáo Yìjīn as military commissioner.
At that time, Guā and Shā were intermixed with Tǔbō inhabitants,
and Yìjīn sent envoys via bypaths to present tribute,
hence the appointment.
In the eighth year of Xiántōng of Táng Yìzōng,
Zhāng Yìcháo entered the court,
leaving his clansman Zhāng Wéishēn to guard Guīyì.
In the thirteenth year,
Wéishēn died,
and Yìjīn was appointed acting interim military governor.
From the thirteenth year of Xiántōng to now is fifty-four years,
so Cáo Yìjīn must already be old.
Jiàn (bypath),
is read with the ancient pronunciation of xiàn.
