41 The vanguard of Lǐ Sìyuán's large army reached Lù Prefecture,
as dusk had already fallen;
just as the army was settling in camp,
Zhāng Tíngyùn led over a hundred fierce warriors from his command to cross the moat, scale the ramparts, and climb the wall.
The defenders could not resist,
and they immediately broke through the gate and let the army in.
By dawn,
when Sìyuán and Lǐ Shàoróng arrived,
the city had already been taken,
and Sìyuán and the others were displeased.
This was because Zhāng Tíngyùn did not wait for their arrival before taking the city.
On Bǐngyín,
Sìyuán reported that Lù Prefecture was pacified.
In the sixth month,
on Bǐngzǐ,
Yáng Lì and his associates were dismembered at Zhènguó Bridge.
The walls and moats of Lù Prefecture were high and deep,
and the Emperor ordered them leveled.
Yí (level),
means to make flat.
42 On Bǐngxū,
they appointed Wǔníng military commissioner Lǐ Shàoróng as Guīdé military commissioner and concurrently participating in determining government matters.
Liáng had its capital at Biàn,
and moved the Xuānwǔ Army to Sòng Prefecture;
after Táng destroyed Liáng,
Biàn Prefecture was again made the Xuānwǔ Army,
and Sòng Prefecture was made the Guīdé Army.
He received deep favor and treatment.
The Emperor sometimes went to his home with the Empress Dowager and Empress.
The Emperor had a favored consort,
beautiful in appearance,
who had once borne a child,
and Empress Liú was jealous of her.
It happened that Shàoróng had lost his wife.
One day,
while attending in the palace,
the Emperor asked Shàoróng:
"Will you remarry?
I will seek a wife for you."
The Empress then pointed to the favored consort and said:
"Since Your Majesty pities Shàoróng,
why not bestow her upon him!"
The Emperor found it difficult to say no,
and faintly assented.
The Empress urged Shàoróng to bow in thanks.
By the time he rose,
looking back at the favored consort,
she had already been carried out of the palace in a sedan chair.
The Emperor, because of this, feigned illness and refused to eat for several days.
The history states that the Emperor feared Empress Liú's jealousy and ferocity.
43 On Rénchén,
they appointed Tiānpíng military commissioner Lǐ Sìyuán as Xuānwǔ military commissioner,
replacing Lǐ Cúnshěn as Fan-Han Internal and External Cavalry and Infantry Commander-in-Chief.
He was promoted from deputy commander-in-chief to full commander-in-chief.
44 In autumn,
the seventh month,
on Rényín,
Shǔ appointed Minister of Rites Xǔ Jì as Vice Director of the Secretariat and concurrently participating in determining government matters.
45 Kǒng Qiān again spoke ill of Wáng Zhèngyán to Guō Chóngtāo,
and also heavily bribed the court entertainer-officials,
seeking the position of Commissioner for Tax Collection and State Monopolies,
but ultimately did not obtain it.
Discontented,
on the Guǐmǎo day,
he submitted a memorial requesting to be relieved of his duties.
The Emperor was angry,
considering it an evasion of responsibility,
and intended to punish him according to the law.
Jǐng Jìn intervened to save him,
and he was spared.
46 The breach in the Yellow River made by Liáng had for years been a disaster for Cáo and Pú.
(The Liáng breach of the river is seen in scroll 270, the fourth year of Jūnmíng of Emperor Mò of Liáng.)
Pú,
Bó mù fān.
On the Jiǎchén day
, he ordered Right Gate Guard Senior General Lóu Jìyīng to supervise Biàn and Huá troops to block it.
Not long after,
it broke again.
47 On the Gēngshēn day,
the Wēisài Army was established at Xīnzhōu.
48 The Khitan, relying on their strength,
sent an envoy to the Emperor to request Yōuzhōu to settle Lú Wénjìn.
At that time, the various tribes in the northeast were all subservient to the Khitan,
only Bóhǎi was not submissive.
The Khitan ruler planned to invade,
but feared Bóhǎi would attack his rear.
(Bóhǎi was at that time the powerful state of Hǎidōng,
with five capitals, fifteen prefectures, and sixty-two districts,
possessing all the lands of Gāolí and Sùshèn.)
Jǐ,
Jū yǐ fān.
He sent his general Tūněi and Lú Wénjìn to occupy Yíng, Píng and other prefectures to harass the Yān region.
49 In the eighth month,
on the Wùchén day,
the Shǔ ruler appointed Right Dìngyuǎn Army Commander Wáng Zōng'è as the Campaign Commander of Cavalry and Infantry,
leading twenty-one armies to station at Yángzhōu.
On the Yǐhài day,
he appointed Long-term Straight Cavalry Army Commander Lín Sī'è as Military Commissioner of Zhāowǔ,
garrisoning Lìzhōu to prepare against Táng.
50 Commissioner for Tax Collection and State Monopolies Wáng Zhèngyán suffered from a wind illness,
dazed and unable to manage affairs.
Jǐng Jìn repeatedly spoke about it.
On the Guǐyǒu day,
Deputy Commissioner and Commandant of the Guards Kǒng Qiān was appointed Commissioner for Tax Collection and State Monopolies,
and Right Valiant Guard General-in-Chief Kǒng Xún was appointed Deputy Commissioner.
Xún was originally Zhào Yīnhéng.
After Liáng perished,
he resumed his original name.
(The Ouyáng History says: Kǒng Xún's family background is unknown.
Orphaned young,
he drifted to Biànzhōu,
where the wealthy man Lǐ Ràng found him by chance,
and raised him as a son.
Liáng Tàizǔ adopted Lǐ Ràng as a foster son,
so Xún assumed the surname Zhū,
and served in Tàizǔ's tent.
One of the wet nurses of Tàizǔ's sons favored him,
and raised Xún as her son.
The wet nurse's husband was surnamed Zhào,
so he again assumed the surname Zhào,
named Yīnhéng.
After Liáng perished,
he served Táng,
and finally changed his name to Kǒng Xún.
According to records, in the second year of Tiānyòu of Táng, Zhào Yīnhéng was already provisionally managing the Xuānhuīyuàn,
see scroll 265.) He imposed heavy taxes and urgent levies to satisfy the Emperor's desires,
and the people had no means to live.
On the Guǐwèi day,
Qiān was granted the title "Meritorious Subject Who Enriches Wealth and Sustains the State."
(The Record says: Better to have ministers who steal than ministers who amass wealth.
Yet to use this as a title of merit to honor Kǒng Qiān,
the rulers and ministers of Táng did not know it was wrong.
With the people in distress and the army resentful,
how could it last long!
This sets the stage for Emperor Míngzōng's execution of Qiān.)
51 The Emperor again sent envoy Lǐ Yǎnchóu into Shǔ.
In the ninth month,
on the Jǐhài day,
he reached Chéngdū.
52 On the Guǐmǎo day,
the Emperor hunted in the near suburbs.
At that time, the Emperor frequently went out hunting.
The accompanying cavalry damaged the people's crops.
The Magistrate of Luòyáng, Hé Zé, lay hidden in the thicket,
(grass growing densely is called cóng;
trees and grass interwoven is called bó)
and stopped the horse to remonstrate, saying:
"Your Majesty's taxes and levies are already harsh.
Now the crops are about to ripen,
yet you trample them again.
How can your officials govern,
and how can the people survive!
I wish to be granted death first."
The Emperor consoled him and sent him away.
(The remonstrance against hunting was the same.
The Magistrate of Zhōngmóu nearly did not escape death,
yet the Magistrate of Luòyáng received consolation and dismissal.
It must be that some entertainer-official interceded for him.
Examining Hé Zé's lifelong conduct,
he was truly not an upright and honest man.
He was from Guǎngzhōu.
The Old History of the Five Dynasties: Hé Zé,
from Guǎngzhōu,
in the Zhēnmíng era of Liáng, Qīnghǎi Military Commissioner Liú Zhì recommended his talent,
and he passed the jìnshì examination.)
53 The Khitan attacked Bóhǎi,
but achieved nothing and returned.
54 The former Shannan Military Commissioner and Secretariat Director of Shǔ, Wáng Zōngchóu, due to the Shǔ ruler's lack of virtue,
plotted with Wáng Zōngbì to depose and install a new ruler.
Zōngbì hesitated and did not decide.
On the Gēngxū day,
Zōngchóu died of worry and indignation.
Zōngbì said to the Bureau of Military Affairs Commissioners Sòng Guāngsì and Jǐng Rùnchéng, etc.:
"Zōngchóu urged me to kill you all.
Today, you have no worries."
Guāngsì and the others bowed low, weeping and thanking him.
Zōngbì's son Chéngbān heard of this,
and said to someone:
"Our family will find it hard to escape calamity."
55 On the Yǐmǎo day,
the Shǔ ruler appointed former Zhènjiāng Army Military Commissioner Zhāng Wǔ as Campaign Commander of the Xiá Route Reinforcements.
(Shǔ established the Zhènjiāng Army at Kuízhōu.)
56 On the Dīngsì day,
Yōuzhōu reported that the Khitan had invaded.
57 In winter,
the tenth month,
on the Xīnwèi day,
Tiānpíng Military Commissioner Lǐ Cúnbà and Pínglú Military Commissioner Fú Xí said:
"The subordinate prefectures often claim to directly receive orders from the Commissioner for Tax Collection and State Monopolies to handle public affairs,
which the Commissioner's office is completely unaware of,
disrupting established regulations."
(Commissioner's office refers to the Military Commissioner's office.
Wěn,
yīn wèn.)
Recently, it had become customary for orders to be issued directly.
(At that time, the Commissioner for Tax Collection and State Monopolies issued orders to the various prefectures for requisitions and levies,
bypassing the Military Commissioners and Surveillance Commissioners.
This was called 'direct issuance'.
Xià,
hù jià fān.)
"According to the court's established practices,
imperial edicts and decrees are not issued to subordinate commanderies.
(The military governor's seat is the huìfǔ,
and the various prefectures under its jurisdiction are the subordinate commanderies.)
What the two circuits now report
is the old regulation of our dynasty.
What the Commissioner for Tax Collection and State Monopolies proposes
is a recent practice of the false court.
(At that time, Liáng was considered the false court,
and thus denigrated.)
All matters must be reported by the circuit.
The requisitions and levies by the Commissioner for Tax Collection and State Monopolies must also be communicated to the Surveillance Commissioner."
(The Táng system: Military Commissioners handled military affairs,
Surveillance Commissioners handled civil affairs.
Therefore, edicts for requisitions and levies by the Commissioner for Tax Collection and State Monopolies were only communicated to the Surveillance Commissioner's office.)
In the end, this was not implemented.
(The history records that tax collection was severe and urgent,
only aiming for quick completion,
and ultimately the edict was not followed.)
58 Yìdìng reported that the Khitan had invaded.
59 The Shǔ Xuānhuī North Bureau Commissioner Wáng Chéngxiū requested selecting twelve thousand brave and fierce soldiers from the various armies,
to establish forty armies of infantry and cavalry under the Left and Right Lóngwǔ Guards of the Imperial Escort,
with weapons and supplies all superior to other armies.
Chéngxiū was appointed Commander of the Lóngwǔ Army Cavalry and Infantry,
with Deputy General Ān Zhòngbà as his deputy.
The old generals were all indignant and ashamed.
(Zhòngbà was from Yúnzhōu,
and through cunning, flattery, and bribery served Chéngxiū,
so Chéngxiū favored him.
This sets the stage for Ān Zhòngbà betraying Wáng Chéngxiū and surrendering to Táng.)
60 The King of Wúyuè, Qián Liú, resumed offering tribute to our court.
(Qián Liú was originally a minister of Táng.
After Táng perished, he served Liáng.
After Liáng perished, he again served Táng,
hence it says 'resumed offering tribute to our court'.)
On the Rénwǔ day,
the Emperor, following the official titles and ranks of Liáng, appointed him.
Liú offered generous tribute,
and also bribed powerful officials,
seeking a gold seal, jade tablets, imperial edicts that did not use his personal name, and the title of King of a State.
The responsible officials said:
"According to precedent, only the Son of Heaven uses jade tablets.
Princes and dukes all use bamboo tablets.
(Bamboo tablets are made by weaving bamboo,
to preserve ancient meaning.)
There is no precedent for enfeoffing a King of a State."
The Emperor indulged all of Liú's wishes.
61. The King of Wú went to Báishā to inspect the tower ships,
and renamed Báishā as Yíngluánzhèn.
According to *Lù Zhèn's Records of the Nine States*: Yáng Pǔ inspected Báishā,
and the Grand Academy Doctor Wáng Gǔ submitted a memorial requesting to change Báishā to Yíngluán.
The summary stated:
"Where the sun and moon pass,
all stars become the ecliptic;
where the imperial carriage stops,
every village becomes a Red County."
Báishā
was in the territory of Yángzǐ County.
At the end of the Five Dynasties, Yángzǐ was renamed Yǒngzhēn County.
In the second year of the Qiándé era of the Sòng dynasty, Yíngluánzhèn in Yǒngzhēn County of Yángzhōu was made Jiàn'ānjūn.
In the sixth year of the Dàzhōngxiángfú era, it was elevated to Zhēnzhōu,
and Yǒngzhēn County was previously changed back to Yángzǐ.
The place is sixty *lǐ* east to Yángzhōu,
borders the Great River to the south,
and crossing the river south to Jīnlíng is also sixty *lǐ*.
Gēng,
pronounced as gēng.
Wēn appointed his close subordinate Zhái Qián as the Commissioner of the Palace Gates, Palace City, and Military Equipment,
to monitor the king's daily activities.
Zhái Qián restricted the king very strictly.
Ordering Zhōng Tàizhāng to kill Zhāng Hào, closing the inner city gates to attack Zhū Jǐn,
were all actions of Zhái Qián,
hence Xú Wēn trusted and employed him closely.
Zhái,
pronounced as zhái.
The king, when speaking to Wēn, changed the word for "rain" (yǔ) to "water" (shuǐ),
and Wēn asked the reason.
The king said:
"It is the name of Zhái Qián's father,
I have become accustomed to avoiding it."
Then he said to Wēn:
"Your loyalty,
I am well aware of,
but Zhái Qián is disrespectful;
the needs of the palace and the imperial clan are often not met."
"Needs" refers to
what one desires,
what one seeks.
He requested to execute him.
The king said:
"Execution is too severe,
distant exile would suffice."
So he was exiled to Fǔzhōu.
62. In the eleventh month,
the Shǔ ruler sent his Hanlin Academician Ōuyáng Bīn as an envoy.
*Textual Analysis*: According to the *Veritable Records*:
"In the seventh month,
on the Wùwǔ day,
the Shǔ ruler sent the Vice Minister of Revenue Ōuyáng Bīn as an envoy,
using the protocol of a rival state in correspondence."
The *Shǔ History, Annals of the Later Ruler* states:
"In the eleventh month,
on the Yǐwèi day,
he appointed Hanlin Academician and Vice Minister of War Ōuyáng Bīn as envoy to establish friendly relations with the Táng state."
We follow this account.
He was from Héngshān.
He also sent Lǐ Yànchóu back east.
Lǐ Yànchóu arrived in Shǔ; see the ninth month above.
Huán,
pronounced as huán,
or as in the original character.
63. On the Guǐmǎo day,
the emperor led his personal troops hunting at Yīquē.
Yīquē County was over two hundred *lǐ* south of Luòyáng.
There is Yīquē Mountain,
excavated by the Great Yǔ.
In the Sòng dynasty, Yīquē County was demoted to a town,
incorporated into Yīyáng County.
Shuài,
read as shuài.
They traversed mountainous and treacherous terrain,
continuing for several days without stop,
sometimes conducting night encirclements;
many soldiers fell from cliffs and ravines to their deaths or suffered fractures and injuries.
The historian remarks that the emperor was obsessed with hunting and showed no compassion for his soldiers.
Zhé,
pronounced as zhé.
On the Bǐngwǔ day
they returned to the palace.
64. Because Shǔ had established friendly relations with Táng,
they disbanded the garrison at Wēiwǔchéng,
recalling Guān Hóngyè and twenty-four armies back to Chéngdū.
On the Wùshēn day,
they also disbanded the thirty-seven armies of the Wǔdìng and Wǔxīng pacification commissioners Liú Qián and others.
65. On the Dīngsì day,
the emperor bestowed an iron pledge to the military commissioner of Hùguó, Lǐ Jìlín,
appointing his sons Lìngdé and Lìngxī both as military commissioners.
All his sons who had grown out of childhood clothes were given official posts,
his favor surpassing all other feudal lords.
The favor shown to Zhū Yǒuqiān
was precisely what hastened his disaster.
He had changed sides many times,
how could he escape retribution!
Guàn,
pronounced as guàn.
66. On the Gēngshēn day,
Yùzhōu reported that the Qìdān had invaded.
67. On the Xīnyǒu day,
the Shǔ ruler disbanded the Tiānxióngjūn pacification force,
ordering Wáng Chéngqiān and twenty-nine armies back to Chéngdū.
68. In the twelfth month,
on the first day, Yǐchǒu,
the Shǔ ruler appointed Vice Director of the Right Zhāng Gé to concurrently serve as Vice Minister of the Secretariat and participated in determining governmental matters.
Earlier,
when Zhāng Gé had been found guilty,
the event is recorded in the 270th scroll of the *History of the Later Liang*, under the fourth year of the Zhēnmíng era of Emperor Jūn.
When he again became chief minister and held power,
he had him beaten to death.
Xǔ Jì said to others:
"Minister Zhāng has great talent but shallow insight.
By killing one Lǔ Róu,
who else would dare feel secure!
This is the beginning of inviting disaster."
Zhāng Gé was indeed at fault,
but Xǔ Jì, who also served as chief minister,
failed to recognize that Shǔ was on the verge of collapse.
He only knew that Zhāng Gé was inviting disaster.
When Shǔ fell,
could those serving as chief ministers avoid disaster?
69. The Shǔ ruler disbanded the garrison at Jīnzhōu,
ordering Wáng Chéngxūn and seven armies back to Chéngdū.
The Shǔ ruler, relying on peace with Táng, removed border defenses,
which is like taming tigers and leopards without setting up sturdy cages.
70. On the Jǐsì day,
the emperor ordered the military commissioner of Xuānwǔ, Lǐ Sìyuán, to lead 37,000 imperial guard troops to Biànzhōu,
and then proceed to Yōuzhōu to defend against the Qìdān.
He ordered Lǐ Sìyuán to lead troops to his garrison,
and from there proceed north to guard the border.
71. On the Gēngwǔ day,
the emperor and empress visited the residence of Zhāng Quányì.
Quányì presented a great display of tribute;
when the wine was flowing freely,
the empress memorialized:
"I lost my parents in childhood,
and whenever I see elderly people, I think of them.
I request to honor Quányì as a father."
The emperor consented.
Quányì was alarmed and firmly declined,
but after repeated insistence,
he finally accepted the empress's bow,
and again presented tribute to express gratitude.
The next day,
the empress ordered Hanlin Academician Zhào Fèng to draft a letter of thanks to Quányì.
Fèng secretly memorialized:
"Since ancient times, there has never been a mother of the realm bowing to a subject as father."
The emperor praised his forthrightness,
but ultimately proceeded with it.
From then on, the empress and Quányì daily sent messengers back and forth, exchanging gifts without cease.
72. Earlier,
during the reigns of Emperors Xīzōng and Zhāozōng of Táng,
although eunuchs were powerful,
none had ever been appointed as a military commissioner.
Shǔ's Ān Zhòngbà urged Wáng Chéngxiū to seek the military commission of Qínzhōu.
Chéngxiū said to the Shǔ ruler:
"Qínzhōu has many beautiful women,
I request to select some for Your Majesty."
The Shǔ ruler agreed.
On the Gēngwǔ day,
he appointed Chéngxiū as military commissioner of Tiānxióng,
enfeoffing him as Duke of Lǔ;
the historian remarks that the disorder of Shǔ's government exceeded even that of the late Táng.
In the tenth month of this year,
Shǔ had just established the Lóngwǔ Army.
73. On the Yǐhài day,
the Shǔ ruler appointed the former military commissioner of Wǔdé and concurrently Grand Secretary Xú Yánqióng as the Capital Inside and Outside Infantry and Cavalry Commander-in-Chief.
Shǔ considered the city of Chéngdū as the capital.
The multitude was discontent.
The Shǔ ruler's mother and
his wife were both from the Xú clan.
The testament of Shǔ's founder, Wáng Jiàn, ordered that the Xú brothers not be put in charge of troops.
Although Wáng Yǎn was foolish and dissolute,
none of Shǔ's ministers reminded Yǎn of Jiàn's testament.
How could Wáng Zōngbì be entrusted with responsibility!
The reason the multitude was discontent with Xú Yánqióng
was simply due to the irregularity of the appointment.
74. On the Rénwǔ day,
Běijīng reported that the Qìdān had raided Lánzhōu.
At the beginning of the Tóngguāng era,
Zhènzhōu was made the Northern Capital,
and Tàiyuán the Western Capital;
soon the Northern Capital was abolished and reverted to Zhènzhōu,
with Tàiyuán becoming Běijīng.
Lán,
pronounced as lán.
75. On the Xīnmǎo day,
the Shǔ ruler changed the next year's era name to Xiánkāng.
76. The military commissioner of Lúlóng, Lǐ Cúnxián, died.
77. This year,
the Shǔ ruler transferred Prince Pǔ Zōngrén to Prince of Wèi,
Prince Yǎ Zōnglù to Prince of Bīn,
Prince Bāo Zōngjì to Prince of Zhào,
Prince Róng Zōngzhì to Prince of Hán,
Prince Xīng Zōngzé to Prince of Sòng,
Prince Péng Zōngdǐng to Prince of Lǔ,
Prince Zhōng Zōngpíng to Prince of Xuē,
Prince Zī Zōngtè to Prince of Jǔ;
Zōnglù, Zōngzhì, and Zōngpíng were all relieved of military duties.
1. Spring,
the first month,
on the first day, jiawu,
Shǔ granted a general amnesty.
2. On bingshen,
the emperor ordered the relevant officials to rebury Emperor Zhāozōng and the Young Emperor,
because they had been murdered by Zhū Wēn,
and their burials were thus deficient in many respects.
Shào,
read as shào.
Later Táng, considering itself the successor to Táng,
ultimately failed to rebury Emperor Zhāozōng and the Young Emperor;
Later Hàn, considering itself the continuation of Hàn's legacy,
yet throughout the Qiányòu reign, Chánglíng and Yuánlíng received not a single offering.
The histories record this to express criticism.
3. The Qìdān raided Yōuzhōu.
4. On gēngzǐ,
the emperor departed from Luòyáng;
on gēngxū,
he arrived at Xìngtáng.
At that time, Wèizhōu was designated as Xìngtáng Prefecture.
5. An edict ordered Pínglú military commissioner Fú Xí to repair the distant dikes at Suānzǎo to guard against the bursting of the Yellow River.
Distant dikes are those
built far from level ground to hold back water.
Zhì,
read as zhí.
6. Previously,
when Lǐ Sìyuán campaigned north,
referring to the time last year when he defended against the Qìdān in the north.
the Eastern Capital's treasury had fine armor for imperial use,
Sìyuán sent a dispatch to deputy garrison commander Zhāng Xiàn requesting five hundred sets;
Xiàn, due to the military campaign,
did not have time to memorialize and issued them;
the emperor angrily said:
"Xiàn did not obey the edict,
but hastily gave my armor to Sìyuán;
what was his intention!"
He fined Xiàn one month's salary
and ordered him to personally go to the army to retrieve them.
To go to Sìyuán's army and retrieve the fine armor.
The emperor, because Yìwǔ military commissioner Wáng Dū was about to come to court,
wanted to clear a polo field.
Xiàn said:
"Recently, the palace courtyard has been used as a polo field;
the year before last, Your Majesty ascended the throne here,
that altar cannot be destroyed.
I request clearing a polo field west of the palace."
After several days,
it was not completed,
so the emperor ordered the destruction of the accession altar.
Xiàn said to Guō Chóngtāo:
"This altar
is where the sovereign performed rites to the Supreme Deity
and first received the Mandate;
how can it be destroyed!"
Chóngtāo calmly spoke to the emperor about it,
but the emperor immediately ordered the two yúhòu to destroy it.
The two yúhòu
are the cavalry yúhòu and infantry yúhòu;
another interpretation: the left and right yúhòu.
"To forget Heaven and turn against one's roots—
no inauspiciousness is greater than this."
7. Second month,
on jiǎxū,
Héng Hǎi military commissioner Lǐ Shàobīn was appointed as Lúlóng military commissioner.
Lǐ Shàobīn, during Emperor Míngzōng's reign, had his surname restored to Zhào,
and was given the name Déjūn.
Déjūn's defense of Yōuzhōu was not without merit;
but later, he took advantage of peril to make demands of his sovereign,
externally making deals with the Qìdān,
not only did father and son become captives,
Yōuzhōu also fell to the captors.
8. On bǐngzǐ,
Lǐ Sìyuán memorialized a victory over the Qìdān at Zhuōzhōu.
9. The emperor was worried about the Qìdān,
and consulted with Guō Chóngtāo.
Since renowned veteran generals were nearly all gone,
and Lǐ Shàobīn's rank and prestige were always low,
he wanted to transfer Lǐ Sìyuán to garrison Zhēndìng,
to provide support for Shàobīn.
Chóngtāo deeply considered this appropriate.
At the time, Chóngtāo commanded Zhēndìng;
the emperor wanted to transfer Chóngtāo to garrison Biànzhōu,
intending for the two men to exchange military provinces.
"I internally manage the pivotal affairs,
externally participate in major governance;
my wealth and honor have reached their peak.
Why must I also command a frontier region?
Moreover, some of Your Majesty's veteran officials have followed you for many years,
having experienced a hundred battles,
yet what they obtained was merely a single prefecture.
I have no merit of sweating horses in battle,
but merely by attending Your Majesty's side,
occasionally offering sagely counsel,
I have reached this position,
and I am often uneasy about it.
Now, by entrusting responsibilities to meritorious worthies,
allowing me to relinquish my command insignia,
is truly my great wish.
Furthermore, Biànzhōu is a vital strategic point east of the pass;
Biànzhōu lies east of Chénggāo Pass,
connecting south to Huái and Sì,
north to Huá and Wèi—
a crucial strategic location.
If I do not go to my post,
merely having another person act in my position,
how is it different from an empty city?
This is not the way to solidify the state's foundation."
The emperor said:
"I deeply understand your loyalty and dedication,
but you devised strategies for me,
capturing Wènyáng by surprise,
securing and fortifying the river crossings;
subsequently, from this route directly
advancing to Dàliáng,
accomplishing my imperial enterprise—
how can the merit of a hundred battles compare?
Now that I am honored as the Son of Heaven,
how can I let you not possess even a foot of land?"
Chóngtāo firmly declined repeatedly,
and the emperor then permitted it.
On gēngchén,
Lǐ Sìyuán was transferred to become Chéngdé military commissioner.
10. The ruler of Hàn, hearing that the emperor had destroyed Liáng, became fearful,
and sent palace garden commissioner Hé Cí to present tribute,
also to spy on the strength and weakness of the Central Kingdom.
On jiǎshēn,
Cí arrived at Wèi.
The emperor was at the Wèi capital at the time.
He reported that the emperor was arrogant, dissolute, and lacked governance,
and was not worthy of fear.
The Hàn ruler was greatly pleased,
and from then on, no longer had contact with the Central Kingdom.
11. The emperor's nature was stubborn and fond of winning;
he did not want power to lie with his ministers.
After entering Luòyáng,
believing the slanders of actors and eunuchs,
he became quite distant and suspicious of veteran generals.
Lǐ Sìyuán's family was in Tàiyuán.
Third month,
on dīngyǒu,
he memorialized to appoint Wèizhōu prefect Lǐ Cóngkē as Běijīng inner yá cavalry and infantry commander-in-chief for the convenience of his family.
The emperor angrily said:
"Sìyuán holds military authority,
commands a major garrison;
military administration lies with me.
How can he submit a request for his son!"
He then demoted Cóngkē to commander of the assault cavalry,
leading several hundred men to garrison Shímén Fort.
Shímén Fort was the Héngshuǐ Stockade of the Táng.
Shuài,
read as shuài.
Sìyuán submitted a memorial pleading his case,
and after a long time, the matter was resolved.
On xīnchǒu,
Sìyuán requested to come to the Eastern Capital for an audience,
but it was not permitted.
Guō Chóngtāo, because Sìyuán had high merit and rank,
also was wary of him,
privately saying to others:
"Commander-in-Chief Línggōng will not remain subordinate for long."
Lǐ Sìyuán was Zhōngshū Lìng and commander-in-chief of all inner and outer cavalry and infantry of the Fán and Hàn armies,
hence the form of address.
He secretly urged the emperor to summon him for palace guard duty,
stripping him of his military authority,
and further urged the emperor to eliminate him.
The emperor did not follow either suggestion.
This lays the groundwork for Lǐ Sìyuán's suspicion and fear.
Did Guō Chóngtāo also know he was resented by actors and eunuchs?
12. On jǐyǒu,
the emperor departed from Xìngtáng,
crossed the river from Déshèng,
passed by Yángcūn and Qīchéng,
viewing the former battle sites,
pointing them out to his veteran officials for amusement.
This is the same attitude
as when the emperor himself said,
"I gained the empire on my ten fingers."
Lè,
pronounced luò.
13 The Luòyáng palaces were vast and deep.
The eunuchs, wishing to have the imperial consorts and concubines increased and the palaces expanded,
deceitfully claimed that ghosts and strange creatures were seen in the palace at night.
The Emperor intended to have exorcists perform incantations to ward them off.
The use of talisman water and curses,
was done by shamans and sorcerers who deceived the world with their arts.
"Ward off" means
to repel.
"Your servant once had the opportunity to serve during the reigns of the Xiántōng and Qiánfú Emperors.
'Dài' means
'to reach' or 'to have the opportunity'.
Xiántōng was
the reign title of Emperor Yìzōng of Táng;
Qiánfú was
the reign title of Emperor Xīzōng.
The noble and lowly women of the Six Palaces numbered no less than ten thousand.
Now, more than half of the Rear Palace is empty,
hence ghosts and creatures wander there."
The Emperor then ordered the eunuch Wáng Yǔnpíng and the entertainer Jǐng Jìn to select and gather women from among the common people,
reaching as far as Tàiyuán, Yōu, and Zhèn,
to fill the Rear Palace.
They numbered no fewer than three thousand,
with no questions asked about their origins.
When the Emperor returned from Xìngtáng,
they were transported in ox-carts,
forming a continuous line filling the roads.
Zhāng Xiàn memorialized:
"Over a thousand women have fled from the various military camps.
I fear they have been taken and hidden by the various escorting armies to travel with them."
In reality, they had all entered the palace.
"Various camps"
refers to the various camps in Wèi Prefecture.
The historian states that the Emperor's grievances with the Wèi troops were not due to a single incident.
"Cóng"
is pronounced with the initial consonant of "cái" and the tone of "yòng".
On the Gēngchén day,
the Emperor arrived in Luòyáng;
on the Xīnyǒu day,
an edict was issued to again make Luòyáng the Eastern Capital,
and Xìngtáng Prefecture the Yè Capital.
During the prosperous era of the Táng,
Luòyáng was made the Eastern Capital.
At the beginning of the Tóngguāng era,
Jìnyáng was made the Western Capital,
Wèi Prefecture the Eastern Capital,
and soon after, Luòyáng was made the Luò Capital.
Now, restoring the old Táng system by making Luòyáng the Eastern Capital,
then also meant restoring Cháng'ān as the Western Capital.
Jìnyáng's designation as Western Capital had earlier been changed to Northern Capital.
Since Luòyáng was restored to its former status as Eastern Capital,
Wèi Prefecture's Eastern Capital was changed to the Yè Capital.
However, Xiàng Prefecture was the ancient Yè territory.
Wèi Prefecture's seat was at Yuánchéng,
which is not Yè territory.
Yè,
during the Warring States period, was a city of Wèi.
In the Hàn, it was Yè County,
the seat of Wèi Commandery.
At the end of the Hàn, Cáo Cāo, as King of Wèi,
resided in Yè.
The Former Yān Mùróng Wěi made Yè his capital,
establishing Guìxiāng County,
which belonged to Chānglè Commandery.
This is the Guìxiāng mentioned in the Shuǐjīng Zhù in relation to the Shāqiū Weir.
In the third year of the Suí Kāihuáng era, Chānglè Commandery was abolished,
and Guìxiāng County was placed under Wèi Prefecture,
subsequently becoming the prefectural seat.
At this time, it was established alongside Xìngtáng County within the city walls.
Xìngtáng was originally Yuánchéng.
Emperor Zhuāngzōng, making Wèi Prefecture the Yè Capital,
specifically named it so because the Hàn Wèi Commandery was administered from Yè and Cáo Cāo, as King of Wèi, had his capital at Yè.
However, since the Suí dynasty, Xiàng Prefecture's seat had been at Ānyáng,
with Yè as a subordinate county.
Neither the seats of Wèi Prefecture nor Xiàng Prefecture were the ancient Yè.
14 In summer,
the fourth month,
on the Guǐhài day, the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
15 Earlier,
the Wǔtái monk Chénghuì, using sorcery and deceit to delude people,
claimed he could subdue heavenly dragons,
command the wind, and summon rain.
The Emperor revered and believed in him,
personally leading the Empress, his imperial brothers, and sons to bow to him.
Chénghuì sat calmly without rising,
and none of the assembled ministers dared not to bow.
At that time, there was a great drought.
The Emperor had Chénghuì brought from the Yè Capital to Luòyáng,
to pray for rain.
Officials and commoners looked up to him morning and night,
but for several decades, no rain fell.
Someone said to Chénghuì:
"Said" here means
to tell or inform.
"The authorities, because the Master's rain prayers have proven ineffective,
intend to burn you."
"Authorities"
refers to Emperor Zhuāngzōng;
"Master"
refers to Chénghuì.
Ashamed and afraid, he died.
The historian states that heterodox teachings are generally deceitful and not to be believed.
16 On the Gēngyín day,
Zhōngshū Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāng Shì Zhào Guāngyǐn died.
17 Since the Empress Dowager parted from Tài,
in the first month of the second year,
the Empress Dowager left Jìnyáng.
Although amusements and entertainments were before her,
she never showed a joyful expression.
After Tài parted from the Empress Dowager,
he also became melancholy and fell ill.
The Empress Dowager dispatched palace messengers and physicians with medicine continuously along the road.
Hearing his illness had worsened slightly,
she would then not eat,
and also said to the Emperor:
"My bond with Tài is like that of brothers.
I wish to go personally to inquire after him."
The Emperor, citing the summer heat and the long distance,
earnestly remonstrated,
and only after a long time did she desist.
Instead, she sent the Emperor's brother Cún Wò and others to go and receive and attend to him.
In the fifth month,
on the Dīngyǒu day,
the Northern Capital reported that Tài had passed away.
The Empress Dowager, in sorrow and grief, did not eat for several days.
The Emperor comforted and explained, never leaving her side.
From then on, the Empress Dowager fell ill.
She also wished to personally attend Tài's burial,
but the Emperor strenuously remonstrated and she stopped.
18 The King of Mǐn, Wáng Shěnzhī, fell seriously ill.
He ordered his son, the Deputy Military Commissioner Yánhàn, to temporarily administer the military prefecture affairs.
19 From spring to summer, there was a great drought.
In the sixth month,
on the Rénshēn day,
rain finally fell.
20 The Emperor suffered from the oppressive summer heat.
He selected places within the palace that were high and cool,
but none satisfied his wishes.
A eunuch therefore said:
"Your servant has seen Cháng'ān in its full flourishing age.
The towers and pavilions of the Dàmíng and Xìngqìng Palaces numbered in the hundreds.
The Táng capital was Cháng'ān.
The Dàmíng Palace was the Eastern Palace,
the Xìngqìng Palace the Southern Palace.
"Guān"
is pronounced with the initial of "gōng" and the tone of "huàn".
The splendor of our current palaces does not even match the mansions of the chief ministers and high officials of that time."
The Emperor then ordered the Palace Gardens Commissioner Wáng Yǔnpíng to build another tower for escaping the summer heat.
The eunuch said:
"Guō Chóngtǎo often frowns with displeasure,
arguing with Kǒng Qiān about insufficient funds.
I fear that even if Your Majesty wishes to undertake construction,
it will ultimately be impossible."
The Emperor said:
"I will use funds from the inner treasury,
unrelated to the state budget."
"State budget"
refers to the regular allocations of the state,
the expenses for which rely on the Tax and Transport Commissioners.
He sent a palace messenger to tell him:
"This year's intense summer heat is exceptionally severe.
In the past, when I was at the river,
confronting the Liáng forces,
the marching camp was low and damp.
Wearing armor and riding horses,
personally facing arrows and stones,
I still did not feel such heat.
Now residing deep within the palace, yet the heat is unbearable.
What is to be done?"
He replied:
"When Your Majesty was at the river in the past,
formidable enemies were not yet destroyed.
You deeply contemplated the enmity and humiliation.
Although there was intense heat,
it did not occupy your sacred thoughts.
Now, external troubles have been eliminated,
and all within the seas submit as guests.
Therefore, even in precious towers and leisurely lodges, one still feels stifling heat.
If Your Majesty does not forget the times of hardship,
then the summer heat will naturally dissipate."
Guō Chóngtǎo's words,
which pointed out how one's living environment changes a person,
can be said to be tactful and earnest.
But what could be done since the Emperor would not listen!
The eunuch said:
"Chóngtǎo's residence
is no different from the imperial palace.
No wonder he does not understand the heat felt by the Supreme Emperor."
The Emperor finally ordered Yǔnpíng to construct the tower.
Ten thousand laborers were employed daily,
and the expenses amounted to tens of thousands.
Chóngtǎo remonstrated:
"Currently, floods and droughts plague the lands north and south of the Yellow River.
Military provisions are insufficient.
I hope you will temporarily halt the corvée labor,
and wait for a year of abundance."
The Emperor did not listen.
21 The Emperor intended to campaign against Shǔ.
On Xīnmǎo,
he issued an edict ordering the empire to requisition and purchase warhorses.
22 Chén Yànqiān, the Judge of the Wú Zhènhǎi Military Command and the Tuanlian Commissioner of Chǔ Prefecture, fell ill.
Chén Yànqiān
was someone trusted and favored by Xú Wēn.
Medicines, gold, and silk were sent to him,
with messengers constantly on the road.
On his deathbed,
Yànqiān secretly left a letter for Xú Wēn,
requesting that his posthumously born son be made his heir.
He sought to move Xú Wēn with the bond of flesh and blood between father and son.
23 The Empress Dowager's illness grew severe.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
on Jiǎwǔ,
Lǐ Sìyuán, the Military Commissioner of Chéngdé, citing that border affairs had somewhat subsided,
submitted a memorial requesting to come to court to inquire after the Empress Dowager's health.
The Emperor did not permit it.
On Rényín,
the Empress Dowager passed away.
The Emperor was overcome with grief and mourning,
and did not eat for five days.
24 In the eighth month,
on Guǐwèi,
Luó Guàn, the Magistrate of Hénán County, was beaten to death with the rod.
Previously,
Guàn had been a Vice Director in the Ministry of Rites.
His nature was strong and upright,
and he was recognized by Guō Chóngtāo,
who appointed him as Magistrate of Hénán County.
In governing, he did not avoid the powerful and influential.
Requests and entreaties from actors and eunuchs
piled up on his desk,
but he did not respond to a single one.
Instead, he showed them all to Chóngtāo,
who memorialized about them.
Consequently, the actors and eunuchs gnashed their teeth in hatred.
Zhāng Quányì, the Governor of Hénán, also disliked Guàn for his lofty and unbending character,
and resented him.
He sent a maidservant to complain to the Empress.
Empress Liú treated Zhāng Quányì as a father,
hence his maidservant could come and go within the palace.
The Emperor harbored anger but had not yet acted.
It happened that the Emperor personally went to Shòu'ān to inspect the workers on the Kūn Mausoleum.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Shòu'ān County is located seventy lǐ southwest of Luòyáng.
The Wǔdài Huìyào says: The Emperor wished to inter the Empress Dowager at the Tàizǔ's garden mausoleum in Dàizhōu.
The Secretariat-Chancellery submitted a memorial of discussion stating:
"A sovereign regards the Four Seas as his home;
he should not distinguish between north and south.
Luòyáng is the dwelling of emperors and kings.
For the seasonal court visits and worship,
it is reasonable that it should be convenient and nearby;
one cannot travel far to Dàizhōu.
The various mausoleums of the Hàn dynasty were all near Qín and Yōng;
our state's garden tombs are distributed throughout the capital region.
After Emperor Wén of the Later Wèi moved the capital from Dài to Luò,
the garden mausoleums were all south of the [Yellow] River.
Moreover, an edict was issued forbidding meritorious ministers' families from being buried in the north.
Now, the various mausoleums of the Wèi clan are still within the capital region.
To inter [the Empress Dowager] in Dàizhōu
is, in principle, not appropriate."
Therefore, the Kūn Mausoleum was constructed.
Many bridges were damaged.
The Emperor asked who was in charge,
and the eunuchs replied it fell under Hénán [County's jurisdiction].
The Emperor was enraged,
and had Guàn imprisoned.
The jailers beat and tortured him,
leaving no part of his body intact.
The next day,
an imperial edict was transmitted ordering his execution.

He emptied his family’s gold, silk, and concubines to bribe Zōngbì,

Zōngbì’s offering,
Jìjí’s keeping,

The Veritable Records and Xuē Shǐ are mistaken.

“But there is no need to worry.

As for Jīngnán’s fortune, it is not heard of.

Hénglù refers to the foot of Mount Héng;

2 Regarding the merit of pacifying Shu,
Lǐ Shàochēn contributed the most,
and his rank was above Dǒng Zhāng's.
However, Zhāng had always been on good terms with Guō Chóngtāo,
and Chóngtāo frequently summoned Zhāng to discuss military affairs.
Shàochēn felt discontented about this.
He said to Zhāng:
"I have the merit of pacifying Shu,
yet you all, who merely followed along like simpletons,

plotting to harm and undermine me.
I am the chief commander.
The Emperor appointed Lǐ Shàochēn as the Commander-in-Chief of the Mobile and Infantry Forces of the Campaign Army,
and Dǒng Zhāng as the Left Wing Patrol Officer.
Hence, he spoke thus.
Zhāng complained to Chóngtāo.
In the twelfth month,
Chóngtāo memorialized to appoint Zhāng as the Military Commissioner of Dōngchuān.
Textual Analysis: The Zhuāngzōng Veritable Records state:
"On the bǐngyín day of the twelfth month,
Jìngnán Military Commissioner Dǒng Zhāng was appointed as Deputy Envoy of the Military Commissioner of Dōngchuān."
Also, the Biography of Kāng Yánxiào states:
"Guō Chóngtāo appointed Dǒng Zhāng as Military Commissioner of Dōngchuān.
Yánxiào and Huázhōu Military Commissioner Máo Zhāng went to see Chóngtāo,
requesting that Minister of Works Rén Shàngshū be appointed as the commander of Dōngchuān.
Chóngtāo angrily said:
'Is Shàochēn rebelling,
that he dares to disobey my command!'
Within less than twenty days,
Chóngtāo was killed by Jìjí."
According to this, the main army entered Xīchuān on the dīngsì day, the twenty-eighth day of the eleventh month,
and by the bǐngyín day, the eighth day of the twelfth month, Dǒng Zhāng was appointed to Dōngchuān,
a total of ten days.
On the eighth day of the first month of the following year, Chóngtāo was killed,
which was sixty days from then.
Yet it says
"within less than twenty days, Chóngtāo was killed,"
which does not match the dates at all.
It is likely that the bǐngyín day of the twelfth month was when Chóngtāo first memorialized to appoint Zhāng as Military Commissioner of Dōngchuān,
not the day the imperial decree was issued.
The statement
"within less than twenty days"
is also likely an error.
By relieving Dǒng Zhāng of his military duties,
Lǐ Shàochēn could no longer command him by military law. This was how Chóngtāo protected Dǒng Zhāng.
Shàochēn said:
"I braved the white blades,

How can Zhāng sit back and claim the rewards!"
He then went to see Chóngtāo and said:
"Dōngchuān is an important region.
Minister Rén possesses both civil and military talents.
You should memorialize to appoint him as commander."
Rén Huán was then Minister of Works participating in military planning.
Shuài (commander),
pronounced similarly to shuài (lead).
"Is Shàochēn rebelling,
that he dares to disobey my command!"

Earlier,
the Emperor sent the eunuch Lǐ Cóngxí and others to accompany Prince Wèi, Lǐ Jìjí, on the campaign against Shu.
Although Jìjí was the overall commander,

Chóngtāo spent the whole day handling affairs,

the gates were quiet and deserted.
Cóngxí and others felt deeply humiliated by this.

the high-ranking officials and generals of Shu vied to present treasures, goods, singing girls, and musicians to Chóngtāo and his son Tínghuì.

Cóngxí and others grew even more resentful.
When Wáng Zōngbì made himself the Provisional Governor of Xīchuān,

Chóngtāo ostensibly agreed.
Textual Analysis: The Veritable Records and the Old History of the Five Dynasties both state that Chóngtāo promised him the position of Shu commander.
Considering that Chóngtāo was a man of insight and strategy,
how could he lead a great army to capture Xīchuān,
only to give it to Zōngbì!
This is something even a mediocre person would not do.
At that time, Zōngbì still held Chéngdū.
Chóngtāo likely feared that Zōngbì might regret his submission and resist,

Zōngbì then led the people of Shu to submit a petition to Jìjí,

Cóngxí and others thus said to Jìjí:

His intentions are unfathomable.
Your Highness must take precautions."
Jìjí said to Chóngtāo:
"The Sovereign relies on you, Imperial Attendant, as upon a mountain.
You cannot leave the court.
Guō Chóngtāo held the title of Imperial Attendant,
hence Jìjí addressed him as such.
Lí (leave),
pronounced lì zhì fān.
Moreover, this is not something I dare decide.
Please have the petitioners go to the capital and present their request themselves."
From then on, Jìjí and Chóngtāo became suspicious of each other.
This section, from "Regarding the merit of pacifying Shu" onward,
lays the groundwork for Lǐ Shàochēn's rebellion.
The section from "Earlier, the Emperor sent Lǐ Cóngxí to accompany Jìjí" onward,

"The Northern Capital is indispensable without Zhāng Xiàn.

To appoint a Governor to handle garrison affairs

Wáng Zhèngyán was senile and muddle-headed.

This is evidence of that.

Jìn,

The Tax Commissioner Kǒng Qiān daily waited outside the Shàngdōng Gate

on Jǐchǒu, the first day,
Mèng Zhīxiáng arrived in Luòyáng,

11. The Emperor, due to insufficient military supplies,
consulted with his close ministers.
Dòu Lú Gé and those below him all did not know what plan to propose.
The Minister of Personnel Lǐ Qí submitted a memorial,
stating:
"In ancient times, they measured income to determine expenditure,
and calculated agricultural resources before raising troops.
Therefore, even when there were floods or droughts, there was no worry of shortage.
In recent times, they tax agriculture to support the military.
There has never been a case where agriculture was wealthy and sufficient, yet the military was lacking,
or where agriculture was impoverished and wasted, yet the military was well-fed and ample.
Now, even if we cannot abolish or reduce taxes,
we should at least eliminate the methods of zhé nà and niǔ pèi.
Zhé nà
refers to forcing the people to convert and pay what they do not have;
niǔ pèi,
refers to calculating amounts and imposing levies accordingly."
The Emperor immediately ordered the relevant officials to act as Lǐ Qí suggested,
but in the end, it could not be implemented.
12. On Dīngyǒu,
an edict was issued: Officials appointed by the former Shǔ court of the fourth rank and above were to be demoted to varying degrees;
those of the fifth rank and below who lacked talent or background were all to be released to return to their fields and villages.
Those who had surrendered earlier or had merit
were entrusted to Guō Chóngtāo to reward and employ according to circumstances.
An edict was also bestowed upon Wáng Yǎn,
roughly stating:
"We shall certainly grant you land and enfeoff you,
and will definitely not treat you harshly in times of danger.
The three celestial bodies are above,
not a single word is false."
He swore by the three celestial bodies but ultimately killed him,
which was not keeping faith.

16. Guō Chóngtāo had always detested eunuchs.
He once secretly said to Prince of Wèi Jìjí:
"When Your Highness gains the empire in the future,
you should not even ride a gelded horse,
let alone employ eunuchs!
You should completely remove them,
and exclusively use scholars."
Lǚ Zhīróu secretly listened
and heard this.
Lǚ Zhīróu was then the Tōngyè of the Commander-in-Chief's Yáshǔ.
Although Chéngdū had been captured,
bandits in Shǔ rose in swarms,
filling the mountains and forests.
Guō Chóngtāo, fearing that after the main army departed,

The Emperor sent the eunuch Xiàng Yánsì to urge him,
but Chóngtāo did not go out to the suburbs to welcome him.
When they met,
his etiquette was also arrogant.
While eunuchs are certainly detestable,
when the Son of Heaven sends them as envoys,
respecting them is how one respects the sovereign.
How could one meet them arrogantly!
Táng Zhuāngzōng sending a penal official as an envoy to a high minister was wrong,
and Guō Chóngtāo meeting him arrogantly was also wrong.
Alas!
Sending penal officials as envoys
had been the norm since the Kāiyuán era of the Táng.
Lǐ Cóngxí said to Yánsì:
"Prince of Wèi
is the Crown Prince;
may the Sovereign enjoy boundless blessings,
yet Guō holds power so arbitrarily.
Guō Tínghuái moves about with followers,
daily drinking intimately with bold generals of the army and local magnates of Shǔ,
pointing at heaven and drawing on the earth.
Recently, I heard he told his father to request appointing himself as the military governor of Shǔ;
he also said
'Shǔ is rich and fertile,
Father should properly plan for yourself.'
Now all the army officers are part of Guō's faction.
Your Highness is lodged in the mouth of tigers and wolves;
should a sudden change occur,
we do not know where our bones will be abandoned."
Thereupon, they faced each other and wept.
Yánsì returned
and fully reported this to Empress Liú.
The Empress tearfully pleaded with the Emperor,
asking to quickly save Jìjí from death.
Previously, the Emperor had heard that the people of Shǔ requested Chóngtāo as military governor,
and was already displeased.
Upon hearing Yánsì's words,
he could not help but be suspicious.
The Emperor examined the registers of the Shǔ treasury,
saying:
"People say the treasures in Shǔ are countless,
why are they so few?"
Yánsì said:
"Your servant heard that when Shǔ fell,
its treasures all went to Chóngtāo and his son.
Chóngtāo has ten thousand taels of gold,
four hundred thousand taels of silver,
a million strings of cash,
a thousand famous horses,
and other goods in proportion.
What Tínghuái took
is additional;
therefore, what the imperial treasury obtained is not much."
The Emperor then showed anger on his face.
When Mèng Zhīxiáng was about to depart,
the Emperor said to him:
"I hear Guō Chóngtāo has rebellious intentions.
When you arrive,
execute him for me."
Zhīxiáng said:
"Chóngtāo
is a meritorious veteran of the state,
he should not be like this.
Wait until your servant reaches Shǔ to investigate;
if he has no other intentions, then send him back."
The Emperor agreed.
On the Rénzǐ day,
Zhīxiáng set out from Luòyáng.
The Emperor then also sent the Armory Commissioner Mǎ Yànguī
galloping to Chéngdū to observe Chóngtāo's actions:
if he obeyed the edict to withdraw the army, then let it be;
if there were signs of delay or arrogance,
then join with Jìjí to deal with him.
Considering how Zhuāngzōng thus ordered Mèng Zhīxiáng and Mǎ Yànguī,
even if Lǐ Cóngxí and others had not acted on Empress Liú's instruction,
and Chóngtāo had managed to return east,
he certainly could not have preserved himself.
It was said:
"Your servant sees that according to Xiàng Yánsì, the situation in Shǔ is precarious day and night.
Now the Sovereign hesitates when he should decide.
This means the Emperor's edict is ambiguous,
without a decisive order to kill Chóngtāo.
Decisive,
reading as 'duàn'.
The crisis allows not a hair's breadth;
how can one await orders from three thousand lǐ away in urgent situations!"
From Chéngdū to Luòyáng is 3,216 lǐ,
see the Old Táng Book, Treatise on Geography.
The Emperor said:
"These are rumors,
their truth is unknown;
how can we rashly be decisive!"
The Empress, failing to get her request,
withdrew,
and personally issued an instruction to Jìjí,
ordering him to kill Chóngtāo.
Zhīxiáng traveled to Shíháo,
Shíháo Village is east of Shǎnxiàn and west of Xīn'ānxiàn,
the place mentioned in Dù Shàolíng's poem
"At dusk I lodge at Shíháo Village"
Jiǔyù Zhì: Shǎnzhōu Shǎnxiàn has Shíháo Town.
Urging Zhīxiáng to hurry to his post,
Zhīxiáng secretly sighed:
"Disorder is about to arise!"
Then he traveled day and night.
Mèng Zhīxiáng traveling at double speed
was not to save Guō Chóngtāo from death,
but fearing that after Chóngtāo's death, other changes would arise.
17. Earlier,
after King Chǔ, Mǎ Yīn, obtained Húnán,
he did not tax merchants,
thus merchants from all directions gathered like spokes to a hub.
Húnán had much lead and iron.
Yīn adopted the strategy of Army Chief Adjutant Gāo Yù,
Army Chief Adjutant
means chief adjutant of all armies.
Gāo Yù in Mǎ Yīn's administration
held a position above that of Army Marshal.
When merchants traveled beyond the borders,
they had no use for these,
so they exchanged them for other goods and left.
Thus, he could use the surplus goods within the territory to exchange for all kinds of goods under heaven,
and the state became rich.
The people of Húnán did not engage in sericulture.
Yù ordered that people paying taxes use silk instead of cash.
Not long after,
weaving looms became widespread among the people.
18. King of Wúyuè, Qián Liú, sent envoy Shěn Tǎn with a letter,
announcing to Wú that he had received the jade register and been enfeoffed as King of Wúyuè.
The people of Wú, because his state name was the same as theirs,
disliked that he resided in Yuè yet bore the name Wú.
They sent Tǎn back.
And ordered the borders not to allow passage to Wúyuè envoys and merchants.
Emperor Míngzōng, Shèngdé Héwǔ Qīnxiào Huángdì, First Part, First Scroll
His personal name was Sìyuán,
a native of Yìngzhōu.
His ancestry was from barbarian tribes,
without a surname.
His father was Diàn,
a commander at Yànmén.
The Emperor's childhood name was Miǎojíliè.
Tàizǔ raised him as a son,
so he took the surname Lǐ,
and was named Sìyuán.
After ascending the throne, he changed his name to Dǎn.
First year of Tiānchéng
(Bǐngxū, 926)
The era name was changed in the fourth month this year,
see the next scroll.
1. Spring,
first month,
Gēngshēn day,
Prince of Wèi, Lǐ Jìjí, sent Lǐ Jìyǎn and Lǐ Yán to escort Wáng Yǎn and his clan and hundreds of officials, several thousand people, to Luòyáng.
2. The Military Commissioner of Hézhōng, Chief Minister Lǐ Jìlín, relied on his old friendship with the Emperor
and his meritorious service.
In the second year of Qiánhuà of the Liáng dynasty,
Zhū Yǒuqiān had already attached Hézhōng to Jìn,
hence he relied on this old connection.
Ever since attaching to Jìn,
when the Prince of Jìn fought the men of Liáng on the Yellow River,
Fén and Jìn had no worries about their rear,
and this was considered his merit.
He also relied on this.
He therefore refused to comply.
When the great army was campaigning against Shǔ,
Jìlín reviewed his troops
and sent his son Lìngdé to lead them in following.
Jǐng Jìn and the eunuchs slandered him, saying:
"Jìlín heard the great army was mobilizing,
thinking it was to attack him,
so he was alarmed and fearful,
and reviewed his troops to defend himself."
They also said:
"The reason Guō Chóngtāo dared to act arrogantly in Shǔ
was because of a secret plot with Hézhōng,
with internal and external coordination."
Jìlín heard this and was afraid;
he wanted to go to the court in person to clear himself.
His close associates stopped him,
but Jìlín said:
"Chief Attendant Guō's merit is higher than mine.
Now the situation is becoming dangerous;
if I can see the sovereign,
and personally state my utmost sincerity,
then the slanderers will be punished."
Chief Attendant Guō
refers to Chóngtāo.
Higher merit
refers to his achievements in destroying Liáng and Shǔ,
which he himself could not match.
Slanderers
refers to the actors and eunuchs.
On the guǐhài day
Jìlín entered the court.
This sets the stage for Jìlín's misfortune.
3. Prince of Wèi Jìjí was about to depart from Chéngdū,
and ordered Rén Yuán to temporarily take charge of remaining affairs,
awaiting Mèng Zhīxiáng.
The arrangements for the various armies were already settled,
meaning the arrangements for those departing and staying were already settled.
Mǎ Yànguī arrived
and showed the Empress's instruction to Jìjí.
Jìjí said:
"The great army is about to depart;
'about to depart'
means on the verge of departure.
How can we do such a treacherous deed!
Gentlemen, say no more.
Moreover, the sovereign has issued no edict;
to kill the Pacification Commissioner solely based on the Empress's instruction,
is that permissible?"
Lǐ Cóngxí and others wept and said:
"Since there is already this evidence,
if by any chance Chóngtāo hears of it,
and causes a mutiny along the way,
it will be even more irremediable."
Together they cleverly explained the advantages and disadvantages,
and Jìjí, having no alternative, complied.
At dawn on the jiǎzǐ day,
Cóngxí, on Jìjí's order, summoned Chóngtāo to discuss matters,
and Jìjí went upstairs to avoid him.
Just as Chóngtāo was ascending the steps,
Jìjí's attendant Lǐ Huán smashed his head,
and also killed his sons Tínghuì and Tíngxìn.
Those outside still did not know.
The Assistant Officer of the Commander-in-Chief, from Fǔyáng, Lǐ Sōng, said to Jìjí:
"Now we are on campaign three thousand lǐ away,
with no imperial edict whatsoever,
you have rashly killed a great general.
How could Your Highness undertake such a dangerous act!
Could you not have endured until reaching Luòyáng?"
Jìjí said:
"What you say is right,
but regret is now useless."
Sōng then summoned several clerks,
went upstairs and removed the ladder,
forged an edict,
used a wax seal to promulgate it,
meaning he carved a replica of the Secretariat seal in wax,
used it to seal the edict and promulgated it.
Chóngtāo's attendants all fled and hid;
only his Chief Secretary, Zhāng Lì from Fǔyáng, went to the Prince of Wèi's residence and wept bitterly for a long time.
Zhāng Lì was Chief Secretary in Chóngtāo's administration.
History records that he served his lord faithfully to the end.
4. Prince of Wèi's aide Lǐ Tíng'ān presented over two hundred Shǔ musicians.
Among them was one Yán Xù,
whom Wáng Yǎn had appointed as Prefect of Péngzhōu.
The Emperor asked him:
"How did you obtain the prefectship?"
He replied:
"Through singing."
The Emperor had him sing, and finding it good,
promised to restore him to his former post.
People all said that the Emperor conquered Shǔ but did not understand why Shǔ perished,
hence his own downfall followed swiftly;
they did not realize this was the Emperor's habitual disposition,
as can be seen from the affairs of Lǐ Cúnxián and Zhōu Zā.
5. On the wùchén day,
Mèng Zhīxiáng reached Chéngdū.
At that time, Guō Chóngtāo had just been killed,
and people's hearts were unsettled.
Zhīxiáng comforted and pacified the officials and people,
rewarded and bestowed upon the officers and soldiers,
and those departing and staying were all calm and orderly.
History records Mèng Zhīxiáng's talent,
which is why he was able to possess Shǔ.
'Reward'
is pronounced kào.
6. The Mǐn people defeated Chén Běn,
and beheaded him.
Chén Běn had besieged Tīngzhōu,
see last year, twelfth month.
7. The Khitan ruler attacked the Jurchens and Balhae.
The Jurchens first appear here.
Their state originally was the Sushen people;
in the Eastern Hàn they were called Yìlóu,
in the Northern Wèi they were called Wùjí,
in Suí and Táng they were called Mòhé,
and in the Five Dynasties period they first were called Nǚzhēn.
The Jurchens had several kinds;
those living south of the Hùntóng River were the 'ripe' Jurchens,
those north of the river were the 'raw' Jurchens.
The Hùntóng River is the Yālù River.
On the wùyín day,
he sent Méi Lǎoxiélǐ to repair relations.
8. Mǎ Yànguī returned to Luòyáng,
and then an edict was issued exposing Guō Chóngtāo's crimes,
and also killing his sons Tíngshuō, Tíngràng, and Tíngyì.
These were Guō Chóngtāo's sons who were in Luòyáng.
Shuō
is read as yuè.
Rumors and discussions were rampant,
and the Emperor sent eunuchs to secretly investigate.
The Military Commissioner of Bǎodà, Prince of Mù Cún Yì,
was Chóngtāo's son-in-law;
the eunuchs wanted to completely eliminate Chóngtāo's faction,
and said
"Cún Yì, facing the generals, bared his arms and wept,
proclaiming Chóngtāo's injustice,
his words resentful and discontented."
On the gēngchén day,
Cún Yì was confined to his residence,
and soon killed.
Jǐng Jìn said:
"Someone from Hézhōng reported a rebellion,
saying Lǐ Jìlín and Guō Chóngtāo plotted rebellion;
after Chóngtāo died,
he also conspired with Cún Yì."
The eunuchs therefore together urged the Emperor to quickly eliminate him,
and the Emperor transferred Jìlín to be Military Commissioner of Yìchéng.
That night,
he sent the Fan and Han Cavalry and Infantry Commander Zhū Shǒuyīn to surround his residence with troops.
The Historical Records of the Five Dynasties says
"surrounded his lodging,"
probably because Zhū Yǒuqiān had no private residence in Luòyáng.
He restored his original name to Zhū Yǒuqiān.
When Emperor Zhāozōng of Táng moved to Luò,
the imperial carriage entered the palace through the Huī'ān Gate.
The Six Codes of Táng: the two northern gates of the Eastern Capital,
the eastern one called Yánxǐ,
the western one called Huī'ān.
Zhū Yǒuqiān being granted a surname is recorded in the 272nd scroll, first year.
Lìngdé was made Military Commissioner of Wǔxìn,
Lìngxī was made Military Commissioner of Zhōngwǔ;
an edict ordered Prince of Wèi Jìjí to execute Lìngdé in Suìzhōu,
and Prefect of Zhèngzhōu Wáng Sītóng to execute Lìngxī in Xǔzhōu.
The Táng established the Zhōngwǔ Army in Xǔzhōu and the Kuāngguó Army in Tóngzhōu,
but by the time of Liáng the two army names were swapped,
and when Later Táng destroyed Liáng,
both were restored to their original names.
Shàoqí went to his home,
and Yǒuqiān's wife, née Zhāng, led over two hundred members of the household to see Shàoqí
and said:
"The Zhū clan deserves to die,
but I hope innocent people are not indiscriminately implicated."
She then separated a hundred servants,
and with a hundred members of the clan went to execution.
Née Zhāng also took out the iron certificate to show Shàoqí, saying:
"This was bestowed by the Emperor last year;
I am a woman,
I cannot read,
and do not know what it says."
Shàoqí was also ashamed for her.
Yǒuqiān's former generals Shǐ Wǔ and six others,
who were then prefects,
were all executed along with their clans.
At that time, the various armies in Luòyáng were starving and in dire straits,
and they recklessly spread rumors.
The court musicians collected these rumors and reported them to the emperor,
which led to the disasters that befell both Zhū Yǒuqiān and Guō Chóngtāo.
Lǐ Sìyuán, the military governor of Chéngdé and concurrently Zhōngshū Lìng, was also implicated by the rumors.
The emperor sent Zhū Shǒuyīn to investigate him;
Shǒuyīn privately said to Sìyuán:
"Your Excellency's achievements have shaken the ruler.
You should plan to return to your own territory to avoid disaster."
"Shaken,"
should be interpreted as
"startled."
"Avoid,"
pronounced as "yuàn" in the sense of "to keep away."
"My heart bears no guilt toward heaven and earth.
When fortune or disaster comes,
there is no way to avoid it;
I entrust it all to fate."
Lǐ Sìyuán's response to Zhū Shǒuyīn's words,
showing equanimity in the face of life, death, fortune, and disaster,
reveals a heroic perspective and magnanimity that others could not match.
The meritorious veterans could not protect themselves,
and Sìyuán was in grave danger on several occasions.
He relied on Xuānhuī Shǐ Lǐ Shàohóng to protect and assist him from all sides,
and thus he was able to survive.

9. Prince of Wèi, Jìjí, left the infantry and cavalry commander-in-chief, Lǐ Rénhǎn of Chénliú; the cavalry commander-in-chief, Pān Rénsì of Dōngguāng; the left-wing commander-in-chief, Zhào Tíngyǐn; the right-wing commander-in-chief, Zhāng Yè of Jùnyí; the commander of the inner guards, Wǔ Zhāng of Wénshuǐ; and the commander of the elite troops, Lǐ Yánhòu of Píng'ēn to garrison Chéngdū.
This laid the groundwork for the generals in Shǔ to eventually pledge their loyalty to Mèng Zhīxiáng.
On Jiǎshēn,
Jìjí departed from Chéngdū,
ordering Lǐ Shàochēn to lead twelve thousand men as the rear army,
whose movements were always thirty lǐ behind the central army.
Thirty lǐ is one shè.
They lagged thirty lǐ behind the central army.
"Lead,"
pronounced as "shuài."
10. In the second month,
on Jǐchǒu, the first day,
Lǐ Shàohóng, the Xuānhuī Nányuàn Shǐ, was appointed as the Shūmì Shǐ.
He replaced Guō Chóngtāo.
11. Yáng Rénzhěng, the commander of Wèibó,
led his troops to garrison Wǎqiáo.
After more than a year, they were due to return,
but upon reaching Bèizhōu,
because Yèdū was undefended,
it was feared that the troops might cause unrest upon arrival.
An imperial decree ordered them to remain stationed in Bèizhōu.
At that time, no one in the empire knew the crime of Guō Chóngtāo,
and among the people, rumors spread:
"Chóngtāo killed Jìjí,
and declared himself king in Shǔ,
which is why his family was exterminated."
Zhū Yǒuqiān's son, Jiànhuī, was the prefect of Chánzhōu.
The emperor secretly ordered Shǐ Yànqióng, the supervisor of Yèdū, to kill him.
Chánzhōu
was under the jurisdiction of Wèibó,
hence the secret order to the supervisor of Wèibó to kill Zhū Jiànhuī.
"Chán,"
pronounced as "shí lián."
"Shǐ Wǔdé rode out of the city on horseback at midnight,
without saying where he was going."
Shǐ Yànqióng, as a military commissioner, served as a supervisor,
referring to his inner court position.
"The empress blamed the emperor for Jìjí's death,
and had already assassinated the emperor,
hence urgently summoning Yànqióng to discuss matters."
The people grew even more terrified.
Rumors were just beginning to spread,
and Shǐ Yànqióng's actions were suspicious and alarming,
which caused the rumors to intensify,
and chaos followed.
Huángfǔ Huī, a soldier under Yáng Rénzhěng, lost at gambling with his companions one night.
Taking advantage of the people's unrest,
he started a rebellion,
seizing Rénzhěng and saying:
"The reason the sovereign gained the empire
was due to the strength of our Wèi army;
meaning they relied on the military power of Wèibó to defeat Liáng.
For over ten years, our horses never left the saddle.
Now that the empire is pacified,
the Son of Heaven does not remember our past labors,
but instead grows more suspicious and jealous.
We have been stationed far away for over a year,
and just as we were delighted to be relieved and return,
with home just a stone's throw away,
we are not allowed to see it.
This refers to the order to remain stationed in Bèizhōu,
not permitting them to return to Wèizhōu.
According to the Jiǔyù Zhì: Bèizhōu is 225 lǐ south of Wèizhōu.
The capital is already in chaos.
The officers and soldiers wish to return with you,
and we will submit a memorial to inform the court.
If the Son of Heaven is fortunate,
and raises an army to attack us,
with the military strength of our Wèibó, we can certainly resist them."
Huángfǔ Huī
was a soldier of the Yínqiāng Xiàojié unit,
who fought with Zhuāngzōng on the Hé River,
and was accustomed to seeing Zhuāngzōng's military tactics,
as well as the bravery and cowardice of the various armies.
Therefore, he dared to say this.
Rénzhěng did not comply,
and Huī killed him;
then he seized a junior officer,
who also did not comply,
and he killed him as well.
Zhào Zàilǐ, the commander of the Xiàojié unit, heard of the rebellion.
Without even having time to fasten his clothes,
he climbed over the wall to flee.
Huī caught up with him,
dragged him down by his feet,
and showed him two heads,
the heads of Yáng Rénzhěng and the junior officer.
The rebellious soldiers then made him their leader,
and they looted and burned Bèizhōu.
Huī
was from Wèizhōu;
Zàilǐ
was from Zhuōzhōu.
At dawn the next day,
Huī and others escorted Zàilǐ south toward Línqīng, Yǒngjì, and Guàntáo,
plundering along the way.
"Toward,"
pronounced as "qī yù."
"Plunder,"
pronounced as "pǐ miào."
On the evening of Rénchén,
someone came from Bèizhōu to report that the army had rebelled and was about to attack Yèdū.
The chief patrol inspector, Sūn Duó, and others urgently went to Shǐ Yànqióng,
requesting armor and permission to man the city walls for defense.
Yànqióng suspected that Duó and others had ulterior motives,
and said:
"The informant said the rebels would reach Línqīng today.
Calculating the distance, they should only arrive on the evening of the sixth day."
According to the Jiǔyù Zhì: Línqīng County is 150 lǐ south of Wèizhōu city.
Huángfǔ Huī and others reached Línqīng on Rénchén.
Shǐ Yànqióng thought they would only reach Wèizhōu on the evening of the sixth day,
because an army marches 50 lǐ per day,
so he calculated it would take three days to arrive.
Rénchén was the fourth day of the second month.
The sixth day
refers to the sixth day of the second month,
which was Jiǎwǔ.
Sūn Duó said:
"Since the rebels have started a rebellion,
they will certainly take advantage of our lack of preparedness,
marching day and night at double speed.
How could they possibly travel according to a fixed schedule?
I request that the Púyè lead the troops to man the city walls."
Shǐ Yànqióng likely held the title of Púyè,
which is why Sūn Duó addressed him as such.
"Lead,"
pronounced as "shuài."
"Once the rebels' momentum is thwarted,
they will certainly disperse,
and then we can suppress and attack them."
"If we wait until they reach the city walls,
and by chance there are traitors acting as inside agents,
then the situation will be perilous."
Yànqióng said:
"Just strictly guard the city with soldiers.
Why engage in preemptive battle?"
That night,
the rebel vanguard attacked the north gate,
with arrows and crossbow bolts flying chaotically.
At the time, Yànqióng was stationed with his troops at the north gate tower.
Upon hearing the rebels' shouts,
they immediately panicked and scattered.
Yànqióng fled alone on horseback to Luòyáng.
On Guǐsì,
the rebels entered Yèdū.
Sūn Duó and others resisted but were defeated,
and they fled.
Zhào Zàilǐ occupied the palace city.
The emperor had ascended the throne in Wèizhōu,
using the yáchéng as the palace city.
He allowed his soldiers to loot extensively.
Jìn
was from Dìngzhōu.
Wáng Zhèngyán was just sitting at his desk summoning clerks to draft a memorial,
but none arrived.
Zhèngyán grew angry,
and his family members said:
"The rebels have already entered the city,
killing and plundering in the markets.
The clerks have all fled and scattered.
Whom are you still calling for?"
Zhèngyán exclaimed in shock:
"I had no idea at all."
He then asked for a horse,
but could not obtain one.
So he led his subordinates on foot out of the prefectural gate to pay respects to Zài Lǐ,
bowing twice to beg for forgiveness.
Zài Lǐ also bowed in return,
saying:
"The soldiers merely wish to return home.
Your Excellency is of high virtue;
do not humble yourself!"
He comforted and admonished them before sending them away.
Wáng Zhèngyán had been appointed as the acting governor in his capacity as Minister of Revenue,
hence Zhào Zài Lǐ addressed him as such.
The crowd pushed Zài Lǐ to become the acting military governor of Wèi-Bó,
and they submitted a memorial reporting the situation.
The acting governor of Běijīng, Zhāng Xiàn, had his family in Yèdū.
Last year, Zhāng Xiàn had been transferred from acting governor of Yèdū to Běijīng,
so his family still remained in Yèdū.
Zài Lǐ sent an envoy with a letter to entice Xiàn,
but Xiàn did not open the seal,
instead beheading the envoy and reporting it.
On the 12th, jiǎwǔ,
Jǐng Jìn was appointed as Silver青光禄大夫, Acting Right散骑常侍兼御史大夫, and Shàngzhùguó.
On the 13th, bǐngshēn,
Shǐ Yànqióng arrived in Luòyáng.
He had fled from Yèdū to Luòyáng.
Shào Hóng again requested the employment of Lǐ Shàoqīn.
During the campaign against Shǔ,
Lǐ Shàohóng had already recommended Lǐ Shàoqīn but he was not used,
hence the mention of "again."
He was ordered to submit a strategic plan.
The deputy commanders requested by Shàoqīn
were all old Liáng generals,
men he was on good terms with,
so the Emperor grew suspicious and stopped it.
The Empress said:
"This is a minor matter;
it is not worth troubling a senior general.
Shàoróng can handle it."
Shàoróng
was Yuán Xíngqín.
Troops were also levied from various circuits,
in preparation for any disobedience.
After Guō Chóngtāo's death,
Lǐ Shàochēn said to Dǒng Zhāng:
"Whose door do you plan to whisper at again?"
Zhāng grew fearful
and apologized.
When Prince of Wèi Jìjí's army returned to Wǔlián,
they encountered an imperial envoy
who informed them that Zhū Yǒuqiān had already been executed,
and ordered Dǒng Zhāng to lead troops to Suìzhōu to execute Zhū Lìngdé.
At that time, Shàochēn was commanding the rear army at Wèichéng.

Prince Xuē Cúnlǐ, and Emperor Zhuāngzōng's young sons Jìsōng, Jìtóng, Jìchán, and Jìshān[AS-FBEC]yáo,

One chancellor was entrusted with exclusive authority over these matters.
Under the Táng system: the Ministry of Revenue and the Bureau of Budget were managed by their respective directors and vice-directors,
and the Salt and Iron Transport Commissioner was also established.
Later, due to military campaigns,
state finances became paramount,
and the chancellors took charge of these duties.
After the Gānfú era,

state finances became increasingly strained,

Military campaigns were irregular,
and taxes were levied as needed,
ceasing once the campaigns ended.
When the Liáng dynasty rose,
the Tax Commissioner was established,
overseeing the realm's finances and grain,

After Zhuāngzōng destroyed Liáng,
this system remained unchanged.
When Míngzōng ascended the throne,
he executed the Tax Commissioner Kǒng Qiān and abolished the position,
entrusting one high official to manage the Revenue, Budget, and Salt and Iron offices,
known as the Commissioner of the Three Offices.
By the first year of the Chángxīng era,

The Secretariat followed Táng precedent,
appointing Yánlǎng as Tejin and Minister of Works,

an edict appointed Yánlǎng as Commissioner of the Three Offices,

The establishment of the Commissioner of the Three Offices
began with the Liáng dynasty.

61 Under the old system,

for both civil and military officials, as well as officials of various circuits and recommended military officers,
after the imperial edict was issued,

and only then would they receive their appointment letters.
Lù Yóu said: Jiāng Línjǐ's Jiāyòu Miscellany states that in the Tang dynasty, appointment letters were initially made of paper,
during the reign of Emperor Suzōng, silk was sometimes used,

I once saw in Chéngdū the appointment letter for Liú Rénshàn's promotion to Zhōngshū Lìng by Emperor Shìzōng of the Later Zhōu, which was still made of paper,
kept at the home of the son of Minister Jīn Yànhēng.
Poor officials only received the edict document,
and often did not take the appointment letter.
They used the edict document to verify their appointment and perform their duties,
merely to obtain temporary salary and benefits;
as for the appointment letter,
if they lacked the money, they would not receive it.

"The appointment letter contains words of praise, criticism, instruction, and admonition,

assistant directors and vice directors refer to the Left and Right Assistant Directors of the Department of State Affairs and the twenty-four bureau directors,
supervising secretaries refer to the Supervising Secretaries,
and remonstrance officials refer to the Remonstrance Officials.
They should be granted appointment letters.
Later, the chief ministers deliberated,
believing that the vermilion glue and silk scroll
did not cost much,
and since the court granted them official salaries,
why begrudge such a small expense!
"Shòu"
should be
"shòu"
(to grant).
The History of the Five Dynasties states: According to precedent,
for appointment letters issued by the Ministry of Personnel, the appointee had to pay for the vermilion glue and silk scroll before receiving it,
while those of high rank were granted them.
Poor officials could not afford to pay,
often receiving only the edict document without the appointment letter.
During the chaos of the Five Dynasties,
this became customary,
and low-ranking officials no longer received appointment letters;
the Secretariat merely recorded the wording of the appointment and compiled it into the edict registry.
Liú Yuè proposed,
arguing that
"the wording of the appointment either acknowledges the appointee's talent and ability,
or praises their achievements and conduct,
or offers instruction and admonition,
yet those receiving appointments are not given the appointment letter,
so they do not know the reason for their appointment,
which contradicts the intention of the imperial proclamation.
I request that they all be granted appointment letters."
From then on, all officials were granted appointment letters,
starting with Liú Yuè.
"All those appointed to office no longer had to pay money;
they were all granted appointment letters."
At that time,
besides regular officials,
the rest, such as probationary titles and honorary designations, were only used to honor and motivate military officers.

Honorary designations

As appointments increased,
even ordinary soldiers in the army,
clerks in prefectures, towns, and garrisons,
were granted silver and blue ranks and surveillance officials,
with tens of thousands of appointment letters granted annually.
The history, due to the text on granting appointment letters,
comments on the excessive appointments of the time.

65 Zhào Jìliáng and others transported one billion in gold and silk from Shǔ to Luòyáng.
The Book of Songs says: "Ten thousand yì and zǐ."
The commentary explains: Ten thousand yì is called a zhào.
Kǒng Yǐngdá said: "Ten thousand yì is called a zhào" means,
according to mathematical methods,
the number yì has two systems, large and small.
In the small system, ten is the base,
so one hundred thousand is called yì,
and one billion is called zhào.
In the large system, ten thousand is the base,
so counting ten thousand to ten thousand is yì,
meaning one hundred million is yì,
and counting from yì to ten thousand yì is zhào.
Therefore, the Máo commentary on the Book of Songs says,
counting ten thousand to ten thousand is yì,
counting yì to yì is zǐ,
and zhào lies between yì and zǐ,
which is the large system.
The Odes of Wèi criticize the greed and cruelty of those in power:
"Why take three hundred yì of grain!"
The state of Wèi was small,
so the amount should not be excessive;
thus, the small system is used,
explaining that one hundred thousand is yì.
Now, Zhào Jìliáng transported one billion in gold and silk.
If calculated using the small yì, it would only be one million,
how could that relieve the court's shortages?
If calculated using the large yì,
it would be ten billion.
It is unclear which is correct.
The court relied on this to get by.

making Zhīxiáng go to the capital.
Dǎn
I have already executed him."
The Nèi Bāzuò Shǐ Yáng Lìngzhī was on business in Shǔ.
Bāzuò Shǐ
oversees the craftsmen of the eight workshops in the Bāzuò Sī.
Hearing of Yán's death,
he fled back.
Zhū Hóngzhāo was in Dōngchuān.
Zhū Hóngzhāo was the deputy of Dōngchuān,

He also feared,
