When it came to dividing commands and increasing troops,

Cóngróng heard this

Since he was now the administrator of the capital region

his position was close and his power great,
Cóngróng disliked his encroachment,
hence his displeasure.
This sets the stage for Cóngróng's jealousy of Cónghòu.

Shūmìshǐ An Chonghuì was additionally appointed Shìzhōng,

Shìzhōng Xú Zhīgào deliberately made a mistake in reporting daily affairs in the side hall,

The King of Wú issued a gracious edict not to inquire further,

from then on, both inside and outside the court, order was restored.
When laws are not upheld,
it is because those above violate them;
when laws are upheld by those above,
then both inside and outside the court, order is restored.
10. The Khitan changed their reign era to Tiānxiǎn,
and buried their ruler Ābǎojī at Mùyè Shān.
The Khitan ruler designated his residence as Shàngjīng,
and built a tower there,
named Xī Lóu.
He also built Dōng Lóu a thousand *li* to the east,
Běi Lóu three hundred *li* to the north,
and Nán Lóu at Nán Mùyè Shān.
According to records, at Mùyè Shān,
the Khitan established Jǐnzhōu.
The *Xūzhī* of the Xiongnu states: Jǐnzhōu is four hundred *li* northeast to Dōngjīng,
and Mùyè Shān is three hundred *li* southwest to Shàngjīng.
This indicates Jǐnzhōu and Mùyè Shān are two separate places.
Later, the *Zizhi Tongjian* records that when the Jìn dynasty's Prince of Qí was moved north to Jǐnzhōu,
the Khitan ordered him to pay respects at Ābǎojī's tomb,
which then seems to suggest Mùyè Shān was in Jǐnzhōu.
Historical works like the *Ōu Shǐ* state the Khitan built Nán Lóu at Nán Mùyè Shān,
which would be south of Shàngjīng.
The *Xūzhī* states Mùyè Shān is three hundred *li* southwest to Shàngjīng,
which would be northeast of Shàngjīng.
Could it be that among the Khitan there was both a Nán Mùyè Shān and a Běi Mùyè Shān?
The Empress then often said:
"Convey my words to the Late Emperor!"
Upon reaching the tomb site, they would be killed,
and over a hundred people were killed this way.
Finally,
it was the turn of Zhào Sīwēn from Píngzhōu to go,
but Sīwēn refused.
The Empress said:
"You served the Late Emperor closely,
why do you refuse to go?"
He replied:
"None were as close as Your Majesty.
If Your Majesty goes,
then your servant will follow."
The Empress said:
"It is not that I do not wish to follow the Late Emperor underground,
but considering the heir is young and weak,
and the state lacks a ruler,
I cannot go."
She then severed one of her wrists,
and ordered it placed in the tomb.
Sīwēn was thus spared.

At that time, Lú
[Lú] Zhīwēn incited the troops under Lóng Zhì's command to kill Wū Zhèn at the banquet,

Incited,

The mutineers looked at each other, their faces pale,

Common speech,

Acting Judge,

Later Student Tiāntāi
The second year of Tiānchéng
(Dīnghài, 927)
1 In autumn,
the seventh month,
Guīdé Military Commissioner Wáng Yànqiú was appointed Deputy Northern Campaign Commander.
After Wū Zhèn died,
Wáng Yànqiú replaced him.
According to the Old History of the Five Dynasties,
an edict issued on the Jiǎchén day of the seventh month this year stated:
"In our dynasty, imperial princes have held military governorships in absentia,
leading to the positions of Deputy Grand Envoy and Administrator of Military Affairs.
This practice has been passed down for generations,
and has persisted without change.
Henceforth, for Xīchuān and Dōngchuān, the title of Deputy Grand Envoy shall be dropped,
and they shall simply be called Military Commissioners."
Soon after, all military governorships were formally appointed as Military Commissioners.
2 On the Bǐngyín day,
Kuízhōu was elevated to Níngjiāng Army,
and Xīfāng Yè was appointed its Military Commissioner.
This was a reward for defeating Gāo Jìxīng's army,
and recapturing Kuí, Zhōng, and Wàn.
Shǔ had designated Kuízhōu as Zhènjiāng Army;
now it was changed to Níngjiāng Army.
3 On the Guǐsì day,
the cession of Kuí, Zhōng, and Wàn to Gāo Jìxīng was deemed the crime of Dòulú Gé and Wéi Shuō.
In the first year, these three prefectures were given to Jìxīng,
while Gé and Shuō were still serving as chancellors,
hence they were charged with this crime.
4 Duàn Níng was exiled to Liáozhōu,
Wēn Tāo to Dézhōu,
and Liú Xùn to Púzhōu.
Since the end of the Táng,
those sentenced to exile or demotion never actually reached their designated places.
Liáo, Dé, and Pú were all within Táng territory.
These three men were all made to proceed to their places of exile.
5 Rèn Huán requested to retire and reside in Cízhōu,
which was granted.
6 In the eighth month,
on the Jǐmǎo day, the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
7 When the envoys for the investiture ceremony arrived at Chángshā,
the Prince of Chǔ, Mǎ Yīn, began to establish his state.
The enfeoffment of the Prince of Chǔ, Mǎ Yīn, as King is recorded in the sixth month of this year in the previous scroll.
He established all official posts,
all similar to those of the Son of Heaven,
though some names were slightly altered:
to show he did not dare to emulate the imperial court.
Gēng,
pronounced gōng xíng fān.
The "Drafter of Edicts" was called "Administrator of Edicts and Compositions,"
the Bureau of Military Affairs was called the "Left and Right Office of Critical Affairs,"
subordinates addressed him as "Your Highness,"
and his orders were called "Instructions."
Yáo Yànzhāng was appointed Left Chancellor,
Xǔ Déxūn as Right Chancellor,
Lǐ Duó as Minister of Education,
Cuī Yǐng as Minister of Works,
Tuòbá Héng as Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs,
and Zhāng Yànyáo and Zhāng Yíng were appointed to adjudicate the Office of Critical Affairs.
The person upon whom Mǎ Yīn relied to govern the state was Gāo Yù.
Yet when establishing the state and appointing officials,
Yù was not included.
Why was this?
Could it be that Mǎ Yīn's sons already harbored jealousy towards Yù?
Only the Military Commissioners of Lǎng and Guì were appointed first and then approval was sought afterwards.
Lǎng,
Wǔpíng Army,
Guì,
Jìngjiāng Army,
both were under Chǔ at the time.
The names were altered to avoid the taboo of Mǎ Yīn's father's name.

the Emperor said to Ān Zhònghuì:
"Among Cóngróng's attendants, there are those who falsely proclaimed Our decree,
ordering him not to associate with Confucian scholars,
fearing it would weaken a man's will and spirit.
We, considering Cóngróng young and governing a major commandery,
(Cóngróng was appointed to guard Yèdū in the third month of this year,
the matter is recorded in the previous scroll.)
Shǎo,
pronounced shì zhào fān.
Now treacherous people speak such words!"
He wanted to execute them;
Zhònghuì requested only a stern warning.
Ān Zhònghuì was not a Confucian,
hence he was lenient towards the speaker's crime.
Did he not consider that falsely proclaiming the Emperor's decree
is punishable by the constant laws of the state!

was the son of Lǐ Cúnshěn;

the tenth month,
on the Yǐyǒu day,

intending to go to Biànzhōu;
on the Dīnghài day,
he arrived at Xíngyáng.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: Xíngyáng County is sixty *lǐ* west of Zhèngzhōu,
and one hundred and forty *lǐ* east to Dàliáng.
Among the people, rumors spread that the Emperor intended to personally attack Wú,
and also that he intended to reorganize the eastern feudal lords.
The Xuānwǔ Military Commissioner, Acting Palace Attendant Zhū Shǒuyīn became suspicious and fearful.
His Administrative Assistant, Sūn Chéng from Gāomì, urged Shǒuyīn to rebel.
Gāomì
was an ancient county of the Hàn,
abandoned during the chaos of the Suí,
re-established at Yìchéng Fortress in the third year of Wǔdé of the Táng,
and moved in the sixth year to the old site of Yí'ān City,
which was the ancient Gāomì County,
belonging to Mìzhōu.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: It is 120 *lǐ* northeast of the prefecture.
*Kǎoyì* states: The *Jiāngnán Lù* records it as
"Sūn Jì."
Now we follow Wáng Pǔ's *Zhōu Shìzōng Shílù*.
Chéng,
pronounced chéng zhèng fān.
The Emperor sent Palace Attendant Fàn Yánguāng to go and admonish him.
Yánguāng said:
"If we do not attack him early,
then the walls of Biàn City will be fortified;
I wish to take five hundred cavalry and go with them."
The Emperor agreed.
Yánguāng set out at dusk,
and before dawn had traveled two hundred *lǐ*,
reaching the walls of Dàliáng.
He engaged the people of Biàn in battle,
greatly startling them.
On the Wùzǐ day,
the Emperor reached Jīngshuǐ.
Jīngshuǐ is east of Xíngyáng,
west of Suǒshuǐ.
Since the Liáng dynasty,
there have been the Imperial Guard Army, the Imperial Guard Cavalry, and the Imperial Guard Infantry.
Someone said to Ān Zhònghuì:
"Those who have lost their positions and are outside the capital,
taking advantage before the rebels are defeated,
might cause trouble.
It would be better to eliminate them."
Zhònghuì considered this reasonable,
and memorialized to send an envoy to bestow death upon Rèn Huán.
Rèn Huán's dismissal from the chancellorship is recorded in the sixth month of this year in the previous scroll.
"Rèn Huán is a righteous man,
how could he possibly rebel!
Your indiscriminate punishment like this,
how can it assist the state!"
When the envoy reached Cízhōu,
Huán gathered his clan for a hearty drink,
and then died,
his spirit and expression unwavering.
13 On the Jǐchǒu day,
the Emperor reached Dàliáng,
attacking from all sides.
Many officials and people descended the walls by rope to surrender.
Shǒuyīn, knowing the situation was hopeless,
killed all his family,
then stretched out his neck and ordered his attendants to behead him.
Those defending the walls saw the imperial carriage,
and led each other in opening the gates to surrender.
Sūn Chéng fled to Wú,
where Xú Zhīgào treated him as a guest.
This sets the stage for Sūn Chéng's loyal service in Jiāngnán.
14 On the Wùxū day,
an edict was issued remitting nearly two million strings of cash in arrears owed to the Three Bureaus.
15 On the Xīnchǒu day,

the Grand Chancellor of Wú, Commander of All Armies Within and Without, Commander of All Circuits, Military Commissioner of Zhènhǎi and Níngguó, concurrently Secretariat Director, Prince of Dōnghǎi, Xú Wēn, died.
7. Zhāng Yún arrived at Cháng'ān.
Last year, Zhāng Yún was transferred to remain in charge of the Western Capital.
This was the Emperor's intention.
He was appointed as General of the Left Guard.
8. On Rénchén,
Níngjiāng Military Commissioner Xīfāng Yè attacked and captured Guīzhōu.
Not long after,
Jīngnán recaptured it.
Guīzhōu
was under the jurisdiction of Gāo Jìxīng.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: From Kuízhōu east to Guīzhōu is 330 lǐ.
Jǐ,
read as jū qǐ fān.
Fù,
read as fú yòu fān;
below, yí fù is the same.
9. Privy Councilor and Tongpíngzhāngshì Kǒng Xún,
was cunning and flattering by nature,
and Ān Zhònghuái trusted him.
The Emperor wanted to arrange a marriage between a prince and Ān Zhònghuái's daughter.
Kǒng Xún said to Ān Zhònghuái:
"Your position is close to the Emperor,
it is not appropriate to also form a marriage alliance with a prince."
Ān Zhònghuái declined the offer.
After some time,
someone said to Ān Zhònghuái:
"Kǒng Xún is skilled at sowing discord among people,
he should not be placed in a confidential position."
Kǒng Xún learned of this,
and secretly sent someone to contact Wáng Dé,
seeking to have his daughter accepted;
Wáng Dé requested to marry Kǒng Xún's daughter as a wife for his son Cónghòu,
and the Emperor approved it.
Wáng Dé was favored by the Emperor,
and whatever he said was carried out,
later he was promoted to Shū.
On Yǐwèi,
Kǒng Xún was appointed as Tongpíngzhāngshì,
serving concurrently as Zhōngwǔ Military Commissioner and overseer of the Eastern Capital.
This removed him from his confidential position.
Ān Zhònghuái was stubborn and obstinate by nature.
Qínzhōu Military Commissioner Huá Wēnqí came to court,
requesting to remain in the capital,
and the Emperor praised him for this.
At that time, most military commanders preferred to remain in their regional commands where they could act arbitrarily,
only Huá Wēnqí came to court and requested to stay,
hence the Emperor praised him.
Huá,
read as hù huà fān.
He was granted additional monthly allowances of money and grain.
Beyond his regular salary, he was granted additional money and grain.
The Emperor said to Ān Zhònghuái:
"Huá Wēnqí is an old acquaintance,
we should select an important command for him."
Huá Wēnqí had already served as a military commissioner under the Liáng,
hence the Emperor spoke thus.
Chǔ,
read as chāng lǚ fān.
Another day,
the Emperor mentioned it repeatedly,
Ān Zhònghuái said angrily:
"I have repeatedly reported that there are no vacancies,
only the position of Privy Councilor could be given to him."
The Emperor said:
"That could work too."
Ān Zhònghuái had no reply.
Huá Wēnqí's ability was truly insufficient to hold an important command,
Ān Zhònghuái, relying on the harmonious relationship between ruler and minister,
should have explained clearly in his memorials,
and Míngzōng would likely have complied;
but now the words exchanged between superior and subordinate failed to convey their intentions clearly,
they only provoked each other,
this was due to lack of learning reaching this point.
For several months, Ān Zhònghuái did not appear at court.
Ān Zhònghuái disliked Chéngdé Military Commissioner and Tongpíngzhāngshì Wáng Jiànlì,
and reported that Wáng Jiànlì was colluding with Wáng Dū,
harboring disloyal intentions.
Wáng Jiànlì also reported that Ān Zhònghuái was monopolizing power,
and requested to come to court to personally explain the situation,
the Emperor summoned him;
after he arrived,
he said that Ān Zhònghuái had formed a marriage alliance with Xuānhuīshǐ and concurrent Sānsī official Zhāng Yánlǎng,
they were acting in collusion,
and abusing power.
In the third month,
on Xīnhài,
the Emperor saw Ān Zhònghuái,
his expression was very angry,
and said to him:
"Now I will give you a military command to rest,
and have Wáng Jiànlì replace you,
Zhāng Yánlǎng will also be appointed to an external post."
Ān Zhònghuái said:
"I have served Your Majesty through hardships for decades,
witnessed Your Majesty's ascension,
and filled the vacancy in confidential matters,
'filled the vacancy' means
filling someone else's lack,
meaning that at the time there was a lack of suitable people,
so I was able to take charge of confidential matters.
Now to suddenly discard me to an external command,
I wish to hear my crime!"
The Emperor, displeased, stood up and left.
This section, from Kǒng Xún onward, describes how Ān Zhònghuái and Kǒng Xún opposed each other,
from Huá Wēnqí onward, it explains the origin of the suspicion between ruler and minister.
It seems Ān Zhònghuái relied on his long-standing relationship,
clung to power and was unwilling to step down,
while Míngzōng had gradually been influenced by slanderous words,
wanted to distance him but could not,
until the rupture occurred,
then it became irreparable.
Zhū Hóngzhāo said:
"Your Majesty has always treated Ān Zhònghuái like your own hands,
how can you discard him over a minor grievance!
I hope you will reconsider."
Zhū Hóngzhāo's words today,
show he knew Ān Zhònghuái's favor had not yet declined;
his memorial from Fèngxiáng,
shows he knew Ān Zhònghuái's power was already gone.
The wisdom of petty men,
changes with the times,
how fearsome!
The next day,
Wáng Jiànlì bid farewell to return to his command,
the Emperor said:
"You recently memorialized wanting to come and share my worries,
now why are you leaving again!"
It happened that Menxià Shìláng concurrent Xíngbù Shàngshū and Tongpíngzhāngshì Zhèng Yù requested to retire,
on Jǐwèi,
Zhèng Yù was appointed as Zuǒ Púyè and retired;
on Guǐhài,
Wáng Jiànlì was appointed as Yòu Púyè concurrent Zhōngshū Shìláng, Tongpíngzhāngshì, and concurrent Sānsī official.
10. Mèng Zhīxiáng repeatedly disputed with Dǒng Zhāng over salt profits.
In Shǔ, there are well salts,
within the jurisdictions of both the Eastern and Western Chuān circuits,
each wanted to monopolize and secure the profits,
hence the dispute.
According to the prosperous period of the Táng,
there were thirteen wells in Qióng, Jiā, and Méi,
overseen by the Jiànnán Xīchuān office;
there were 460 wells in Zǐ, Suì, Mián, Hé, Chāng, Yú, Lú, Zī, Róng, Líng, and Jiǎn,
overseen by the Jiànnán Dōngchuān office.
The salt profits of Dōngchuān were greater than those of Xīchuān.
Mèng Zhīxiáng was troubled by this,
so he established three tax stations in Hànzhōu to impose heavy levies,
Hànzhōu borders Dōngchuān to the southeast,
hence he set up three stations to tax salt merchants.
Merchants no longer went to Dōngchuān.
Zhī,
means to go.
11. The King of Chǔ, Mǎ Yīn, went to Yuèzhōu,
and sent Six Armies Commander Yuán Quán,
Deputy Commander Wáng Huán, and Supervisor Mǎ Xīzhān to lead the naval forces to attack Jīngnán.
Gāo Jìxīng met them with his naval forces.
They reached Liúláng Fú.
At Shā Bù in Shíshǒu County, Jiānglíng Prefecture, there is Liúláng Pǔ,
where the former ruler of Shǔ married a woman from Wú.
Fú,
read as fáng liù fān.
A swirling current is called fú.
At dawn the next day,
the two armies engaged in battle,
Mǎ Xīzhān maneuvered his warships to attack from the flank,
Gāo Jìxīng was heavily defeated,
with thousands captured or killed,
and they advanced to press on Jiānglíng.
Gāo Jìxīng requested peace,
and returned Shǐ Guāngxiàn to Chǔ.
Gāo Jìxīng captured Shǐ Guāngxiàn, see the previous year's entry above.
The King of Chǔ, Mǎ Yīn, reproached Wáng Huán for not taking the opportunity to seize Jīngnán,
Wáng Huán said:
"Jiānglíng lies between the Central Dynasty, Wú, and Shǔ,
the Central Dynasty,
refers to the Táng,
being in the Central Plains,
and also the Celestial Court.
It is surrounded by enemies on all sides,
making it a contested territory.
During the Sòng, Chancellor Zhào Pǔ advised Tàizǔ to delay taking Tàiyuán,
with the same intention.
Wáng Huán in every battle,
led from the front,
sharing hardships with his troops;
he often kept needles and medicine by his seat,
after battle,
he would summon the wounded before his tent,
and personally apply treatment.
Soldiers under Wáng Huán's command congratulated each other, saying:
'We have found a place to die.'
Therefore, wherever he went, he achieved success.
History shows that generals who win the utmost loyalty of their soldiers are victorious.
12. The state of Chǔ launched a large-scale naval attack against Hàn,
besieging Fēngzhōu.
Sòng Bái states: Fēngzhōu was originally Guǎngxìn County of Cāngwú Commandery under the Hàn dynasty,
the Liáng dynasty established Liángxìn Commandery there,
the Suí dynasty established Fēngzhōu,
located on the north bank of the Fēng River.
Encountering the "Dàyǒu" [omen],
the tortoise shell was used for divination,
the milfoil stalks for yarrow-stalk divination.
Using forty-nine stalks, they were randomly divided,
observing whether the resulting numbers were odd or even,
three transformations formed a single line,
eighteen transformations formed a complete hexagram.
[The ruler of Hàn] changed the reign era to Dàyǒu;
he ordered the Left and Right Street Commissioner Sū Zhāng to lead three thousand crossbowmen and one hundred warships to relieve Fēngzhōu.
The capital of Hàn was Pānyú,
modeled after the Tang dynasty's capital,
establishing Left and Right Street Commissioners.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: From Guǎngzhōu west to Fēngzhōu is six hundred and ten *lǐ*.
[Sū Zhāng] sank iron cables in the water,
constructing large winches on both banks to haul the cables,
and built a long embankment to conceal them,
hiding strong warriors within the embankment.
Zhāng engaged the enemy with light boats,
feigning defeat,
the Chǔ forces pursued him,
entering the area within the embankment;
[his men] turned the winches and raised the cables,
the Chǔ warships could neither advance nor retreat,
[Zhāng's forces] shot at them with powerful crossbows from both sides of the river,
the Chǔ troops were utterly defeated,
lifted the siege and fled.
The ruler of Hàn appointed Zhāng as the Tuánliànshǐ of Fēngzhōu.
13. In summer,
the fourth month,
[the emperor] appointed the Yèdū Liúshǒu Cóngróng as the Hé dōng Jiédùshǐ and Běidū Liúshǒu,
appointed the Guest Reception Commissioner Féng Bīn of Tàiyuán as Deputy Liúshǒu,
and appointed the Jiámǎ Zhǐhuīshǐ Yáng Sīquán of Xīnpíng as the Bùjūn Dūzhǐhuīshǐ to assist him.
On the Wùyín day,
[he] appointed the Xuānwǔ Jiédùshǐ Shí Jìngtáng as Yèdū Liúshǒu and Tiānxióng Jiédùshǐ,
adding the title of Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì;
appointed the Shūmìshǐ Fàn Yánguāng as Chéngdé Jiédùshǐ.
On the Bǐngxū day,
[he] appointed the Shūmìshǐ Ān Zhònghuì to concurrently serve as Hénán Yǐn,
appointed the Hénán Yǐn Cónghòu as Xuānwǔ Jiédùshǐ,
still in charge of the affairs of the Six Armies and various guard units.
Cónghòu was originally the Hénán Yǐn in charge of the affairs of the Six Armies and various guard units,
now he was transferred to the Biànzhōu garrison but remained in charge of the Six Armies and various guard units as before.
14. The Wú state's Right Xióngwǔ Army Commander Miáo Lín and Jìngjiāng Tǒngjūn Wáng Yànzhāng led a naval force of ten thousand to attack the Chǔ state's Yuèzhōu,
reaching Jūnshān.
Yuèzhōu administered Bālíng,
Dòngtíng Lake lies west of Bālíng,
Jūnshān is in Dòngtíng Lake,
measuring sixty *lǐ* square.
Déxūn said:
"The Wú forces caught us unprepared,
but upon seeing our main army,
they will certainly fear and flee."
He then secretly moved his army to Jiǎozǐ Lake,
ordering Wáng Huán to lead three hundred warships at night,
to cut off
the Wú army's retreat route.
At dawn,
the Wú forces advanced to Jīngjiāngkǒu,
intending to join forces with Jīngnán troops to attack Yuèzhōu.
On the Dīnghài day,
they reached Dàorénjī.
Déxūn ordered the Zhànzhào Dūyúhòu Zhān Xìn to take three hundred light boats and emerge behind the Wú army,
while Déxūn confronted them from the front with his main force,
attacking them from both sides,
the Wú army was utterly defeated,
and [Déxūn's forces] captured Lín and Yànzhāng and returned.
15. Earlier,
the Yìwǔ Jiédùshǐ and concurrently Zhōngshū Lìng Wáng Dū had governed Yìdìng for over ten years.
In the first year of the Liáng Emperor Jūndì's Lóngdé era,
Wáng Dū obtained Dìngzhōu,
making it nine years by this time.
All taxes and levies were used to support his own army.
When Ān Zhònghuì came to power,
he gradually used laws and regulations to restrain him;
the Emperor also despised Dū for usurping his father's position.
[He] despised him.
Wáng Dū imprisoned his father Chùzhí and usurped his position,
see the first year of the Later Liáng Emperor Jūndì's Lóngdé era in scroll 271.
Despise,
wū lù fān.
The imperial court stationed many troops between Yōu and Yì,
with major generals coming and going between Wǎqiáo and Lú
[lú]
Dū secretly made preparations against them,
gradually leading to suspicion and estrangement.
Dū feared the court would transfer him to another garrison,
his confidant Hé Zhāoxùn urged Dū to devise a plan for self-preservation,
so Dū sought a marriage alliance with the Lúlóng Jiédùshǐ Zhào Déjūn.
He also knew that the Chéngdé Jiédùshǐ Wáng Jiànlì had a rift with Ān Zhònghuì,
so he sent an envoy to form a sworn brotherhood with him,
secretly plotting with him to restore the old practices of Héběi,
wishing to restore the situation like in the Táng dynasty where the various Héběi garrisons were hereditary,
not paying tribute and taxes to the court,
not accepting conscription orders from the court.
Dū also sent sealed wax letters to the five commanders of Qīng, Xú, Lù, Yì, and Zǐ,
to sow discord among them.
At that time, the Qīng commander was Huò Yànwēi,
the Xú commander was Fáng Zhīwēn,
the Lù commander was Máo Zhāng,
the Yì commander was Mèng Zhīxiáng,
the Zǐ commander was Dǒng Zhāng,
all were stubborn and difficult to control.
Send,
wéi jì fān;
the following "jīn yí" is the same.
Sow discord,
gǔ xiàn fān.
Yànqiú did not comply;
[Dū] then sent gold to Yànqiú's tent,
to have him plot [against the court],
but it was unsuccessful;
on the Guǐsì day,
Yànqiú reported Dū's rebellious actions,
an edict ordered the Xuānhuīshǐ Zhāng Yánlǎng to discuss punitive measures with the northern generals.
The northern generals,
refers to the Zhāotǎoshǐ Wáng Yànqiú and the various generals under his command stationed between Yōu and Yì, as well as the Yōuzhōu commander Zhào Déjūn.
16. On the Wùxū day,
Wú transferred Prince Chángshān Měng to be Prince Línchuān.
17. On the Gēngzǐ day,
an edict was issued stripping Wáng Dū of his official titles and ranks.
On the Rényín day,
[the emperor] appointed Wáng Yànqiú as the Běimiàn Zhāotǎoshǐ,
acting administrator of Dìngzhōu Prefectural affairs,
appointed the Héng Hǎi Jiédùshǐ Ān Shěntōng as Deputy Zhāotǎoshǐ,
appointed the Zhèngzhōu Fángyùshǐ Zhāng Qiánzhāo as Dūjiān,
and mobilized troops from various circuits to jointly attack Dìngzhōu.
That day,
Yànqiú attacked Dìngzhōu,
capturing its northern gate city.
The acting administrator of Dìngzhōu Prefectural affairs:
because they had not yet taken Dìngzhōu city,
Wáng Yànqiú was made to act as administrator of prefectural affairs outside the city,
to pacify and recruit the people of Dìngzhōu.
It seems this order had not yet been issued,
when Yànqiú's troops had already reached the walls of Dìngzhōu.
Tūněi was the one who besieged Emperor Zhuāngzōng,
a fierce tribal chieftain.
Chieftain,
cí qiū fān.
Tūněi led ten thousand cavalry in a sudden charge into Dìngzhōu;
Yànqiú retreated to defend Qūyáng.
Qūyáng,
was Shàngqūyáng County in the Hàn dynasty,
the Suí dynasty changed it to Héngyáng;
the Táng dynasty renamed it Qūyáng in the fifteenth year of the Yuánhé era,
to avoid the personal name of Emperor Mùzōng,
and placed it under Dìngzhōu.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: The county is sixty *lǐ* west of the prefecture.
Yànqiú engaged him in battle at the foot of Jiāshān,
inflicting a major defeat,
Tūněi fled back to Dìngzhōu with two thousand cavalry.
Yànqiú pursued him to the city gate,
and then launched an attack,
capturing the western gate city.
Dìngzhōu's walls were strong,
and could not be taken by assault,
so Yànqiú reinforced and expanded the western gate city to serve as his headquarters,
establishing the Zhāotǎoshǐ's headquarters and the Dìngzhōu prefectural office in the western gate city.
The three prefectures,
are Dìng, Qí, and Yì.
Wáng Yànqiú's attack on Dìngzhōu,
aimed to wear it down through a protracted siege,
this was his predetermined strategy.
18. On the Xīnyǒu day,
[the emperor] appointed the Tiānxióng Jiédù Fùshǐ Zhào Jìngyí as Shūmìshǐ.
Wáng Yànqiú heard that the Khitan had dispatched troops to rescue Dìngzhōu,
so he led his main army towards Wàngdū,
sending Zhāng Yánlǎng to divide his forces and retreat to defend Xīnlè.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: Wàngdū County is located sixty *lǐ* northeast of Dìngzhōu,
and Xīnlè County is fifty *lǐ* southwest of the prefecture.
"Zhī" means
"to go."
In the early years of Tóngguāng,
the Northern Capital was established at Zhènzhōu,
with Zhènzhōu becoming Zhēndìng Prefecture.
Soon after, the Northern Capital was abolished, but Zhēndìng Prefecture remained.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: From Xīnlè County, it is seventy *lǐ* southwest to Zhēndìng.
The Khitan had already entered Dìngzhōu via another route,
and together with Wáng Dū, they launched a night attack on Xīnlè,
capturing it,
and killing Jiàn Fēng.
On the Yǐchǒu day,
Wáng Yànqiú and Zhāng Yánlǎng met at Xíngtáng.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: Xíngtáng County is located fifty-five *lǐ* north of Zhēndìng Prefecture.
On the Bǐngyín day,
they reached Qūyáng.
From Xíngtáng, it is about thirty *lǐ* northwest to Qūyáng.
Wáng Dū gathered all his forces and, together with five thousand Khitan cavalry, totaling over ten thousand men,
intercepted Yànqiú and others at Qūyáng.
On the Dīngmǎo day,
they fought south of the city.
Yànqiú assembled his generals and officers and ordered them:
"Wáng Dū is reckless and arrogant,
and can be captured in a single battle.
Today,
is the time for all of you to repay the state.
Discard all bows and arrows,
and attack them with short weapons.
Anyone who looks back will be executed!"
Thereupon, the cavalry advanced first,
brandishing whips and swinging swords,
charging straight into their formation,
and utterly defeated them,
with corpses covering the fields.
Using short weapons meant the officers and soldiers were all resolved to fight to the death;
charging straight into their formation meant the enemy had no time to resist.
What the northerners relied on were bows and arrows.
Once inside their formation,
these could not be used,
and wherever the whips and swords reached,
if not dead, they were wounded.
This is why they were so badly defeated.
"Zhuā"
is pronounced "zhuā."
"Jiāng"
is pronounced "jiāng."
"Chén"
is read as "zhèn."
The remaining troops fled north;
Wáng Dū and Tǔněi, with only a few riders,
barely escaped.
The Lúlóng military governor Zhào Déjūn intercepted and attacked the Khitan,
and those fleeing north were almost completely annihilated.
The state of Wú sent an envoy to seek peace with Chǔ,
requesting the return of Miáo Lín and Wáng Yànzhāng.
The King of Chǔ, Mǎ Yīn, returned them,
and had Xǔ Déxūn host a farewell banquet for them.
Déxūn said to the two men:
"Although the state of Chǔ is small,
its veteran ministers and seasoned generals are still present.
I hope the Wú court does not take this lightly.
You must wait until the young colts fight over the stable and manger,
and only then can you make plans."
At that time, Yīn had many favored concubines,
with no distinction between legitimate and illegitimate sons,
and his various sons were arrogant and extravagant.
This is why Déxūn spoke of this.
In the sixth month,
on the Xīnsì day,
Gāo Jìxīng again requested to become a vassal of Wú.
Xú Wēn of Wú discussed not accepting Gāo Jìxīng's submission as a vassal,
as seen in the previous volume from May of last year.
The Emperor ordered the King of Chǔ, Mǎ Yīn, to attack him.
Yīn sent Xǔ Déxūn to lead troops against Jīngnán,
with his son Xī Fàn as the army supervisor,
and they encamped at Shātóu.
Encamping at Shātóu
meant they were already pressing close to Jiānglíng.
Gāo Jìxīng requested a decisive challenge with Xī Fàn,
and the deputy commander Liào Kuāngqí went out to fight him,
and killed him by pulling him apart.
Jìxīng became fearful,
and the next day,
requested peace.
Déxūn then withdrew.
Kuāngqí
was from Gàn.
Wáng Yànqiú knew that Dìngzhōu was well-defended
and not easy to attack hastily.
Zhū Hóngzhāo and Zhāng Qiánzhāo publicly declared that the great general was timid;
an edict was issued urging him to attack the city.
Yànqiú had no choice,
and on the Yǐwèi day,
attacked,
resulting in three thousand casualties among his officers and soldiers.
Zhāng Qiánzhāo did not learn from the lesson of Dìngzhōu;
later, he urgently attacked Fèngxiáng,
leading to the defeat of the state,
and he himself became a captive.
His errors greatly harmed the state of Emperor Míngzōng.
Previously,
an edict had been issued to dispatch troops from Xīchuān to garrison Kuízhōu,
as a precaution against Gāo Jìxīng.
"Xiān"
is pronounced "xiān."
Shortly after,
Mèng Zhīxiáng memorialized,
"Kuí, Zhōng, and Wàn prefectures have already been pacified.
I request to recall the garrison troops,
to reduce the burden of transporting supplies."
Mèng Zhīxiáng feared that the garrison troops would be detained by Táng,
weakening himself,
hence he requested their recall.
Zhīxiáng secretly sent someone to lure them,
and Zhòng Wēi led his troops, clamoring, and fled back.
The Emperor ordered an investigation into their crime,
but Zhīxiáng requested and obtained their pardon.
This shows that the authority and orders of Táng did not extend into Shǔ.
The Shǎnzhōu military administrator Wáng Zōngshòu requested to bury the former Shǔ ruler Wáng Yǎn.
Wáng Yǎn died in Cháng'ān,
as seen in volume 274, year one.
"Shǎn"
is pronounced "shǎn."
In the seventh month,
Yǎn was posthumously honored as Duke Shùnzhèng,
and buried with the rites of a feudal lord.
Wáng Zōngshòu
was originally from a commoner family in Xǔzhōu.
Wáng Jiàn, because they shared the same surname,
adopted him as a son.
He served Wáng Yǎn,
and repeatedly offered straightforward remonstrance,
but Yǎn did not listen,
leading to the state's downfall.
After Yǎn's death,
Zōngshòu traveled east,
reaching Miǎnchí,
where he heard that Emperor Zhuāngzōng had been assassinated,
and fled into the Xióng'ěr Mountains.
At this time, he reappeared,
went to the capital,
and requested to bury Yǎn's clan.
The Emperor praised his loyalty,
and appointed him as the Bǎoyì military administrator.
He obtained eighteen coffins of Yǎn's clan,
and buried them at Sānzhàocūn south of Cháng'ān.
The northern expedition commander Ān Shěntōng died.
Under "expedition commander,"
there should be
"deputy"
written.
In the Eastern Capital, some people were found guilty of privately producing yeast,
and the留守 Kǒng Xún executed their entire clans.
Some requested to allow the people to make yeast,
and to collect five coins per *mǔ* in the autumn tax;
on the Jǐwèi day,
an edict was issued to follow this.
According to records, in early Táng, there was no law for monopolizing wine.
In the third year of Jiànzhōng under Emperor Dézōng, the monopoly on wine throughout the empire was first established,
with all wine required to be officially brewed,
each *hú* collected at three thousand cash,
and even if rice was cheap, it could not be reduced below two thousand;
prefectures and counties were entrusted to oversee this,
with varying penalties for thin wine or private brewing;
the capital was specially exempted from the monopoly.
In the sixth year of Yuánhé,
the capital prefecture memorialized that the wine monopoly money, aside from the official wine households,
would all be levied according to the two-tax system and the green shoots tax based on household registration.
An edict in the sixth year of Huìchāng stated:
"In eight circuits including Yángzhōu, establish yeast monopolies and set up official shops to sell wine,
in place of the common people paying the wine monopoly tax,
and use it to support military expenses.
Those who privately sell wine or produce yeast privately,
the punishment applies only to the individual."
At this time,
because Kǒng Xún had excessively implemented harsh laws,
an edict was issued:
"All households in villages of the three capitals, Yèdū, and various circuit prefectures and counties,
shall pay five full coins per *mǔ* on their summer and autumn crop fields as yeast money,
and are allowed to produce yeast and brew wine for their own households.
This money shall be collected along with the summer and autumn taxes,
and shall not be commuted.
In the capital and various circuit county towns, market boundaries, and border markets within passes and cities,
the official yeast and wine-selling households that operate annually
are permitted to produce their own yeast and brew wine for sale.
All yeast offices,
shall reduce the selling price by eight-tenths,
and shall not request further official capital for production."
"Qū"
is pronounced "qū."
On the 27th day, the Rénxū day,
the Khitan again sent their chieftain Tìyǐn leading seven thousand cavalry to rescue Dìngzhōu.
Wáng Yànqiú engaged them in battle north of the Táng River,
and inflicted a major defeat upon them.
On the Jiǎzǐ day,
he pursued them as far as Yìzhōu.
At that time, prolonged rain had caused the waters to rise,
and the number of Khitan soldiers captured, beheaded, drowned, or killed by the Táng forces
was beyond count.
On the 28th day, the Wùchén day,
Wáng Yánjūn, the Military Commissioner of Wēiwǔ, was appointed King of Mǐn.
The Khitan fled northward,
but the roads were muddy and treacherous,
and both men and horses were hungry and exhausted.
When they entered the territory of Yōuzhōu,
in the eighth month,
on the Rén
xū day,
Zhào Déjūn dispatched his officer Wǔ Cóngjiàn with elite cavalry to intercept them,
dividing his troops to secure the strategic passes.
They captured alive Tìyǐn and several hundred others;
the remaining troops scattered and fled into villages,
where the villagers attacked them with wooden clubs,
and only a few dozen managed to escape and return to their country.
From then on, the Khitan's morale was broken,
and they did not dare to lightly invade the frontier again.
Earlier,
when Emperor Zhuāngzōng campaigned in Héběi,
he captured a young boy,
who was raised in the palace.
When the boy grew up,
he was granted the surname and given name Lǐ Jìtáo.
After the current Emperor ascended the throne,
he was released and sent away.
Wáng Dū obtained him
and had him dressed in a yellow robe and seated atop the city wall,
saying, "This is the son of Emperor Zhuāngzōng,
who has already ascended the throne.
You, sir, received great favor from the previous dynasty;
have you no regard for it?"
Wáng Yànqiú was originally Dù Yànqiú.
After Emperor Zhuāngzōng destroyed the Liáng,
Yànqiú surrendered with his troops,
and Emperor Zhuāngzōng granted him a new surname and name and employed him.
Wáng Dū intended to use this to sway Yànqiú.
"What good does such a petty trick do you?
I will now teach you two strategies:
either gather all your forces for a decisive battle,
or surrender with your hands tied.
There is no other way to survive."
Wáng Jiànlì, being illiterate,
requested to be relieved of his position overseeing the Three Departments,
but his request was denied.
On the Yǐwèi day,
Wú declared a general amnesty.
The King of Wúyuè, Qián Liú, wished to appoint his middle son, Qián Chuánguàn, as his heir.
He said to his sons,
"Each of you speak of your merits,
and I will choose the one with the most to establish as heir."
He then petitioned to grant Chuánguàn two military commands.
In the intercalary month,
on the Dīngwèi day,
an edict appointed Chuánguàn as the Military Commissioner of Zhènhǎi and Zhèndōng.
On the Wùshēn day,
Zhào Déjūn presented the captured Khitan chieftain Tìyǐn and others.
All the generals requested their execution,
but the Emperor said,
"These are all brave commanders among the barbarians.
Killing them would extinguish the barbarians' hopes,
so it is better to spare them to alleviate border troubles."
He then pardoned Tìyǐn and fifty other chieftains
and placed them in the imperial guard.
Later Táng followed the system of the High Táng,
where during court assemblies, the guard of honor consisted of the Qīn, Xūn, and Yì guards.
This laid the groundwork for the Khitan's repeated requests for Tìyǐn and others.
The Khitan sent Méilǎo Jìsù and others to present tribute.
Earlier,
when Lú Wénjìn surrendered,
as recorded in the first year of the previous volume,
he was stationed in Píngzhōu,
and three hundred cavalry were sent to monitor him.
Zhāng Xīchóng was originally a scholar
and served as an officer in Yōuzhōu.
He was captured by the Khitan,
and the Khitan generals gradually trusted him.
He then plotted with his troops to return south.
His troops wept and said,
"Returning is something we never forget even in our sleep and meals,
but the barbarians are many, and we are few.
What can we do?"
Xīchóng said,
"I will lure their generals and kill them,
and their troops will surely disperse.
Their camp is over a thousand lǐ away;
by the time they realize and mobilize troops,
we will be far away."
The troops said,
"Good!"
They first dug a pit
and filled it with lime.
The next day,
they invited the barbarian generals to drink,
got them drunk,
and killed them along with their attendants,
throwing them into the pit.
Their camp was north of the city,
and they quickly dispatched troops to attack it.
These were Hàn troops.
Xīchóng led all his troops, over twenty thousand people, to flee south,
and an edict appointed him as the Prefect of Rǔzhōu.
The Queen Dowager of Wú passed away.
She was the mother of the Wú ruler, née Wáng.
In the ninth month,
on the Xīnsì day,
Jīngnán defeated the Chǔ troops at Báitián,
capturing the Chǔ Prefect of Yuèzhōu, Lǐ Tíngguī,
and sending him to Wú.
At that time, Jīngnán was a vassal of Wú.
On the Yǐwèi day,
an order was issued that Wēn Tāo, for excavating imperial tombs,
and Duàn Níng, for his treachery,
were to be granted death wherever they were.
Last year,
Wēn Tāo was exiled to Dézhōu,
and Duàn Níng was exiled to Liáozhōu.
On the Jǐhài day,
Fáng Zhīwēn, the Military Commissioner of Wǔníng, was appointed concurrently as the Campaign Commander of the Jīngnán Field Headquarters,
overseeing the affairs of the Jīngnán Field Administration.
Palace envoys were separately dispatched to mobilize troops from various circuits to Xiāngyáng
to campaign against Gāo Jìxīng.
Previously, Liú Xùn's campaign against Jīngnán had failed,
so they were now campaigning against it again.
On the Xīnchǒu day,
Dòu Tíngwǎn, the Defense Commissioner of Qìngzhōu, was transferred to be the Prefect of Jīnzhōu.
In winter,
in the tenth month,
Tíngwǎn occupied Qìngzhōu and defied orders.
On the Bǐngwǔ day,
Lǐ Cóngmǐn, the Military Commissioner of Hénghǎi, was appointed concurrently as the Deputy Campaign Commander of the Northern Field Headquarters,
replacing Ān Shěntōng.
He was the Emperor's nephew.
On the Wùshēn day,
an edict ordered Lǐ Jìngtōng, the Military Commissioner of Jìngnán,
to dispatch troops to campaign against Dòu Tíngwǎn.
Qìngzhōu was under the jurisdiction of the Jìngnán Army,
so he was ordered to campaign against it.
Wáng Dū occupied Dìngzhōu,
with strong defenses and strict surveillance.
Although the generals repeatedly plotted to open the city gates and respond to the imperial army,
none succeeded.
The Emperor sent an envoy to urge Wáng Yànqiú to attack the city.
Yànqiú rode alongside the envoy to inspect the city walls,
saying, "The walls are so high and steep
that even if the defenders allowed our troops to climb them,
they could not be reached by ladders or battering rams.
It would cause no harm to the enemy,
so why do this?
It is better to use the taxes from the three prefectures,
care for the people, and nourish the troops while waiting.
They will surely collapse from within."
The Emperor followed his advice.
In the art of war,
attacking a city is the most difficult.
However, there are two strategies for attacking a city: if the city has external reinforcements,
one must exert all efforts to attack swiftly to ensure its capture;
if the city has no external reinforcements,
one should prolong the siege to wear it down,
preserving one's own military strength while achieving complete victory.
Those skilled in the art of war in ancient times all knew this strategy.
In the eleventh month,
the officials requested the establishment of a temple for Emperor Āi,
and an edict ordered a temple to be built in Cáozhōu.
Huò Yánwēi, the Military Commissioner of Pínglú and Duke Zhōngwǔ of Jìn, passed away.
47. The prefect of Zhōngzhōu, Wáng Yǎ, captured Guīzhōu.
At that time, Zhōngzhōu belonged to the Níngjiāng Army of Kuízhōu,
under the command of Xīfāng Yè.
Guīzhōu at that time belonged to the Jīngnán Army,
under the command of Gāo Jìxīng.
48. On the gēngyín day,
the imperial prince Cónghòu married the daughter of Kǒng Xún.
Because of this, Xún was able to go to Dàliáng.
At that time, Kǒng Xún concurrently served as the liúshǒu of the Eastern Capital,
and the emperor was in Dàliáng.
"Was able to" means
was able to go.
Those with official duties are not allowed to leave their posts without authorization.
Now, Xún was able to go to the emperor's temporary residence because of the wedding ceremony.
"Was able to"
in some versions is written as
"was able to reach."
According to this, the Táng capital was Luòyáng,
with Dàliáng as the Eastern Capital.
Kǒng Xún's official duties were in the Eastern Capital,
but it is said that he was able to go to Dàliáng.
This is probably because Ān Zhònghuì was angry with Kǒng Xún,
who was transferred from the Shūmìyuàn to serve as the military governor of Zhōngwǔ and concurrently as the liúshǒu of the Eastern Capital.
At that time, the emperor was in Dàliáng,
and Xún had not yet taken up his post as liúshǒu.
Now, because of his daughter's marriage, he was able to go to the Eastern Capital.
This can be understood from the following text, which urges him to return to his garrison,
as is clear.
He requested to stay.
Ān Zhònghuì reported the matter in detail,
strongly opposing it.
After the ceremony was completed,
meaning the wedding ceremony was completed,
he returned to the Zhōngwǔ Army garrison.
49. On the jiǎwǔ day,
Wáng Jiànlì, the Zhōngshū Shìláng and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì, was appointed as Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì
and concurrently as the military governor of Pínglú.
50. On the bǐngshēn day,
the emperor asked Zhào Fèng:
"Why do emperors bestow iron certificates upon people?"
He replied:
"To make an oath with them,
so that their descendants may enjoy noble titles and emoluments for generations."
The emperor said:
"In the previous reign, only three people received this reward."
According to Xuē Jūzhèng's History of the Five Dynasties: On the jiǎyín day of the first month in the second year of Tóngguāng of Zhuāngzōng,
the emperor held court in the Zhōngxīng Hall,
and personally bestowed an iron certificate upon Guō Chóngtāo;
on the dīnghài day of the second month,
he bestowed an iron certificate upon Lǐ Sìyuán;
in the second year,
he bestowed upon Zhū Yǒuqiān the surname Lǐ and the personal name Jìlín,
enrolled him in the imperial clan register,
and bestowed an iron certificate upon him.
The extermination of their clans is recorded in the 274th scroll, first year.
"Cháo"
is pronounced zhí yáo fān.
The emperor was suspected and guarded against by Zhuāngzōng,
and was also troubled by slander.
The matter began in the 273rd scroll, in the third year of Tóngguāng, when he took the fine armor from Yèdū,
and ended in the 274th scroll, first year, when he left Yèdū and was in Wèi County.
Zhào Fèng said:
"If an emperor maintains great trustworthiness in his heart,
there is certainly no need to engrave it on metal or stone."
51. In the twelfth month,
on the jiǎchén day,
Lǐ Jìngzhōu reported the capture of Qìngzhōu,
and exterminated Dòu Tíngwǎn's clan.
52. The military governor of Jīngnán, Gāo Jìxīng, fell seriously ill.
He ordered his son, the xíngjūn sīmǎ, military governor of Zhōngyì, and Tóng Zhōngshū Ménxià Píngzhāngshì, Cónghuì, to temporarily take charge of the military government affairs.
On the bǐngchén day,
Jìxīng died.
Examination of discrepancies: The Veritable Records of Táng Míngzōng states:
"On the rénwǔ day of the eleventh month in the third year of Tiānchéng,
Fáng Zhīwēn reported that Gāo Jìxīng had died."
The Veritable Records of Lièzǔ also states
"in the second year of Qiánzhēn, eleventh month,
Jìxīng died."
This is probably an error in hearsay.
According to Táo Gǔ's "Stele Inscription for Jìxīng" and the "Bóhǎi Xíngnián Jì,"
both state
"he died on the fifteenth day of the twelfth month."
We follow this.
Gāo Cónghuì,
styled Zūnshèng,
was the eldest son of Jìxīng.
53. The history office compiler and editor Zhāng Zhāoyuǎn submitted a memorial:
"I have observed that in the previous reign,
the imperial brothers and princes all enjoyed entertainers,
indoors they adorned themselves with concubines,
outdoors they boasted of their servants and horses;
with such habits and customs,
how could they become virtuous!
This means by what means could they become virtuous men.
Now, the imperial prince should humble himself and treat them as teachers,
study the classics of ritual and righteousness,
and discuss the principles of safety and danger.
In ancient times, when a ruler ascended the throne, he would establish a crown prince,
in order to clarify the distinction between legitimate and illegitimate,
and block the source of calamity and disorder.
Now, regarding divination for an heir and establishing a crown prince,
I dare not lightly discuss.
However, in matters of bestowing favors and gifts,
and in occasions of marriage and visiting,
distinctions should be made between legitimate and illegitimate, elder and younger,
to demonstrate hierarchical authority,
and cut off their hopes of advancement."
The emperor praised and sighed at his words but could not employ them.
From the Kāipíng era of Liáng,
up to the Tiānchéng era,
only Zhāng Zhāoyuǎn's memorial was able to discuss current affairs based on learning.
Without Confucian scholars,
how can a state be maintained!
It is a pity that his words were not employed.
The history says he praised and sighed but could not employ them.
Alas!
The emperor's praise and sigh
were also because people at the time said Zhāng Zhāoyuǎn was a Confucian scholar, so he praised and sighed,
but how could he know that his words were deeply beneficial to the state!
54. The king of Mǐn, Wáng Yánjūn, exempted twenty thousand people from corvée to become monks,
hence there were many monks in Mǐn.
55. The military governor of Hédōng and liúshǒu of the Northern Capital, Cóngróng,
was young, arrogant, and stubborn,
and did not attend to government affairs.
The emperor sent attendants who had always been on good terms with Cóngróng to stay with him,
to gradually admonish and guide him.
One of them privately said to Cóngróng:
"The lord of Hénán is respectful, cautious, and fond of goodness,
personally treats upright scholars with courtesy,
and has the demeanor of maturity;
Cónghòu was then the yǐn of Hénán,
hence he was referred to as the lord of Hénán.
"Upright scholars" means
righteous scholars.
"Fond of"
is pronounced hǎo.
You should encourage yourself,
and not let your reputation fall below that of Hénán."
Cóngróng was displeased.
After retreating,
he told the infantry commander Yáng Sīquán:
"People in the court all praise Cónghòu and speak ill of me.
Am I to be deposed!"
Sīquán said:
"My lord, you hold strong troops in your hands,
and moreover, I, Sīquán, am here.
What is there to worry about!"
Thereupon, he advised Cóngróng to recruit more troops,
repair armor and weapons,
and secretly prepare for self-defense.
Observing Cóngróng's question and Yáng Sīquán's reply,
the means by which they sought self-preservation were precisely the means by which they endangered themselves.
"The ruler often praises the younger brother and suppresses the elder brother.
How can we not assist him!"
That person was afraid,
and reported it to the deputy liúshǒu Féng Bīn.
Bīn secretly memorialized it.
The emperor sent attendants to admonish and guide Cóngróng,
which shows that he secretly received the emperor's instructions and was most intimate.
Cóngróng's displeasure,
Yáng Sīquán's coercion,
all these circumstances,
that person should have secretly memorialized them.
How could he report it to Féng Bīn and wait for Bīn to memorialize it?
There must be twists and turns in this.
Because of Cóngróng,
he was also not punished.
The emperor did not punish Yáng Sīquán,
and later this became a calamity for Cónghòu.
However, the rift between the two sons had already formed.
Even if Sīquán were punished,
there would be nothing that could be done.
1. In spring,
first month,
Féng Bīn entered the court as Xuānhuīshǐ.
He said to those in power:
"Cóngróng is stubborn, eccentric, and frivolous.
A virtuous and weighty person should be selected to assist him."
2. Wáng Dū and Tūněi wanted to break through the siege and escape,
but could not get out.
In the second month,
on the guǐchǒu day,
the capital commander of Dìngzhōu, Mǎ Ràngnéng, opened the gates and let the government troops in.
Wáng Dū burned himself and his entire family,
and Tūněi and two thousand Khitan people were captured.
Wáng Yànqiú had been attacking Wáng Dū since the fourth month of last year,
and by now had conquered him.
On the xīnhài day,
Wáng Yànqiú was appointed as the military governor of Tiānpíng,
and both he and Zhào Déjūn were additionally given the title of concurrent Shìzhōng.
This rewarded Wáng Yànqiú
for his achievement in pacifying Wáng Dū;
it rewarded Zhào Déjūn
for capturing the Tìyǐn.
They were executed in the market.
3. The Shūmìshǐ Zhào Jìngyí died.
4. On the jiǎzǐ day,
the emperor departed from Dàliáng.
5 On the Dīngmǎo day,
the Menxià Shìláng and Tóng Píngzhāngshì Cuī Xié died at Xūshuǐ.
In the early Táng dynasty, Xūshuǐ County was established;
during the Zhēnguàn era, it was merged into Guǎnchéng County of Zhèng Prefecture.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Zhèng Prefecture's Xíngyáng County has a Xūshuǐ town.
Zú,
pronounced zǐ xù fān.
6 On the Gēngwǔ day,
the Emperor arrived at Luòyáng.
In the winter tenth month of the second year,
the Emperor went to Dàliáng,
and by now had returned to Luòyáng.
7 Wáng Yànqiú was at the walls of Dìng Prefecture,
daily feasting the soldiers with his private wealth,
and from the beginning of the attack until the city was taken, he never executed a single soldier.
In the third month,
on the Xīnsì day,
Yànqiú entered the court,
and the Emperor praised his achievements;
Yànqiú merely apologized for the long trouble of supply transport.
History records that Wáng Yànqiú had merit but did not boast.
8 The Emperor's son, the Right Guard Grand General Cóng Cǎn, had a stubborn nature.
Ān Zhònghuí was in power,
and Cóng Cǎn did not yield to him.
When the Emperor made an eastern tour,
that is, when he went to Dàliáng,
Cóng Cǎn feasted with guests at the Huìjié Garden.
The Huìjié Garden was within the walls of Luòyáng.
Zhāng Quányì had long governed Luò,
and his private residence was in the Huìjié ward.
Its halls, rooms, gardens, and ponds were the grandest of the time,
and he presented it to the government to become the Huìjié Garden.
Cóng Cǎn playfully ascended the imperial couch.
All imperial gardens had imperial couches,
for the emperor to use when visiting.
On the Bǐngxū day,
Cóng Cǎn was ordered to commit suicide.
9 The Héngshān barbarians raided Shào Prefecture.
Shào Prefecture
was Zhāolíng County in the Hàn,
belonging to the Chángshā Kingdom.
In the Eastern Hàn, it belonged to the Chángshā and Línglíng commanderies.
Also, Zhāolíng was changed to Zhāoyáng County.
The Wú established the Shàolíng commandery.
Emperor Wǔ of Jìn changed Zhāoyáng to Shàoyáng County.
The Suí abolished the commandery.
The Táng established Nánliáng Prefecture,
which was changed to Shào Prefecture.
At that time, it was within the territory of Chǔ.
10 The King of Chǔ, Mǎ Yīn, ordered his son, the Wǔ'ān military deputy commissioner and administrator of Chángshā prefectural government, Xīshēng, to oversee governmental affairs,
and to supervise all internal and external military matters.
From then on, state affairs first passed through Xīshēng
before being reported to Yīn.
Xīshēng,
styled Ruò Nè,
was Yīn's second son.
This sets the stage for the killing of Gāo Yù.
11 In summer,
the fourth month,
on the Gēngzǐ day, the first day of the month,
iron and tin coins were banned.
At that time, Húnán exclusively used tin coins.
One copper coin was worth a hundred tin coins.
They flowed into the central states,
and the law could not stop them.
When Mǎ Yīn gained Húnán,
he minted coins from tin,
originally for use within his territory,

The Wǔdài Huìyào states: In the third month of the second year of Tóngguāng, an edict said:
