Both books come from Wénbǎo,
yet they differ so greatly.
Considering that after Zhīgào ascended the throne,
if he wanted to eliminate Zhōu Běn,
he should have used various methods,
not needing such an approach.
Saying he poisoned Zhīxún is more plausible,
so we follow that.
35 Fèngguó military commissioner and administrator of Jiànzhōu, Wáng Yánbǐng, claimed illness and retired to his hometown residence,
requesting that Jiànzhōu be handed over to his son Jìxióng.
On the Gēngzǐ day,
an edict appointed Jìxióng as prefect of Jiànzhōu.
At that time, Wáng Yánbǐng, having together with Wáng Yánjūn assassinated their ruler Yánhàn,
possessed strong military power and heavy authority.
Moreover, Jiànzhōu was located upstream from Fúzhōu,
giving him a position to oppress Yánjūn.
Therefore, he no longer reported to Yánjūn but communicated directly with Luòyáng.
36 After Ān Chónghuì had stationed Lǐ Rénjǔ in Lángzhōu,
he sent him, along with Miánzhōu prefect Wǔ Qiānyù, to lead troops to their posts.
(To "go to one's post" means to proceed to the seat of administration.)
Rénjǔ was an old subordinate of the emperor
and a maternal cousin of Chónghuì.
Chónghuì ordered Rénjǔ to investigate signs of Dǒng Zhāng's rebellion,
and Rénjǔ embellished and reported them.
The court also sent Wǔxìn military commissioner Xià Lǔqí to repair the walls and moats of Suízhōu,
mend armor and weapons,
and increase garrison troops.
Zhāng was greatly alarmed.
At that time, rumors circulated on the roads
that Mián and Lóng would also be made into separate military prefectures,
and Mèng Zhīxiáng also became fearful.
(Splitting Láng and Suí into military prefectures was intended to control Dōngchuān,
hence Dǒng Zhāng's fear.)
Miánzhōu was close to Chéngdū,
and Lóngzhōu was also on the route Dèng Ài took to enter Shǔ.
Since Wǔ Qiānyù was already prefect of Miánzhōu,
this also indicated a trend toward establishing separate prefectures.
Added to the rumors,
Mèng Zhīxiáng also became fearful.
Previously, they had not communicated,
but now,
Zhāng sent an envoy to Chéngdū,
requesting to marry his son to Zhīxiáng's daughter.
Zhīxiáng agreed,
planning to join forces to resist the court.
(This sets the stage for the two Chuān regions joining forces to attack and capture Suí and Láng.)
Diàn Guǎngmíng punctuated, Niè Chóngqí proofread.
Sīmǎ Guāng
compiled by imperial command.
Later
student from Tiāntāi.
First year of Chángxīng (Gēngyín, 930) (The era name was changed in the second month of this year.)
1 In spring,
first month,
Dǒng Zhāng sent troops to build seven forts at Jiànmén.
On the Xīnsì day,
Mèng Zhīxiáng sent Zhào Jìliáng to Zǐzhōu to reestablish friendly relations.
Previously, Dǒng Zhāng in Dōngchuān
and Mèng Zhīxiáng in neighboring prefectures had not communicated;
in the third year of Tiānchéng,
the two prefectures had disputes over salt profits;
last year, Zhāng sent an envoy to seek marriage with Zhīxiáng's family,
and now Zhīxiáng sent a return envoy to reestablish friendly relations.
Both sides set aside grievances to pursue reconciliation,
fearing the court would send troops against them.
(When in the same boat encountering a storm, even Hú and Yuè will cooperate like left and right hands—
this is what it means.)
Ān Chónghuì was troubled by the difficulty of controlling the two Chuān regions,
but instead of exploiting their discord to set them against each other,
he actually brought them together.
Can this be considered good strategy for the state?
The *Art of War* says: When the enemy unites, find ways to divide them.
Ān Chónghuì did the opposite.
Hǎo (好)
is pronounced hū dào fān (呼到翻);
similarly below.
2 Hónglú Shǎoqīng Guō Zàihuī petitioned to cast large coins worth five thousand, three thousand, and one thousand;
the court considered his proposal to treat the imaginary as real,
ignorant and reckless talk,
and demoted him to Wèiwèi Shǎoqīng, tóngzhèng.
(This is what Táng officials called "extra appointment,
equivalent to regular position.")
3 Wú transferred Prince Chè of Píngyuán to become Prince of Déhuà.
(Déhuà County in Jiāngzhōu
was originally Hàn's Xúnyáng County.
Sòng Bái said: changed by Southern Táng.)
4 In the second month,
on the first day, Yǐwèi,
Zhào Jìliáng returned to Chéngdū
and said to Mèng Zhīxiáng:
"Lord Dǒng is greedy, cruel, and fond of winning,
ambitious but short-sighted in strategy,
and will ultimately be a problem for Xīchuān."
(The history records Zhào Jìliáng's words,
setting the stage for Dǒng Zhāng's attack on Mèng Zhīxiáng.)
Capital Commanders Lǐ Rénhǎn and Zhāng Yè wanted to host a banquet and invite Zhīxiáng.
Two days beforehand,
a nun reported that the two generals planned to harm Zhīxiáng on the banquet day.
Zhīxiáng interrogated them,
but found no evidence
(no evidence of plotting harm).
Jié (詰)
is pronounced qù jí fān (去吉翻).
On Dīngyǒu
, the first informants, army officers Dū Yánchāng and Wáng Xíngběn, were identified,
and executed by waist-cutting.
On Wùxū
, he attended the banquet,
dismissed all attendants,
and went alone to Rénhǎn's residence.
Rénhǎn kowtowed and said tearfully:
"This old soldier will only repay your virtue with utmost loyalty unto death."
From then on, all the generals became closely attached and submitted to him.
(The history shows that Mèng Zhīxiáng could open his heart to win people's utmost loyalty.)
5 On the Rénzǐ day,
Mèng Zhīxiáng and Dǒng Zhāng jointly submitted a memorial to the throne, stating:
"The two Chuān regions have heard that the court is establishing a military command in Lángzhōng,
and reinforcing troops in Mián and Suì.
There is no one who is not worried and fearful."
The establishment of a military command in Lángzhōng
refers to setting up the Bǎoníng Army in Láng Prefecture;
reinforcing troops in Mián and Suì
refers to Wǔ Qiányù being appointed as the prefect of Mián Prefecture,
and Xià Lǔqí commanding Suì Prefecture,
both of whom increased troops for defense.
These events are all recorded in the previous year's scroll.
6 On the Yǐmǎo day,
the emperor performed sacrifices at the Circular Mound,
granted a general amnesty,
and changed the era name.
The era name was changed to Chángxīng.
In the third month,
on the Rénshēn day,
an edict was issued to transfer Cóng Yǎn to serve as the military governor of Xuānwǔ.
In the first year of the Tiānchéng era,
Lǐ Cóng Yǎn was reappointed as the military governor of Fèngxiáng,
and was transferred to another command at this time.
7 On the Guǐyǒu day,
the ruler of Wú established Jiāngdū Prince Liǎn as the crown prince.
8 On the Bǐngzǐ day,
Zhū Hóngzhāo, the Commissioner of Palace Affairs, was appointed as the military governor of Fèngxiáng.
9 Kāng Fú reported the capture of Bǎojìng Garrison,
and the execution of Lǐ Kuāngbīn.
Lǐ Kuāngbīn's occupation of Bǎojìng Garrison is recorded in the previous year's scroll.
10 The Ānyì Army was restored as the Zhāoyì Army.
In the second year of the Lóngdé era of Liáng Emperor Jūn,
the Prince of Jìn changed the name of the Zhāoyì Army to Ānyì Army,
as recorded in scroll 271.
11 The emperor intended to establish Cáo Shū as empress,
but Shū said to Wáng Dé:
"I have long suffered from internal restlessness,
internal restlessness
refers to heat and restlessness in the chest.
Let my younger sister take my place."
Dé said:
"The position of empress is the counterpart to the supreme ruler,
who would dare to interfere!"
On the Gēngyín day,
Shū was established as empress.
Dé served the empress with respect and caution,
and the empress also showed compassion toward her.
Initially,
Wáng Dé gained advancement through Ān Zhònghuì,
and often felt indebted to him.
The Ouyáng History states: Dé, surnamed Wáng,
was the daughter of a pancake seller in Bīn Prefecture,
and was known for her beauty,
nicknamed "Huā Jiànxiū" (Flower Shyness).
In her youth, she was sold as a maidservant to the Liáng general Liú Xún.
After Xún's death,
Wáng had nowhere to go.
At that time, the emperor's principal wife, Lady Xià, had already passed away,
and he was seeking another consort.
Someone mentioned Wáng to Ān Zhònghuì,
who informed the emperor, and she was taken into the palace.
As the emperor remained in power for a long time,
palace expenditures gradually became extravagant,
and Zhònghuì often admonished him.
When the emperor took brocade from the outer treasury to make carpets,
Zhònghuì strongly remonstrated,
citing Empress Liú as a warning;
referring to Empress Liú of Zhuāngzōng.
12 Gāo Cóngxù sent an envoy to submit a memorial to Wú,
stating that his ancestral graves were in the Central Plains,
Gāo Jìxīng
was from Xiáshí, Shǎn Prefecture,
hence this statement.
Wú troops were unable to provide timely assistance,
so he declined and severed ties.
Gāo Jìxīng's request to submit to Wú
is recorded in scroll 275 of the second year of the Tiānchéng era.
It did not succeed.
13 Dǒng Zhāng feared that Wǔ Qiányù, the prefect of Mián Prefecture, might spy on his activities,
according to the Jiǔyù Zhì,
Mián Prefecture is 137 li southeast to Zǐ Prefecture.
Due to its proximity,
he feared being spied on.
In the fourth month,
on the first day, Jiǎwǔ,
he submitted a memorial appointing him as concurrent marching commander,
and imprisoned him in the prefectural court.
Using the concurrent marching commander appointment to lure him,
he was imprisoned upon arriving in Zǐ Prefecture.
The prefectural court
refers to the court of Dōngchuān.
14 Xuānwǔ military governor Fú Xí,
relying on his status as a veteran general,
Fú Xí was originally a general of Chéngdé,
and fought alongside Zhuāngzōng at Héshàng,
hence he considered himself a senior veteran.
Zhònghuì sought out his faults,
and reported them;
on the Dīngyǒu day,
an edict was issued for Fú Xí to retire as Grand Preceptor of the Crown Prince.
15 On the Wùxū day,
Mèng Zhīxiáng was additionally appointed as concurrent Secretariat Director,
and Xià Lǔqí as concurrent Vice Director of the Secretariat.
16 Initially,
when the emperor was in Zhēndìng,
in the second year of the Tóngguāng era of Zhuāngzōng,
the emperor governed Zhēndìng.
Cóng Kē assaulted Zhònghuì,
and Zhònghuì fled to avoid harm;
after sobering up,
Cóng Kē regretted and apologized,
but Zhònghuì never forgot the grudge.
By this time,
Zhònghuì was in power,
and even the imperial princes Cóng Róng and Cóng Hòu treated him with respect and caution.
"Bùxiá"
means not daring to be idle.
Zhònghuì repeatedly spoke ill of him to the emperor,
but the emperor did not listen.
Zhònghuì then falsely issued an imperial order to Yáng Yànwēn, the commander of the Hézhōng internal guards, to expel him.
"Hédōng"
should be
"Hézhōng."
Following the previous Wùxū day,
it is referred to as "this day."
Yànwēn led troops to close the gates and block him,
and Cóng Kē sent someone to knock on the gate and question him:
"I have treated you well,
why are you doing this?"
He replied:
"Yànwēn does not dare to betray your kindness,
but is acting on an order from the Bureau of Military Affairs."
The Bureau of Military Affairs used "xuān" (proclamations),
while the Three Departments used "tángtiě" (hall notices).
Today, "tángtiě" is called "shěngzhá" (departmental notes),
and "xuān" is called "mìzhá" (secret notes).
Cóng Kē stopped at Yúxiāng,
according to the Jiǔyù Zhì: Yúxiāng County is 60 li east of Hézhōng Prefecture.
When the envoy arrived,
on the Rényín day,
the emperor asked Zhònghuì:
"How could Yànwēn say such a thing?"
Referring to his claim of acting on an order from the Bureau of Military Affairs.
"This is the false words of a treacherous person,
and he should be swiftly punished."
The emperor was suspicious,
and wanted to lure Yànwēn to interrogate him about the matter,
"xùn"
means to question.
"Yòu,"
pronounced yǒu.
Zhònghuì insisted on sending troops to attack him,
so the emperor ordered Suǒ Zìtōng, the Western Capital garrison commander,
and Yào Yànchóu, the infantry commander, to lead troops against him.
Yào
is a surname,
and there was a Yào Sōng in the Hàn dynasty.
According to the Old History of the Five Dynasties: Yào Yànchóu
was from the three tribes of the Shatuo,
and was certainly not a descendant of Sōng.
The emperor wanted to interrogate him in person.
He summoned Cóng Kē to Luòyáng.
Cóng Kē knew he had been framed by Zhònghuì,
and rushed to the capital to clear his name.
17 Ān Zhònghuì was additionally appointed as concurrent Secretariat Director.
18 When Lǐ Cóng Kē arrived in Luòyáng,
the emperor reprimanded him and ordered him to return to his residence,
cutting off his court attendance privileges.
The Old History of the Five Dynasties states: He returned to his residence in Qīnghuà Lane.
On the Xīnhài day,
Suǒ Zìtōng and others captured Hézhōng,
executed Yáng Yànwēn,
following Ān Zhònghuì's instructions,
executing Yáng Yànwēn to silence him.
This set the stage for Prince Lù's later execution of Yào Yànchóu and Suǒ Zìtōng's suicide by drowning.
On the Guǐchǒu day,
his head was delivered as an offering.
The emperor was angry that Yào Yànchóu had not captured him alive,
referring to not capturing Yáng Yànwēn alive.
An Zhònghuì hinted to Féng Dào and Zhào Fèng to memorialize that Cóng Kē had failed in his defense,
and should be punished.
The Emperor said:
"My son has been undermined by treacherous factions;
the rights and wrongs are not yet clear.
Why do you gentlemen make such statements?
Do you intend not to let him remain among the living?
These are not your own intentions."
He meant that the two men were acting under An Zhònghuì's instigation.
Another day,
Zhào Fèng spoke of it again,
but the Emperor did not respond.
The next day,
Zhònghuì himself spoke of it.
The Emperor said:
"In the past, when I was a minor officer,
my family was poor,
and I relied on this child collecting horse dung to support himself,
until today I became the Son of Heaven.
Can I not even protect him now?
How do you wish to deal with him so that it is convenient for you?"
The Emperor also used these words to provoke An Zhònghuì.
(Note on pronunciation: 處, read as chǔ.)
"Between Your Majesty and your son,
how dare I speak!
It is only for Your Majesty to decide!"
The Emperor said:
"Letting him live idly in his private residence is also acceptable;
what need is there to say more!"
On Bǐngchén,
Suǒ Zìtōng was appointed as military governor of Hézhōng.
Upon arriving at his post,
Zìtōng, following Zhònghuì's instructions,
inventoried the armor and weapons in the military headquarters and reported the numbers upwards,
claiming they were privately manufactured by Cóng Kē.
Thanks to Wáng Déjué's protection from within,
Cóng Kē thereby escaped punishment.
Scholar-officials did not dare to associate with Cóng Kē;
only Lǚ Qí, a Vice Director of the Ministry of Rites and compiler at the Historiography Institute, whose residence was nearby,
occasionally went to visit him.
Whenever Cóng Kē had a petition or request,
he would consult Qí before acting.
(Comment: When Cóng Kē was living in idleness, he consulted Lǚ Qí before submitting petitions; yet when he was on the throne, he treated Qí generously but did not employ him. Why?)
On Wùwǔ,
the Emperor added the honorific title "Sagely Enlightened, Divinely Martial, Cultured and Virtuous, Reverent and Filial Emperor."
An Zhònghuì reported that Zhāoyì military governor Wáng Jiànlì, while passing through Wèi Prefecture, had made statements that stirred the masses.
In the fifth month, on Bǐngyín,
an edict ordered him to retire as Grand Mentor.
(Note: The enmity between An Zhònghuì and Wáng Jiànlì is recorded in the third year of Tiānchéng in the previous scroll.)
Dǒng Zhāng reviewed and assembled militia troops,
having them all cut their hair and tattoo their faces.
He also established Yǒngdìng Pass north of Jiànmén,
arranging beacon fires.
Mèng Zhīxiáng repeatedly petitioned requesting that the thirteen salt inspectorates including Yún'ān be placed under Xīchuān's jurisdiction.

(Note: Yún'ān County was the location of the ancient Qúrǔn County of Bā Commandery in the Hàn dynasty. Emperor Wǔ of the Zhōu dynasty changed it to Yún'ān County, belonging to Bādōng Commandery. In the Táng, it was under Kuí Prefecture, later changed to Yún'ān Inspectorate. Also, Dàchāng County in Kuí Prefecture and the Yúyáng Inspectorate in Nánpǔ County of Wàn Prefecture both had salt officials, subordinate to the patrol jurisdiction of Níngjiāng Army. The exact locations of the so-called thirteen inspectorates are unknown.)
On Xīnmǎo,
this was granted.
In the sixth month, on Guǐsì, the first day,
there was a solar eclipse.
On Xīnhài,
an edict decreed that from now on, defensive commissioners, training commissioners, prefects, army supervisors, and deputy military governors must all be appointed by the court;
the various circuits may not recommend candidates.
Dǒng Zhāng sent troops to raid the garrisons of Suí and Làng.
In autumn, the seventh month, on Wùchén,
the two Chuān regions, because the court continued to station troops in Suí and Làng,
submitted further memorials of protest.
From then on, few merchants from the northeast dared to enter Shǔ.
In the eighth month, on Yǐwèi,

Pěngshèng Army commander Lǐ Xíngdé (Note: According to the Wǔdài Huìyào, in the first year of Yīngshùn, the forty commands of Lóngwǔ and Shénwǔ were changed to the Left and Right Pěngshèng Armies. Based on this, the Pěngshèng Army already existed by this time. Sòng Bái said: In the third year of Chángxīng, the forty commands of Lóngwǔ and Shénwǔ in the capital were changed to the Left and Right Pěngshèng Armies.)
and Ten Gates Arrangement commander Zhāng Qiān (Note: The Ten Gates Arrangement was established in the third year of Tiānchéng, with ten gates in the capital, each under a commander.)
along with others, reported that deputy commander of the Pěngshèng Army Yáo Yánwēn had received secret orders from An Zhònghuì, saying,
"An Zhònghuì is mobilizing troops, claiming he intends to personally campaign against Huáinán."
(They used the fact that An Zhònghuì had once proposed an expedition against Wú in the second year of Tiānchéng to falsely accuse him.)
The Emperor questioned Imperial Guard Commander-in-Chief Ān Cóngjìn and Yào Yǎnchóu.
The two said:
"This is a villain attempting to sow discord between Your Majesty and your meritorious old ministers.

Zhònghuì has served Your Majesty for thirty years (Note: In the second year of Zhēnmíng under Liáng Emperor Jūn, the Emperor first became military governor of Ānguó, appointing An Zhònghuì as his inner gate officer. By this time, it was only sixteen years. Probably because the Emperor and Zhònghuì were both from Yìng Prefecture, they had been associated for a long time.)
Why would he trouble himself to plot rebellion?
We request to guarantee him with our clans."
The Emperor then executed Yánwēn,
summoned Zhònghuì to console and reassure him,
and ruler and minister wept together.
(Comment: By this time, An Zhònghuì's situation was already precarious.)
Former Zhōngwǔ military governor Zhāng Yánlǎng was appointed as Acting Minister of Works,
filling the post of Three Departments Commissioner.

(The title Three Departments Commissioner began from this time. From then until before Xīníng of the Sòng dynasty, the Three Departments Commissioner ranked just below the chief ministers, exclusively controlled state finances, and held heavy authority and responsibility.)

In Wú, Xú Zhīgào, because Hǎi Prefecture commander Wáng Chuánzhěng had a formidable reputation and won the troops' hearts, and as training commissioner Chén Xuān was being dismissed and returning, promised to let Chuánzhěng replace him.
But later he sent Xuān back to Hǎi Prefecture and summoned Chuánzhěng back to Jiāngdū.
Chuánzhěng was angry, thinking Xuān had slandered him.
On Jǐhài,
leading his subordinates to bid farewell to Xuān,
he beheaded Xuān,
set fire to and plundered the city walls,
and led his five thousand troops to surrender.
Zhīgào said:
"This is my fault."
He spared Chuánzhěng's wife and children.
Liánshuǐ military commissioner Wáng Yán led troops into Hǎi Prefecture (Note: Liánshuǐ to Hǎi Prefecture is 180 lǐ.)
and took charge of Hǎi Prefecture.
Chuánzhěng was the son of Wǎn. (Note: Wú had previously appointed Wáng Wǎn to administer Hǎi Prefecture. When Yáng Lóngyǎn established the state, he was promoted to General Who Guards the East.)
Chuánzhěng sent a secret messenger with a letter to Guāng Prefecture.
The messenger was captured and reported,
and he then requested to retire and return.
(Because his nephew had rebelled and he himself was stationed in a border commandery, his position and intentions were precarious and suspect, hence he requested to retire.)
At that time, power lay with the Xú family,
and those commanding troops and guarding the palace were particularly difficult to select.
Zhīgào considered the messenger稳重厚道 and cautious and meticulous,
so he employed him.
On Rényín,
Zhào Fèng memorialized:
"I have privately heard that recently there have been villains falsely accusing great ministers, shaking the pillars of the state, and the punishment has not been fully carried out."
(Meaning they had not been fully executed.)
They were all executed along with their clans.
The Emperor's son Cóng Róng was enfeoffed as Prince of Qín;
on Bǐngchén,
Cóng Hòu was enfeoffed as Prince of Sòng.
31. Dǒng Zhāng's son Dǒng Guāngyè served as Commissioner of the Palace Gardens,
residing in Luòyáng.
Zhāng wrote him a letter saying:
"The court has severed our subordinate prefectures to establish military governors,
appointing Xià Lǔqí to govern Suízhōu,
Lǐ Rénjǔ to govern Lángzhōu,
and it is also rumored that Miánzhōu and Lóngzhōu will be severed.
This means they are certain to kill me.
You must speak on my behalf when you see the key officials:
'Key officials'
refers to the two Bureau of Military Affairs Commissioners.
Dǒng Zhāng's intention specifically pointed to Ān Zhònghuì.
'For'
is pronounced wèi.
I will certainly rebel!
This is my farewell to you."
Guāngyè showed the letter to Bureau of Military Affairs Recipient of Edicts Lǐ Quánhuī.
Not long after,
the court also dispatched another general, Xún Xiányì, to lead troops to garrison Lángzhōu.
Guāngyè said to Quánhuī:
"Before these troops arrive,
my father will certainly rebel.
I dare not cherish myself,
meaning he dares not cherish his own life.
He means he fears military action will be necessary.
'Transfer'
is pronounced tiáo.
My father assures there is no other way."
Quánhuī reported this to Ān Zhònghuì,
but Zhònghuì did not heed it.
When Zhāng heard of this,
he rebelled.
The three military governors of Lìzhōu, Lángzhōu, and Suízhōu reported this to the court,
the Lìzhōu governor being Lǐ Yànqí,
the Lángzhōu governor Lǐ Rénjǔ,
and the Suízhōu governor Xià Lǔqí.
Zhònghuì said:
"Your subject has long known it would come to this,
but Your Majesty has tolerated it and not launched a punitive campaign."
The Emperor said:
"I do not betray others;
if others betray me, then I will campaign against them."
32. In the ninth month,
on the guǐhài day,
the Western Chuān advance memorials official Sū Yuàn informed Mèng Zhīxiáng:
"The court intends to mobilize a large army to campaign against the two Chuān regions."
The advance memorials official was in the capital,
hence he reported this matter to his commander.
Jì Liáng suggested first using Eastern Chuān troops to capture Suízhōu and Lángzhōu,
then combining forces to defend Jiànmén,
so that even if the imperial army comes,
we would have no worries about threats from within.
If the two Chuān regions unite in heart and strength to defend the strategic passes,
then Western Chuān would have no worries about threats from within.
They sent an envoy to arrange with Dǒng Zhāng to raise troops together.
Zhāng issued a moving proclamation to the three military governors of Lìzhōu, Lángzhōu, and Suízhōu,
enumerating their acts of sowing discord with the court,
and led troops to attack Lángzhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: From Zǐzhōu northeast to Lángzhōu is 309 lǐ.
On the gēngwǔ day,
Zhīxiáng appointed Capital Commandant Lǐ Rénhǎn as Field Headquarters Commander-in-Chief,
with Hànzhōu Prefect Zhào Tíngyǐn as his deputy,
and Jiǎnzhōu Prefect Zhāng Yè as Vanguard Commandant,
leading 30,000 troops to attack Suízhōu;
the Jiǔyù Zhì states: From Suízhōu north to Zǐzhōu is 205 lǐ.
33. Ān Zhònghuì had long monopolized great power,
and those at court and beyond who hated him were many;
Wáng Déjí and the Military Virtue Commissioner Mèng Hànqióng gradually gained influence,
and repeatedly spoke ill of Zhònghuì before the Emperor.
Zhònghuì was inwardly anxious and fearful,
and submitted a memorial requesting to be relieved of his duties.
The Emperor said:
"I have no estrangement from you,
and those who slandered you I have already executed,
referring to Lǐ Xíngdé and Zhāng Jiǎn.
On the jiǎxū day,
Zhònghuì again memorialized in person, saying:
"Your subject, from cold and humble origins,
attained this position,
yet was suddenly falsely accused by others of rebellion.

"My younger brother has such intentions,
I have no regrets,
but how can I face the late king underground!"
The late king refers to Xú Wēn.
37. On the day Xīnchǒu,
Fàn Yánguāng, the Bureau of Military Affairs Commissioner, was additionally appointed Co-Director of the Chancellery.
38. On the day Xīnhài,
an edict was issued to release the falcons and hawks of the Five Offices,
and no more were to be presented from inside or outside the palace.
Féng Dào said:
"Your Majesty's benevolence extends even to birds and beasts."
The Emperor said:
"Not so.
In the past, I once accompanied Emperor Wǔ on a hunt.
Emperor Wǔ is the posthumous title of Jìn Prince Lǐ Kèyòng.
A beast fled into a field,
and cavalry were sent to capture it.
By the time the beast was caught,
little of the crops remained.
Reflecting on this,
hunting brings more harm than benefit,
so I do not engage in it."
39. In winter,
the tenth month,
on the day Dīngmǎo,
Lǐ Jìntáng, Commanding Officer of Yángzhōu, attacked Tōngzhōu and captured it.
From Yángzhōu southeast to Tōngzhōu is 739 li.
Previously,
the Shǔ people had once taken Tōngzhōu,
so now they attacked and recaptured it.
In the second year of Qiándé of Sòng, Tōngzhōu was renamed Dázhōu,
because there was already a Tōngzhōu in Huáinán.
40. On the day Rénwǔ,
Wáng Yánzhèng was appointed Prefect of Jiànzhōu.
41. In the eleventh month,
on the day Jiǎshēn, the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
42. On the day Guǐsì,
Sū Yuàn arrived at Chéngdū.
Mèng Zhīxiáng heard that his nephews and other relatives at the court were all safe and sound,
so he sent an envoy to inform Dǒng Zhāng,
wishing to submit a memorial with him to express remorse.
Zhāng angrily said:
"Lord Mèng's relatives are all intact,
so of course he should submit.
But my clan has been exterminated,
referring to the court's execution of his son Dǒng Guāngyè and his family.
The imperial edict was all in Sū Yuàn's belly;
how could Liú Chéng have known beforehand?
How could Zhāng not know this!"
Thus, they became enemies again.
This sets the stage for Dǒng Zhāng's attack on Xīchuān and his subsequent defeat and death.
Again,
pronounced fù.
43. On the day Yǐwèi,
Lǐ Rénhǎn led his troops back to Chéngdū from Kuízhōu.
Since Mèng Zhīxiáng had already obtained all the territory of the former Shǔ's Kuí and Qián,
he did not expand eastward further.
44. Xú Zhīgào, Secretariat Director of Wú, submitted a memorial stating that he had assisted in governance for many years
and requested to retire to Jīnlíng in his old age.
Thus, Zhīgào was appointed Military Commissioner of Zhènhǎi and Níngguó,
stationed at Jīnlíng,
with his other official positions remaining as before,
overseeing court administration following the precedent of Xú Wēn.
Xú Wēn had first been stationed at Jīngkǒu,
overseeing the administration of the Wú court,
and later moved to Jīnlíng.
Court,
pronounced cháo.
He was put in charge of all military affairs inside and outside, left and right,
and remained at Jiāngdū to assist in governance.
Xú Zhīgào followed Xú Wēn's path,
and Jǐngtōng followed Zhīgào's path.
From this point, the Wú throne began to shift to the Lǐ family.
He was additionally appointed Vice Director of the Chancellery,
with Sòng Qíqiū made Vice Director of the Right,
and concurrently Vice Director of the Secretariat,
both serving as Co-Directors of the Chancellery,
and concurrently Commissioner of the Palace Bureau,
to assist Jǐngtōng.
Déshèng Military Commissioner Zhāng Chóng was enfeoffed as the Prince of Qīnghé.
Wú established the Déshèng Army in Lúzhōu.
The people of the prefecture suffered greatly from him.
He frequently went to court,
lavishly bribing influential officials,
thus often managing to return to his post.
He plagued Lúzhōu for over twenty years.
45. In the twelfth month,
on the day Jiǎyín, the first day of the month,
it was first permitted for the common people to cast their own farming tools and miscellaneous ironware.
According to the Old History of the Five Dynasties, miscellaneous ironware refers to cooking utensils and various implements.
Wrought iron was also allowed to be smelted by the people themselves.
Xú Wúdǎng said: The tax on farming tools money
continues to this day.
In summer and autumn, three coins are levied for farming tools.
46. Mǎ Xīshēng, Military Commissioner of Wǔ'ān and Jìngjiāng, heard that Emperor Tàizǔ of Liáng was fond of eating chicken
and admired this.
After succeeding to the position,
he had fifty chickens killed daily for his meals;
during the mourning period, he showed no grief.
On the day Gēngshēn,
King Wǔmù was buried at Héngyáng.
Mǎ Yīn was posthumously titled King Wǔmù.
Héngyáng was originally Zhēngyáng County of Hàn.
Wú established Línzhēng County separately.
Suí changed Línzhēng County to Héngyáng County.
In Táng, it belonged to Héngzhōu and was the seat of administration.
He ate several plates of chicken in one sitting.
Pān Qǐ, former Vice Director of the Ministry of Personnel, mocked him, saying:
"In the past, Ruǎn Jí ate steamed pork while in mourning.
Jìn's Ruǎn Jí was unrestrained by nature but extremely filial.
When his mother died,
before the burial,
he ate a steamed suckling pig,
drank two dou of wine,
and then went to bid farewell,
directly saying
'All is finished!'
He let out a cry,
vomited several sheng of blood,
became emaciated to the bone,
nearly perishing.
However, this cannot be taken as an example."
47. On the day Guǐhài,
Xú Zhīgào arrived at Jīnlíng.
48. Zhào Tíngyǐn, Acting Military Commissioner of Zhāowǔ, reported to Mèng Zhīxiáng that the walls and moats of Lìzhōu were complete.
Recently, at Jiànzhōu, he had shared merit with Li Zhào, Commander of the Palace Guard.
As recorded in the eleventh month of the previous year.
Zhīxiáng praised and instructed him,
but did not grant permission;
Tíngyǐn declined three times.
On the day Guǐyǒu,
Zhīxiáng summoned Tíngyǐn back to Chéngdū
and replaced him with Li Zhào.
49. Chén Shǒuyuán and others of Mǐn, claiming the command of the Bǎohuáng,
said to King Yánjūn of Mǐn:
"If you can abdicate and receive the Dao,
you will be emperor for sixty years."
Yánjūn believed this.
On the day Bǐngzǐ,
he ordered his son, Deputy Military Commissioner Jìpéng, to temporarily take charge of military and administrative affairs.
Yánjūn abdicated to receive the register,
taking the Daoist name Xuánxī.
In Āizhōu, General Yáng Tíngyì had 3,000 adopted sons,
plotting to recapture Jiāozhōu.
The Southern Hàn general guarding Jiāozhōu, Lǐ Jìn, knew of this,
accepted his bribes,
and did not report it.
That year,
Tíngyì raised troops and besieged Jiāozhōu.
The Old Book of Táng: Treatise on Geography states: From Jiāozhōu west to the boundary of Āizhōu at the mouth of the Xiǎohuáng River,
the water route is 416 lǐ.
(The Hàn court) sent troops to relieve it,
but before they arrived,
the city fell.
Jìn fled back,
and the Hàn ruler executed him.
(General) Bǎo besieged Jiāozhōu,
Tíngyì came out to fight,
and Bǎo was defeated and died.
Last year, Hàn captured Jiāozhōu,
now they lost it again.
1 Spring,
first month,
Privy Councilor Fàn Yánguāng said:
"From Língzhōu to Fāngqú Town in Bīnzhōu,
Sòng Bái said: Tōngyuǎn Army was originally Fāngqú Town of Língzhōu.
In the fourth year of Tiānfú of Jìn, it was changed to Wēizhōu.
Mùbō and Mǎlǐng towns were also placed under its jurisdiction.
In the second year of Guǎngshùn of Zhōu, it was changed to Huánzhōu to avoid a taboo name.
In the fourth year of Xiǎndé, it was downgraded to Tōngyuǎn Army.
I request to send troops to attack them."
Jǐchǒu,
sent Yào Yànchóu, Jìngnán Military Commissioner, and Kāng Fú, former Shuòfāng Military Commissioner, to lead 7,000 infantry and cavalry to campaign against the Dǎngxiàng.
2 Yǐwèi,
Mèng Zhīxiáng's wife, the Elder Princess Fúqìng, died.
Ouyáng's History: In the autumn of the first year of Chángxīng,
Zhīxiáng's wife, Elder Princess Qiónghuá, was renamed Elder Princess Fúqìng.
Elder,
read zhǎng.
3 Mèng Zhīxiáng, considering the court's grace and favor were generous,
but Dǒng Zhāng blocked the road through Miánzhōu,
preventing the sending of envoys to express gratitude—
the route from Chéngdū to Jiànzhōu and Lìzhōu
passed through Miánzhōu.
Blocked,
read sāi.
Wanted to send an envoy via the Xiá River to present a memorial.
His secretary, Lǐ Hào, said:
"If you, sir, do not consult with Dōngchuān (Dǒng Zhāng) and send an envoy alone,
then in the future, the blame for breaking the agreement will fall on us."
So he again sent an envoy to speak with him,
but Zhāng did not comply.
Second month,
Zhào Jìliáng and the generals discussed sending Gāo Yànchóu of Tàiyuán, the Military Inspector of Zhāowǔ, to lead troops to attack and capture Bìzhōu.
Old Book of Táng: Treatise on Geography: Nuòshuǐ County of Bìzhōu
was Xuānhàn County of Later Hàn.
Liáng divided Xuānhàn to establish Shǐníng County.
Northern Wèi divided Shǐníng to establish Nuòshuǐ County.
In the early Wǔdé period of Táng, Bìzhōu was established by dividing Shǐníng of Bādōng,
governing Nuòshuǐ.
Sòng abolished Bìzhōu,
incorporating its territory into Zēngkǒu and Tōngjiāng counties of Bāzhōu.
The prefectures behind the mountains,
refer to Bā, Péng, Guǒ, etc.
Lǐ Hào said:
"The court sent Sū Yuàn and others back west,
and we have not yet sent a memorial of thanks.
Now if we send troops to invade,
unless you, sir, care nothing for your ancestral graves and your nephews—
Mèng Zhīxiáng's ancestral graves were in Lónggāng County of Xíngzhōu,
and his nephews were serving at court at the time.
What use is Bìzhōu to you!"
Zhīxiáng then stopped.
Jìliáng from then on disliked Hào.
4 Xīnwèi,
for the first time ordered the Directorate of Education to collate and finalize the Nine Classics,
carve printing blocks, and sell them.
The printing and selling of the Nine Classics began here.
5 Yào Yànchóu and others reported defeating nineteen Dǎngxiàng tribes,
capturing 2,700 people.
6 Enfeoffed Gāo Cónghuì as the Prince of Bóhǎi.
7 Wú's Xú Zhīgào built a Lǐxián Academy at his official residence,
built it at his official residence in Jīnlíng.
To receive scholars and officials,
and discuss current affairs with Sūn Chéng and Chén Jué of Hǎilíng.
8 Mèng Zhīxiáng sent envoys three times to persuade Dǒng Zhāng,
saying that the sovereign had shown courtesy to the two Chuāns,
and if they did not submit memorials acknowledging their fault,
they might face another punitive campaign.
Zhāng did not comply.
Third month,
Xīnchǒu,
sent Lǐ Hào to Zǐzhōu,
to exhaustively explain the advantages and disadvantages.
Zhāng saw Hào,
cursed angrily,
and did not agree.
Hào returned,
and said to Zhīxiáng:
"Zhāng is unwilling to discuss plans,
unwilling to discuss plans,
like people today saying 'won't allow discussion'.
You, sir, should prepare for him."
9 Jiǎchén,
the King of Mǐn, Wáng Yánjūn, resumed his position.
Wáng Yánjūn had abdicated to receive the registers,
see last year.
10 The Martial and Succoring King of Wúyuè, Qián Liú, was ill.
He said to his officers and officials:
"My illness will certainly be fatal.
All my sons are foolish and weak.
Who can be the commander?"
The crowd wept and said:
"The Lord of the Two Commands (Qián Chuànguàn) is benevolent, filial, and has achieved merit.
Who does not love and support him!"
In the third year of Tiānchéng, Qián Liú conferred the two commands upon Chuànguàn,
the matter is seen in the previous scroll.
According to this year's autumn,
the court then added to Chuànguàn the title of Zhōngshū Lìng.
His subordinates prematurely addressed him as such.
Seal,
refers to the seal of the Wúyuè state and the seals of Zhènhǎi and Zhèndōng.
Keys,
refer to the tallies and keys of the various gates of the inner and outer city walls and the palace gates.
"Since the officers and officials recommend you,
you should guard them well."
He also said:
"My descendants must serve the Central State well.
Do not abandon the ritual of serving the greater because of changes of surname."
At that time, the Central State changed surnames every few years.
Qián Liú's meaning,
was that holding a remote corner,
one only knows to serve the greater as the smaller.
If the Central State has a ruler,
then serve him as a subject.
Whether it rises or falls on its own,
we do not ask.
Gēngxū,
he was eighty-one years old.
Chuànguàn and his brothers shared a mourning tent.
The commander of the inner guards, Lù Rénzhāng, said:
"The Lord succeeds to the former king's hegemonic enterprise.
Officers and officials will come morning and evening to pay respects.
He should be in a different place from the other princes."
So he ordered the person in charge to set up another tent,
and supported Chuànguàn to reside there.
He announced to the officers and officials:
"From now on, only pay respects to the Lord.
The attendants of the other princes are forbidden from entering without reason."
Day and night he maintained guard,
never resting.
Although Lù Rénzhāng was unlearned,
his actions unconsciously matched those of Zhào Xǐ.
Only Rénzhāng repeatedly offended him over matters.
At this time,
Chuànguàn rewarded him.
Rénzhāng said:
"When the former king was on the throne,
Rénzhāng did not know to serve you, Lord.
Today, fulfilling my duty,
is still like serving the former king."
Former king,
refers to Liú.
After Chuànguàn succeeded to the position,
he changed his name to Yuánguàn.
Brothers whose names
contained "Chuàn"
all changed it to
"Yuán".
Following the testamentary order, he abolished the rituals of a state—
Wúyuè establishing a state,
see scroll 271, the third year of Lóngdé of Liáng Emperor Mòdì.
He exempted from taxes the fields of the people that were desolate or ownerless.
Desolate:
having an owner but not cultivated.
Ownerless:
the household line extinct, with no owner.
He established the Zénéng Academy,
in charge of evaluating and selecting officials,
appointing Shěn Sōng, Deputy Commissioner of Camp Farms of Zhèxī, to head it.
The Internal Guard Commander Fùyáng Liú Rén
(Fùyáng County was originally the Hàn dynasty's Fùchūn County.
It was renamed Fùyáng during the Jìn dynasty to avoid the taboo of Empress Dowager Zhèng,
and later generations thus followed this.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: Fùyáng County belongs to Hángzhōu,
located seventy-three *lǐ* southwest of the prefectural seat.
Rénzhāng was of a rigid temperament,
and Rén was fond of slandering and disparaging others;
both were disliked by the multitude.
One day,
the various generals together went to the prefectural gate to request their execution;
Yuánguàn sent his nephew Rénjùn to admonish them,
saying:
"These two generals have served the late king for a long time,
and I am just now considering their merits.
How can you all wish to vent personal grievances and kill them?
Is this permissible?
I am your king,
you should obey my commands;
if not,
I shall return to Lín'ān to yield the path to the worthy!"
The Qián clan originally resided in Lín'ān.
He then appointed Rénzhāng as Prefect of Qúzhōu,
and Rén as Prefect of Húzhōu.
There were those both inside and outside the court who submitted letters of accusation and exposure,
but Yuánguàn set them all aside without inquiry,
and from this, the generals and officials became harmonious and united.
11. Initially,
the Qìdān Shèlì Cèlà and Tìyǐn were both captured by Zhào Déjūn.
(Shèlì and Tìyǐn
are both titles for Qìdān military commanders.
Cè,
read as *shìlì*.
Là,
read as *láidá*.)
Their capture is seen in the third year of Tiānchéng in the previous scroll.
The Emperor consulted with his close ministers,
and Déjūn and others all said:
"The reason the Qìdān have not invaded the border for several years and have repeatedly sought peace
is because these men are in the south.
If we release them, border troubles will arise again."
The Emperor asked Jìzhōu Prefect Yáng Tán about this,
who replied:
"Cèlà
is a valiant general of the Qìdān.
Previously, he assisted Wáng Dū in plotting to endanger the state.
We were fortunate to capture him;
if Your Majesty spares his life,
the favor granted is already great.
The Qìdān losing him is like losing hands and feet.
He has been at the court for several years
and knows the strengths and weaknesses of the Central Plains.
If he is allowed to return,
the trouble he will cause will certainly be deep.
As soon as he leaves the frontier,
he will turn south and shoot arrows.
I fear regret will be too late."
The Emperor then desisted.
Tán
was a Shātuó person.
(Yáng Tán later changed his name to Guāngyuǎn.)
12. The Emperor wished to appoint Lǐ Zànhuá to a provincial governorship in Hénán,
but the close ministers all considered it inadvisable.
The Emperor said:
"I made a pact of brotherhood with his father,
therefore Zànhuá came to me.
I am old now.
If later generations of succeeding rulers
wish to summon him,
how could they possibly get him to come!"
In summer,
the fourth month,
on Guǐhài,
he appointed Zànhuá as Military Commissioner of Yìchéng,
and selected court officials to serve as his subordinates and assist him.
Zànhuá merely lived in leisurely comfort, attending to his own needs,
and did not involve himself in government affairs;
the Emperor praised him for this.
Although he occasionally acted unlawfully, he was not questioned about it.
He married him to Xià shì, a consort from Zhuāngzōng's rear palace.
(*Wǔdài Huìyào*: Zhuāngzōng's Zhāoróng Xià shì was enfeoffed as Lady of Guóguó.
The *Old History of the Five Dynasties* says: When Míngzōng entered Luò,
the several hundred women of Zhuāngzōng's palace were all ordered to return to their families,
only Xià shì had nowhere to return to.
Míngzōng, because Xià Lǔqí was of the same clan,
therefore ordered her to be given to him;
now she was given as wife to Zànhuá.)
(Wife,
read as *qīxì*.)
His concubines often had their arms pricked for him to suck the blood;
if maids or servants committed minor faults,
he would sometimes gouge out their eyes,
or cut them with knives or burn them with fire;
Xià shì could not bear his cruelty,
and petitioned to divorce him and become a nun.
13. On Yǐchǒu,
Sòngwáng Cónghòu was additionally appointed Concurrent Zhōngshū Lìng.
14. Dōngchuān Military Commissioner Dǒng Zhāng assembled his generals to plan a surprise attack on Chéngdū.
They all said it would certainly succeed;
former Língzhōu Prefect Wáng Huī said:
"Jiànnán is ten thousand *lǐ* wide,
with Chéngdū as its greatest city.
The time is now the height of summer,
and the army is setting out without just cause;
it will certainly not succeed."
Mèng Zhīxiáng heard of this,
and sent Cavalry Commander Pān Rénsì to lead three thousand men to Hànzhōu to spy on the situation.
When Zhāng entered the territory,
he captured Báiyánglín Garrison.
(Báiyánglín Garrison should be on the border of Hànzhōu.)
His momentum was very strong,
and Zhīxiáng became worried.
Zhào Jìliáng said:
"Zhāng is a person of courage but without kindness,
his soldiers are not attached to him.
If he defends a city, it will be difficult to capture;
if he fights in the field, he will be captured.
Now he is not guarding his lair;
this is to your advantage.
Zhāng's elite troops in battle are all in the vanguard.
You should use weak troops to lure them,
and await them with strong troops.
Initially there may be a minor setback,
but later there will certainly be a great victory.
This is Sūn Bìn's theory of the three teams of horses.
Since ancient times, many have used this to achieve victory.
Chǔ used it to defeat the Wú army and destroy Shūjiū;
Zhōu Fǎng used it to defeat Dù Zēng and pacify Xiāng and Miǎn;
Wáng Màozhāng used it to behead Zhū Yǒuníng;
their strategies all stem from this."
(Weak,
read as *lúnwéi*.
Setback,
read as *nǚliù*.)
"Now his army has suddenly arrived,
and people's hearts are fearful and alarmed.
You should personally go out to resist him,
to strengthen the resolve of the multitude."
Zhào Tíngyǐn considered Jìliáng's words correct,
and said:
"Zhāng is rash and lacks strategy;
raising an army will certainly lead to defeat.
I will capture him for you."
On Xīnsì,
he appointed Tíngyǐn as Field Commander of the Marching Army,
leading thirty thousand men to resist him.
In the fifth month,
on Rénwǔ, the first day of the month,
Tíngyǐn went to bid farewell.
Dǒng Zhāng's proclamation arrived,
and there were also letters left for Jìliáng, Tíngyǐn, and Lǐ Zhào.
(Dǒng Zhāng's letters uniquely did not reach Lǐ Rénhǎn because Zhào Jìliáng was Mèng Zhīxiáng's chief strategist,
and Zhào Tíngyǐn and Lǐ Zhào had once joined Zhāng in defending against Shí Jìngtáng at Jiànzhōu,
therefore he first tried to entice them with letters;
Lǐ Rénhǎn had never served together with him,
therefore he was not included.)
(Left,
read as *wéijì*.)
Jìliáng and Tíngyǐn were in secret communication with him,
summoning him to come.
Zhīxiáng gave the letters to Tíngyǐn.
Tíngyǐn did not look at them,
but threw them on the ground,
saying:
"This is nothing more than sowing discord,
wanting you, my lord, to kill the Deputy Commissioner and me, Tíngyǐn."
(Zhào Jìliáng was the Deputy Military Commissioner,
therefore Tíngyǐn referred to him as such.)
Zhīxiáng said:
"The matter will certainly succeed."
Zhào had never been literate;
he looked at it
and said:
"Zhāng is teaching me to rebel."
He imprisoned the messenger,
but still gathered troops for self-preservation.
(Lǐ Zhào was at that time stationed in Lìzhōu.)
Zhāng's troops reached Hànzhōu.
Pān Rénsì engaged them at Chìshuǐ,
was greatly defeated,
and was captured by Zhāng.
(Chìshuǐ is southeast of Hànzhōu.)
On the Guǐwèi day,
Mèng Zhīxiáng left Zhào Jìliáng and Gāo Jìngróu to guard Chéngdū,
and personally led eight thousand troops towards Hànzhōu.
He reached Mímóu Town.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Xīndū County in Chéngdū Prefecture has Mímóu Town.
Qù (to head towards),
is pronounced qī yù fān.
On the Jiǎshēn day,
at dawn,
Zhào Tíngyǐn deployed his troops at Jīzōng Bridge.
The Biography of Mèng Zhīxiáng in the Jiù Wǔdài Shǐ states: Mèng Zhīxiáng personally led his forces and, together with Zhào Tíngyǐn and others, engaged the enemy in battle at Jīnyàn Bridge,
and Dǒng Zhāng's army was greatly defeated.
According to this, Jīnyàn Bridge is south of Luò County in Hànzhōu.
After Dǒng Zhāng's troops were defeated,
Mèng Zhīxiáng pursued them,
and spent the night at Luò County.
Could it be that Jīnyàn Bridge is the same as Jīzōng Bridge?
Shortly after, Dǒng Zhāng, seeing the strength of the Western Chuān forces,
withdrew and redeployed his troops below the Wǔhóu Temple.
Zhūgě Liàng, the Marquis of Wǔ, had rendered great service to Shǔ,
and the people of Shǔ erected temples for him wherever they were.
"What are we doing here, exposed to the midday sun!"
Dǒng Zhāng then mounted his horse.
As the vanguards began to engage,
the Eastern Chuān Right Wing Cavalry and Infantry Commander Zhāng Shǒujìn surrendered to Mèng Zhīxiáng,
saying
"Zhāng's troops are all here,
there are no further reinforcements,
you should attack them urgently."
Mèng Zhīxiáng climbed a high mound to oversee the battle.
The Left Míngyì Commander Máo Zhòngwēi and the Left Chōngshān Commander Lǐ Táng guarded Jīzōng Bridge.
Mèng Zhīxiáng established the Left and Right Chōngshān camps,
see scroll 275, the first year of the Tiānchéng era.
Zhào Tíngyǐn fought three engagements unfavorably,
and the Deputy Commander of the Yánèi Capital Command Hóu Hóngshí's troops also retreated.
Mèng Zhīxiáng became fearful,
and pointed his horsewhip towards the rear formation.

is pronounced fú yòu fān.

Messenger,

59. The deputy commander Wén Jǐngchēn of Shǔ's Yuán Prefecture rebelled, seizing the city.
A thorough examination of the Old and New Tang Histories, the Jiǔyù Túzhì, and the Huányǔ Jì
reveals none record the reason for Yuán Prefecture's establishment or its location.
The "Geographical Treatise" in the New History of the Five Dynasties states: Regarding prefectures and counties,
those existing in the Tang but abolished during the Five Dynasties,
those established during the Five Dynasties and extant today, and counties whose administrative affiliation changed and remains so now,
should all be listed to complete the geographical record;
all others that were once established but later abolished,
or whose boundaries were altered and later restored,
are not worth recording.
From this, we know Yuán Prefecture was likely established by Shǔ and soon abolished,
which is why it left no record.
When Táng Zhuāngzōng conquered Shǔ,
he obtained sixty-four prefectures.
Only fifty-three of these appear in the "Geographical Treatise."
Prefectures like Yuán were likely among the sixty-four.
According to the Old History of the Five Dynasties,
Later Shǔ's Pān Rénsì was appointed Military Commissioner of Wǔdìng and Surveillance Commissioner, Agricultural Commissioner, etc., of Yuán, Bì, and other prefectures;
when the Zhōu army attacked Qín and Fèng,
Mèng Yíyè stationed troops at Pínglì as reinforcements for Bāo and Yuán.
Thus, Shǔ established Yuán Prefecture under the jurisdiction of the Wǔdìng Army military command.
【Zhāng: Hú's annotation:
"A thorough examination of the Old and New Tang Histories, the Jiǔyù Túzhì, and the Huányǔ Jì reveals none record the reason for Yuán Prefecture's establishment or its location"
and so on.
The Yǐ-shíyī-háng edition
writes
"Qú"
instead of
"Yuán."
The characters for
"Yuán"
and
"Qú"
are similar in stroke. The printing in the Yǐ-shíyī-háng edition is also blurred,
and only upon careful scrutiny did I dare determine it.
Qú Prefecture
was in Shǔ territory,
as seen in the "Geographical Tables" of the New History of the Five Dynasties.
This commentary's purpose throughout the book is solely to list discrepancies,

but generally not incorporating it.
This entry specifically highlights it,
