he declined and did not accept.
62. Military Commissioner of Xióngwǔ, Zhāng Yánlǎng, led troops to besiege Wén Prefecture.
(The Tiānxióng military command was established at Qín Prefecture in the late Táng,
later changed to Xióngwǔ by Later Táng.)
Shǔ's Lǐ Yánhòu led Guǒ Prefecture troops stationed at Xīng Prefecture,
and dispatched Vanguard Commander Fàn Yánhuī with troops to rescue Wén Prefecture.
Yánlǎng lifted the siege and returned.
Xīng Prefecture Governor Féng Huī led garrison troops back from Gànqú to Fèngxiáng.
At that time, both Jiē and Xīng prefectures had already fallen to Shǔ.
It seems Táng had appointed Guō Zhīqióng and Féng Huī as governors of these two prefectures to advance and capture them but failed.
The Old History states: During the Chángxīng era,
Féng Huī was Governor of Xīng Prefecture,
with Gànqú as his administrative seat.
Gàn
is pronounced gān.
63. In the eleventh month,
Xú Zhīgǎo summoned his son, the Minister of Education and Tongpingzhangshi Jǐngtōng, back to Jīnlíng
(from Jiāngdū to Jīnlíng).

He appointed his second son, Commander of the Yá-Nèi Cavalry and Infantry and Tuanlianshi of Hǎi Prefecture, Jǐngqiān, as Commander of the Left and Right Armies, Left Vice Director of the Department of State Affairs, and Cānzhèngshì,
to remain in Jiāngdū assisting in governance.
64. In the twelfth month,
on Jǐsì day,
Ān Shūqiān, Governor of Yì Prefecture, was appointed Military Commissioner of Zhènwǔ,
and Yǐn Huī, Defense Commissioner of Qí Prefecture, was appointed Military Commissioner of Zhāngguó.
Ān Shūqiān for his merit in resisting the Qìdān,
Yǐn Huī as a reward for submitting to (the court) from Fèngxiáng.
(Ān Shūqiān was a Shatuo.)
Sòng Bái said: Ān Shūqiān's native place was within Yún Prefecture boundaries,
his household registered in Huīquán Village of the Fèngchéng Army.
65. On Rénshēn day,
Shí Jìngtáng reported that the Qìdān had withdrawn,
and he disbanded his troops and returned.
(From Bǎijǐng back to Jìnyáng.)
66. On Yǐhài day,
Military Commissioner of Xióngwǔ Zhāng Yánlǎng was summoned to be Vice Director of the Secretariat, Tongpingzhangshi, and in charge of the Three Departments.
67. On Xīnsì day,
the Hàn Empress Mǎ died.
Empress Mǎ
was the daughter of King Yīn of Chǔ.
68. On Jiǎshēn day,
Shǔ interred Emperor Wénwǔ Shèngdé Yīngliè Míngxiào at Héling,
with the temple name Gāozǔ.
69. On Yǐyǒu day,
the Prince of È was buried south of Huīling's city wall.
(According to Táng imperial tomb regulations,
outside the burial grounds a wall was erected,
and cypress trees were planted in rows,
called the Cypress City.)
Onlookers grieved.
Textual Analysis states: The Min Emperor's Veritable Records and the Min Emperor's Annals in the Old History both say:
"When the Jìn Gāozǔ ascended the throne,
he posthumously honored him as Min,
and buried him together with the Prince of Qín and Chóngjí within the Huīling grounds."
Here we follow the Deposed Emperor's Veritable Records.
70. This year, drought occurred in autumn and winter,
causing many people to flee,
with Tóng, Huá, Pú, and Jiàng particularly severe.
71. The Hàn ruler ordered the Prince of Qín, Hóngdù, who was in charge of the Six Armies, to recruit a thousand Imperial Guards,
all scoundrels from the marketplaces.
Hóngdù was close to them.
Tongpingzhangshi Yáng Dòngqián admonished:
"The Prince of Qín
is the state's primary heir.
(Zhǎng means eldest.)
Having him command troops is already excessive,
let alone being close to petty men!"
The Hàn ruler said:
"The child is being taught military affairs,
I trouble you overly with your concern."
He ultimately did not caution Hóngdù.
Dòngqián, upon leaving,
saw guards plundering merchants' gold and silk.
The merchants dared not complain.
He sighed:
"With governance so chaotic,
what use is a Counselor-in-Chief!"
Thereupon, he pleaded illness and returned to his residence;
after a long time,
not being summoned,
he eventually died.
1. Spring,
first month,
on Bǐngshēn, the first day of the month,
Mǐn proclaimed a general amnesty,
and changed the era name to Yǒnghé.
2. Second month,
on Bǐngyín, the first day of the month,
Shǔ proclaimed a general amnesty.
3. On Jiǎxū day,

Fàn Yánguāng, Commissioner of the Bureau of Military Affairs, Military Commissioner of Tiānxióng, and concurrently Palace Attendant, was appointed Military Commissioner of Xuānwǔ and concurrently Director of the Secretariat.
4. On Dīngchǒu day,
Xià Prefecture Military Commissioner Lǐ Yíchāo reported being ill,
and had his elder brother, Army Supervisor Lǐ Yíyīn, temporarily administer military and prefectural affairs;
Yíchāo died soon after.
5. On Wùyín day,
the Shǔ ruler honored his mother, Lady Lǐ, as Empress Dowager.
The Empress Dowager
was from Tàiyuán,
originally a consort in Zhuāngzōng's rear palace,
given to Shǔ's Gāozǔ.
(Mèng Zhīxiáng served Zhuāngzōng,
long enjoying his intimate trust,
hence he was given a consort.)
The history records in detail Lady Lǐ's origin
to distinguish her from the Princess of Fúqìng.
6. On Jǐchǒu day,
the Emperor's mother, Lady Wèi of the State of Lǔ, was posthumously honored as Empress Xuānxiàn.
Lady Wèi
was originally the wife of a Wáng from Píngshān.
Widowed young,
she and the Emperor were both captured by Míngzōng.
7. The Mǐn ruler established the Virtuous Consort Chén as Empress.
Initially,
the Mǐn ruler had married two women of the Liú clan,
both from scholarly families,
beautiful but not favored.
Empress Chén
was originally Jīnfèng, a serving maid of Mǐn's Tàizǔ,
ugly and licentious,
but the Mǐn ruler doted on her,
appointing her clansmen Shǒu'ēn and Kuāngshèng as Palace Commissioners.
(Palace Commissioners were officials established by Mǐn.)
8. Third month,
on Xīnchǒu day,
former Military Commissioner of Xuānwǔ and concurrent Palace Attendant Zhào Yánshòu was appointed Military Commissioner of Zhōngwǔ and concurrent Commissioner of the Bureau of Military Affairs.
9. Lǐ Yíyīn was appointed Military Commissioner of Dìngnán.
(Lǐ Yíyīn later changed his name to Yíxīng to avoid the Sòng dynasty's ancestral temple taboo,
his sons were Lǐ Jìpěng and Lǐ Jìqiān.)
Nàn
is pronounced nǎi dàn.
10. On Jǐyǒu day,
Wúyuè King Qián Yuánguàn's mother, Lady Chén, was posthumously granted the title Lady of the State of Jìn.
Yuánguàn was filial by nature,
honoring and respecting his maternal relatives,
generously bestowing gifts upon them,
but never promoted them to office
or entrusted them with important responsibilities.
On the 11th day, Rénxū,
An Shěnqí, Commander of the Zhāngshèng Capital Command, was appointed to concurrently hold the office of Military Commissioner of Shùnhuà.
According to the *Wǔdài Huìyào*: In the sixth month of the first year of the Qīngtài era,
the Běngshèng cavalry was renamed the Left and Right Zhāngshèng Armies,
and the Yánwèi infantry was renamed the Left and Right Níngwèi Armies.
The Later Liáng had previously changed the Yìchāng Army in Cāngzhōu to the Shùnhuà Army,
but the Later Táng restored the old Táng name,
making it the Hénghǎi Army.
Prior to this, Qián Yuánxiāng of Wúyuè, serving as Prefect of Míngzhōu,
concurrently held the title of Military Commissioner of Shùnhuà;
the Shùnhuà Army held by Shěnqí was likely the one in Chǔzhōu.
He was the son of Ān Jīnquán.
Ān Jīnquán
was a veteran general from Dàiběi.
On the 12th day, Shǐ Zàidé, a Gentleman of the Grand Temple,
was by nature arrogant and unrestrained.
He submitted a memorial criticizing civil and military officials both inside and outside the court.
The *Old History of the Five Dynasties* records Shǐ Zàidé's memorial,
which roughly stated:
"Those appointed to office by the court are mostly promoted indiscriminately;
those called military men are unskilled in strategy,
and though clad in armor and bearing weapons,
they discard their armor in battle,
and desert the army in desperate straits.
Those called literary men mostly lack talent and skill,
and few possess the conduct of scholars.
When asked about strategies, they remain silent;
when writing documents, they rely on others.
This is what is called maintaining superfluous officials,
wasting the state's resources.
Now that Your Majesty has ushered in a new era of reform,
it is the time to rectify these abuses through enlightened governance.
I request that all military personnel under the command of both internal and external authorities,
as long as they are fit to wear armor,
be ordered by their commanding generals
to undergo examinations on their martial skills, strengths and weaknesses,
and the depth of their strategic acumen.
Those in lower positions who possess general talent should be promoted to high command,
while those in high positions lacking strategic ability should be demoted to lower ranks.
As for the civil officials,
I request that policy questions be issued from the palace to the Secretariat, for the chief ministers to personally examine them.
If those in lower positions possess great talent, they should be promoted to high office;
if those in high positions lack great talent, they should be moved to lower positions."
The character "juàn"
is pronounced as in "jì yuàn".
The character "dǐ"
is pronounced as in "dīng lǐ".
(The memorial proposed) promoting or demoting based on ability;
the chief ministers and court officials were greatly angered,
and Lú Wénjì, along with Reminders Liú Tāo and Yáng Zhāojiǎn, among others, all requested that he be punished.
The Emperor said to Academician Mǎ Yìnsūn:
"I have newly ascended to rule the realm,
and it is appropriate to open the path for remonstrance;
if court officials are punished for speaking out,
who would dare to speak again!
You shall draft an edict for me,
to proclaim my intent."
Mǎ Yìnsūn was then a Hanlin Academician.
The character "wèi"
is pronounced as in "yú wèi".
The edict roughly stated:
"In the past, Wèi Zhēng requested rewards for Huángfǔ Déshēn,
see the eighth year of the Zhēnguān era of Emperor Tàizōng, in scroll 194.
The matter is the same, but the words differ;
how far apart they are!
Zàidé's intent was to pour out his heart,
how can he be blamed!"
"Pouring out"
means to pour forth what is in one's heart and mind,
and to offer loyalty to the sovereign.
He was the great-grandson of Yáng Sìfù.
Yáng Sìfù
served as chancellor during Emperor Wénzong's reign.
On the 13th day, Wú appointed Xú Jǐngqiān as Tongpingzhangshi and placed him in charge of military affairs of the Left and Right Armies;
Xú Zhīgào ordered the Secretariat Gentleman Chén Jué to assist him.
*Kǎoyì* states: According to the *Jiāngnán Lù*:
"At that time, the authority and position of the First Ruler (Xú Zhīgào) grew daily,
and everyone inside and outside knew the situation was bound to change,
but because the ruler of Wú was respectful and cautious, adhering to the Way,
(Xú Zhīgào) intended to wait for the heir to succeed.
Xú Jǐngqiān, the second son of the First Ruler,
was the son-in-law of the ruler of Wú,
and was especially beloved by the First Ruler.
Sòng Qíqiū had Chén Jué serve as Jǐngqiān's tutor,
to enhance his reputation.
Sòng Qíqiū participated in deciding government affairs,
and often acted unlawfully,
attributing faults to the heir apparent while greatly praising Jǐngqiān's virtues,
nearly plotting to have him replace the heir.
The reason for this was
that the ruler of Wú was young while the First Ruler was old,
and (Sòng Qíqiū) believed the First Ruler would certainly not live long enough,
so that in the future, when he gained the state,
if he passed it to Jǐngqiān,
(Jǐngqiān) would be easy to control,
and (Sòng Qíqiū) himself, as the senior statesman,
would have supreme authority and power.
This was his day and night scheme.
The First Ruler became aware of this,
so he summoned Sòng Qíqiū to Jīnlíng to serve as his deputy,
concurrently holding the title of Military Commissioner of Shēn and Cài from afar,
but with no involvement in actual affairs,
merely at leisure."
Now we follow the *Shíguó Jìnián*.
(Xú Zhīgào said to Chén Jué:) "In my youth, when debating with Sòng Zǐsōng,
we enjoyed challenging each other,
sometimes I would leave Zǐsōng and return home,
sometimes Zǐsōng would rise and leave in anger.
Zǐsōng carried his clothing box and headed for the Qínhuái Gate intending to leave on several occasions,
and I often ordered the gatekeepers to stop him.
Sòng Qíqiū,
styled Zǐsōng.
Qínhuái Gate,
a gate of Jīnlíng city.
The character "shuò"
is pronounced as in "suǒ jiǎo".
(Chén Jué) is not yet fully versed in current affairs,
let alone Jǐngqiān, who is young and will be governing the state.
Therefore, I am imposing on you, my son, to instruct him."
In summer,
the fourth month,
on the Gēngwǔ day,
Shǔ appointed Wú Zhāoyì, the Palace Censor from Lóngmén, as Vice Director of the Secretariat and Tongpingzhangshi.
Lóngmén County,
originally the Hàn dynasty Píshì County,
renamed during the Later Wèi,
belonged to Hézhōng Prefecture in the Táng.
According to the *Jiǔyù Zhì*: Located 95 *lǐ* northeast of the prefectural seat.
The surname "Wú"
is a surname;
the Wúqiū clan sometimes became the Wú clan,
with prominent branches from Píngchāng and Jùlù.
During the Kāiyuán era, there was a Reminder named Wú Jǐng,
a man of Luòyáng,
also said to be from Wú.
The character "wú"
is pronounced as in "wǔ fū".
On the Guǐwèi day,
Hán Zhāoyìn, Commissioner of the Bureau of Military Affairs and Minister of Justice, was additionally appointed Vice Director of the Secretariat and Tongpingzhangshi.
On the Xīnmǎo day,
Liú Yánhào, Commissioner of the Southern Bureau of the Palace Reception Office, was appointed Minister of Justice
and concurrently Commissioner of the Bureau of Military Affairs.
Yánhào
was the younger brother of the Empress.
On the Guǐsì day,
Liú Yánlǎng, Great General of the Left Guard of the Imperial Insignia Guard, was appointed Superior General of his own guard,
and concurrently served as Commissioner of the Northern Bureau of the Palace Reception Office
and Deputy Commissioner of the Bureau of Military Affairs.
In the fifth month,
on the Bǐngshēn day,
the Qìdān raided Xīnzhōu and Zhènwǔ.
On the Gēngxū day,
Yáng Tán, Military Commissioner of Zhènwǔ, was bestowed the name Guāngyuǎn.
The *Old History* records a memorial from the Secretariat:
"According to an edict of the first month of the third year of the Tiānchéng era,
regarding the taboo characters of the nine temples, only the main characters are to be avoided;
characters with the same radical components are not required to have strokes reduced.
Now, names such as Military Commissioner Yáng Tán of Zhèngzhōu, Tánzhōu, and Jīntán,
considering what is appropriate under the circumstances,
are all requested to be changed.
In memorials and documents, characters with radical components should have strokes omitted,
and all officials whose names involve such radical components are also requested to change their names."
The edict stated:
"Characters with radical components,
though sharing radicals, have different pronunciations and meanings;
only the exact pronunciation should be avoided,
it is not appropriate to change them all.
Yáng Tán shall be bestowed the name Guāngyuǎn,
the rest remain as before."
Note: This was to avoid the radical of the taboo character
"dǎn"
from Emperor Míngzōng's temple name.
Yáng Tán was not then stationed in Dìngzhōu;
we should follow the *Comprehensive Mirror*.
In the sixth month,
Chái Zàiyòng, Military Commissioner of Déshèng and concurrently Director of the Secretariat of Wú, died.
Previously,
the Historiographer Wáng Zhèn once inquired about his military achievements,
Zàiyòng said:
"These minor contributions of a hawk or hound
are all due to the spirit of the state;
what achievements do I, Zàiyòng, have!"
In the end, he did not report them.
To have achievements yet not seek fame—
among military men, one like Chái Zàiyòng can indeed be praised.
The Qìdān raided Yìngzhōu.
The Hedong Jiedushi and Northern Commander-in-Chief Shí Jìngtáng had already returned to his garrison.
Last year in May,
the Emperor ordered Shí Jìngtáng to return to Tàiyuán.
The Emperor enjoyed inquiring about external affairs,
often summoning Duānmíngdiàn Academician Lǐ Zhuānměi, Hànlín Academician Lǐ Sōng, Drafting Official Lǚ Qí, Xuē Wényù, Hànlín Astronomer Zhào Yányì, and others
In the middle period of the Táng dynasty,
the Directorate of Astronomy had two Astronomy Doctors,
rank 8b;
ninety Astronomy Observers,
and fifty Astronomy Students,
all responsible for observing celestial phenomena.
Hànlín Astronomers
resided in the Hànlín Academy to observe celestial phenomena.
He would converse with them, sometimes until late at night.
At that time, Shí Jìngtáng's two sons served as palace attendants,
Empress Dowager Cáo was the mother of the Princess of Jìn,
Shí Jìngtáng's wife, the Princess of Wèi,
was promoted to Princess of Jìn in April of that year.
Zhǎng,
read with the rising tone.
They were ordered to spy on the Emperor's secret plans,
and thus knew of all matters, great and small.
Shí Jìngtáng often declared in front of guests that he was frail and unfit to be a commander,
hoping the court would not suspect him.
At that time, the Qìdān frequently raided the northern borders,
and the Imperial Guards were mostly stationed in Yōu and Bìng provinces.
Shí Jìngtáng and Zhào Déjūn repeatedly requested additional troops and grain supplies,
one request following another.
Shí Jìngtáng requested troops and grain to strengthen Bìngzhōu,
Zhào Déjūn requested troops and grain to strengthen Yōuzhōu.
On Jiǎshēn
an edict was issued to borrow beans and grain from wealthy people in Hédōng.
On Yǐyǒu,
an edict ordered Zhènzhōu to deliver 50,000 bolts of silk to the Commander-in-Chief's headquarters,
to purchase military grain.
The Commander-in-Chief's headquarters was in Jìnyáng,
because Shí Jìngtáng was then the Northern Commander of Cavalry and Infantry.
The *Jiǔyù Zhì* states: From Zhènzhōu northwest to Dàizhōu is 620 *lǐ*.
Chéng,
read with the falling tone.
At that time, floods and droughts caused famine among the people,
and Shí Jìngtáng sent envoys to press for supplies urgently and harshly,
causing the people east of the mountains to scatter.
This refers to the area east of Tàiháng and Chángshān mountains.
The historian narrates the cause of the disorder.
Shí Jìngtáng led a large army and stationed it at Xīnzhōu.
The court sent envoys to bestow summer clothing upon the soldiers,
conveying an imperial edict to pacify and instruct them.
The soldiers shouted "Long live!" four times.
At that time, the arrogant soldiers were accustomed to such scenes,
and also wanted to support Shí Jìngtáng's ascension in hopes of rewards.
His advisor from Hénèi, Duàn Xīyáo, requested the execution of the ringleaders.
Shí Jìngtáng ordered his Chief Military Inspector Liú Zhīyuǎn to behead thirty-six men, including the Assistant Horse Commander Lǐ Huī, as a warning.
Xīyáo
was from Huáizhōu.
When the Emperor heard of this,
he became even more suspicious of Shí Jìngtáng.
On Rénchén,
an edict was issued:
"For theft, regardless of the amount stolen,
as well as for arson and robbery,
the severest punishment shall be applied."
In Mǐn, Prince Fú Jì Péng had an illicit affair with a palace woman named Lǐ Chūnyàn.
Jì Péng requested her from Empress Chén,
and the Empress informed the King of Mǐn, who then bestowed her upon him.
In autumn,
the seventh month,
Privy Councilor Liú Yánhào was appointed as Tiānxióng Jiedushi.
On Yǐsì,
Wǔníng Jiedushi Zhāng Jìngdá was appointed as Deputy Commander of the Northern Campaign Headquarters,
leading troops to station at Dàizhōu,
in order to divide Shí Jìngtáng's power.
This sets the stage for ordering Zhāng Jìngdá to attack Shí Jìngtáng.
The Emperor was deeply worried about the current situation,
and once casually reproached Lú Wénjì and others for offering no advice or suggestions.
On Dīngsì,
Wénjì and others submitted a memorial:
"We officials attend court every five days,
appearing in two groups,
and briefly have the opportunity to respond to Your Majesty.
With guards filling the space before us,
even if we have foolish ideas,
we dare not fully present them.
We note that since the Shàngyuán era of previous dynasties,
the Yányīngdiàn was established.
If the chief ministers wished to memorialize,
or the Son of Heaven wished to consult,
with no attendants nearby,
people could thus speak their minds fully.
We hope to restore this old practice,
allowing only confidential ministers to attend at your side."
Confidential ministers
refers to the Privy Councilors.
"According to the old system of attending court every five days,
after all officials withdraw,
only the chief ministers remain.
If it concerns routine matters, they can naturally present them.
If a matter requires secrecy,
and not on that day,
on another day they can submit a memorial at the palace gate,
and all attendants should be dismissed,
awaiting them in a side hall.
Why must we follow the name Yányīngdiàn!"
In Wú, the Tuánliànshǐ of Rùnzhōu, Xú Zhī'è,
associated with petty men,
indulged in pleasure and neglected his duties.
He established a market street west of the Yáchéng,
and personally engaged in trade.
When Xú Zhīgào heard of this, he was furious.
He summoned Zhī'è,
and his attendants interrogated and reprimanded him;
Zhī'è was frightened.
Someone said to Zhīgào:
"The Loyal and Martial Prince loved Zhī'è most dearly."
Xú Wēn was posthumously titled Loyal and Martial Prince.
Xú Zhīgào's rise to power
stemmed from quelling the rebellion of Zhū Jǐn.
If Xú Wēn, on his deathbed, handed power to Zhīgào,
it was not his original intent.
This matter is recorded in the 276th scroll, in the second year of Tiānchéng of Emperor Míngzōng.
This refers to summoning Xú Zhīxún back to Yángzhōu from Shēngzhōu.
If Zhī'è had gained a reputation for capable governance,
training troops and nurturing the people,
what benefit would that be to you?"
Zhīgào was moved to realization,
and thereafter treated him more generously.
In the ninth month,
on Bǐngshēn,
Wú issued a great amnesty,
and changed the era name to Tiānzuò.
On Jǐyǒu,
Xuānhéyuàn Southern Commissioner Fáng Gǎo was appointed Minister of Justice,
and concurrently served as Privy Councilor;
Xuānhéyuàn Northern Commissioner Liú Yánlǎng was appointed Southern Commissioner,
still concurrently serving as Deputy Privy Councilor.
From then on, Yánlǎng and Privy Council Academician Xuē Wényù and others wielded power within the court.
Although Gǎo and Zhào Yánshòu were the senior officials,
the Privy Councilor is the head of the Privy Council.
Zhǎng,
read with the rising tone.
Gǎo merely followed the prevailing opinion,
never taking the initiative.
Whenever envoys from Yōu and Bìng came to present memorials,
the various Privy Councilors would sit in a circle to discuss it.
Gǎo would often lower his head and doze off.
By the time he awoke,
stretching his neck and straightening his clothes,
the envoys would already have left.
Matters of appointment and promotion
were all handled by Yánlǎng.
This sets the stage for Liú Yánlǎng's execution by Jìn and Fáng Gǎo's survival.
However, both were the Emperor's close ministers.
Yánlǎng's greed for wealth was wrong,
but Gǎo's avoidance of responsibility was also wrong.
One had to first bribe Yánlǎng,
then discuss the tribute to be offered.
Those who bribed heavily were appointed first,
obtaining posts in the interior;
those who bribed lightly were appointed later,
obtaining posts on the frontiers.
Consequently, all the generals and commanders were resentful and angry,
but the Emperor failed to perceive it.
In Shǔ, the Jīnzhōu Defense Commissioner Quán Shīyù attacked Jīnzhōu,
capturing the water fortress.
According to the *Yuánhé Jùnxiàn Zhì*,
the Hàn River flows a hundred paces from Jīnzhōu city,
hence the Táng established a water fortress to defend against Shǔ troops.
Army Supervisor Chén Zhīyǐn used another matter as a pretext and led three hundred troops to flee downstream;
Defense Commissioner Mǎ Quánjié exhausted his personal wealth to supply the army,
employing clever tactics and fighting desperately,
whereupon the Shǔ troops withdrew.
On Wùyín,
an edict was issued to execute Zhīyǐn.
Earlier, the King of Mǐn had a favored minister named Guī Shǒumíng,
who had access to the inner chambers.
In his later years, the King of Mǐn suffered from a wind illness.
Empress Chén had illicit relations with Shǒumíng and the Director of the Hundred Artisans Institute, Lǐ Kěyīn.
All the people of the state detested this,
but none dared speak of it.
Li Kěyīn had previously slandered the Imperial City Commissioner Lǐ Fǎng to the King of Mǐn.
Chén Kuāngshèng, a relative of the queen, had shown disrespect to Prince Fú, Jì Péng.
Both Lǐ Fǎng and Jì Péng harbored hatred for them.
The King of Mǐn was gravely ill,
and Jì Péng showed a pleased expression.
Lǐ Fǎng believed the King of Mǐn would certainly not recover.
In winter,
the tenth month,
on the day Jǐmǎo,
he sent several strong men armed with white clubs to attack Li Kěyīn,
killing him.
The court and the populace were shocked.
On the day Gēngchén,
the King of Mǐn's illness slightly abated.
[The character] jiàn [is pronounced] according to its usual reading.
The King of Mǐn forced himself to attend court despite his illness,
and inquired about the circumstances of Kěyīn's death.
Lǐ Fǎng, frightened, left the court.
Shortly after,
he led his troops, clamoring, into the palace.
Hearing of the disturbance,
the King of Mǐn hid under the Nine Dragon Canopy.
The King of Mǐn had ordered the brocade workers to make a Nine Dragon Canopy.
The people of the state sang about it:
"Who says the Nine Dragon Canopy
holds only one Guīláng?"
Guīláng refers to Shǒu Míng.
The King of Mǐn was writhing, not yet dead.
The palace attendants could not bear his suffering,
so they ended it for him.
That is, they ended his life.
Wèi [is pronounced] yúwèi fān.
This was because Jì Tāo and Jì Péng had long been hostile towards each other.
On the day Xīnsì,
Jì Péng declared that he was to supervise state affairs by order of the Empress Dowager.
On that same day, he ascended the imperial throne.
The Empress Dowager was Huáng Shì, mother of Wáng Lín.
Jì Péng was the eldest son of Wáng Lín.
He posthumously honored his father as Emperor Qísù Míngxiào,
with the temple name Huìzōng.
Afterwards, he proclaimed himself Acting Military Commissioner of Fújiàn,
sent envoys to present memorials to the Táng court,
and granted a general amnesty within his territory.
He established Lǐ Chūnyàn as his consort.
Earlier, the Mǐn Emperor Huìzōng had married the daughter of the King of Hàn, Princess Qīngyuǎn.
Guǎngzhōu has a Qīngyuǎn County.
The Táng records do not mention a Mǐnqīng County;
it was likely first established by the Wáng family.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: Mǐnqīng County belongs to Fúzhōu,
located 150 li northwest of the prefectural seat.
Sòng Bái says: In the first year of the Zhēnyuán era of Táng, ten districts were carved out from Hòuguān County to form the Méixī Administrative Area.
In the first year of the Qiánhuà era of Liáng, it was changed to Mǐnqīng County.
Fān [is pronounced] pān.
The King of Hàn bestowed upon him a grand mansion,
with generous provisions and gifts,
and frequently questioned him about affairs in Mǐn.
Lín Yányù did not answer.
Upon retiring,
he said to others:
"When leaving Mǐn, one speaks of Mǐn;
when leaving Yuè, one speaks of Yuè.
Living within the palace confines of another,
how can one act otherwise!"
The King of Hàn, hearing this, considered him worthy
and appointed him as a Palace Attendant-in-ordinary,
entrusting him with overseeing the affairs of various offices.
When Lín Yányù heard that Emperor Huìzōng had been assassinated,
he requested to return [to Mǐn],
but was not permitted.
He donned plain mourning clothes and wept facing his homeland for three days.
The historian states that Lín Yányù did not forget his former lord.
Jīngnán Military Commissioner Gāo Cónghuì
was intelligent and perceptive by nature,
personally treating worthy scholars with courtesy,
and entrusted responsibilities to Liáng Zhèn,
treating him as an elder brother.
Liáng Zhèn often addressed Cónghuì as "lángjūn."
Disciples and former subordinates address their master's son as "lángjūn."
Liáng Zhèn served Gāo Jìxīng,
Cónghuì's father,
hence he addressed Cónghuì as "lángjūn."
The King of Chǔ, Mǎ Xīfàn, was fond of extravagance and luxury,
and itinerant talkers all boasted of his magnificence.
Cónghuì said to his aides:
"Someone like King Mǎ can indeed be called a great man."
Sūn Guāngxiàn replied:
"For the Son of Heaven and the feudal lords,
there are distinctions in ritual propriety.
That milky-mouthed youth, arrogant, extravagant, and presumptuous,
seeks momentary pleasure,
gives no thought to the long term.
His peril and ruin are not far off.
Is he truly worthy of admiration?"
After some time, Cónghuì came to understand and said:
"Your words are correct."
Another day,
he said to Liáng Zhèn:
"Upon reflection, I realize my usual indulgences
have certainly been excessive."
He then discarded his curios and pleasures,
amusing himself with classics and histories instead,
reduced punishments and lightened taxes,
and the region became peaceful.
Liáng Zhèn said:
"The late king treated me as a friend in plain clothes,
and entrusted the heir king to me.
The late king refers to Gāo Jìxīng.
The heir king refers to Cónghuì.
Shǔ [is pronounced] zhīyù fān.
Not to let his enterprise decline—I am old now,
and will not serve another."
He thus firmly requested to retire.
Cónghuì could not detain him,
so he built a residence for him on Tǔzhōu.
Liáng Zhèn wore a crane-feather cloak,
calling himself the Recluse of Jīngtái.
Whenever he went to the administrative headquarters,
he rode a yellow ox to the audience hall.
Cónghuì often visited his home,
bestowing generous gifts throughout the four seasons.
From then on, he entrusted all governmental affairs to Sūn Guāngxiàn.

Your subject Guāng remarks: Sūn Guāngxiàn, perceiving subtle signs, was able to remonstrate; Gāo Cónghuì, hearing good counsel, was able to change. Gāo Cónghuì's admiration for Mǎ Xīfàn was the sprouting of a mind inclined towards extravagance, yet Sūn Guāngxiàn strenuously spoke against it to prevent its growth. Gāo Cónghuì, following Guāngxiàn's words, discarded curios and pleasures and found joy in classics and histories, contemplating how to enrich the people and protect the borders—this is turning towards goodness. Liáng Zhèn assisted the Gāo father and son, enabling them to preserve their state—this is an achievement. How could there be any cause for the destruction of the state, the ruin of the family, or the loss of life?
Wú enfeoffed Grand Councillor Xú Zhīgào additionally as Shàngfù, Grand Preceptor, Grand Chancellor, and Grand Marshal,
advanced him to the rank of Prince of Qí,
and prepared special ceremonies for him,
designating Shēng, Rùn, Xuān, Chí, Shè, Cháng, Jiāng, Ráo, Xìn, and Hǎi, ten prefectures, as the State of Qí.
Examining the ten prefectures Xú Zhīgào was enfeoffed with:
from Rùn following the river upstream,
reaching Jiāng then cuts through the waist and spine of the state of Wú.
The connection between Jiāngdū and Hóng, È
is severed.
From Cháng, Rùn crossing the sea to the boundary of Huái and possessing Hǎizhōu,
then there is a situation encompassing the whole of Wú.
His planning and scheming considered himself successful.
At that time, if all the people of Wú united in supporting Zhīgào,
why was it necessary to act thus before usurping?
Shè [is pronounced] shūshè fān.
He declined the special ceremonies.
In Mǐn, the Imperial City Commissioner and Supervisor of the Six Armies and Various Guards, Lǐ Fǎng, monopolized court administration,
secretly nurturing desperadoes.
The King of Mǐn, Chǎng, plotted against him with the Commander of the Gǒngchén Guard, Lín Yánhào, and others.
Yánhào and others pretended to be close and submissive to Fǎng,
and Fǎng treated them without suspicion.
In the eleventh month,
on the day Rénzǐ,
when Fǎng entered the court,
Yánhào and others had hidden several hundred guards in the inner hall,
who seized and beheaded him,
displaying his head at the court gate.
Over a thousand of Fǎng's troops, armed with white clubs, attacked the Yìngtiān Gate,
but failed to take it.
They burned the Qǐshèng Gate,
seized Fǎng's head, and fled to Wúyuè.
An edict was issued exposing Fǎng's crimes of assassinating the sovereign and killing Jì Tāo and others,
and proclaiming it to the court and the populace.
This was the edict of the King of Mǐn.
He appointed the Six Armies Judge, Yǒngtài's Yè Qiào, as Palace Proclamation Commissioner and Participant in Determining Governmental Matters.
In the second year of the Xiántōng era of Emperor Yìzōng of Táng,
Yǒngtài County was established by dividing territory from Liánjiāng and Mǐn,
belonging to Fúzhōu.
The Jiǔyù Zhì states: It is 350 li southwest of the prefectural seat.
The Fúzhōu Tújīng states: Yǒngtài County
was established in the second year of the Yǒngtài era of Táng,
named after the era name.
Qiào [is pronounced] qíxiāo fān.
Qiào was erudite and upright in character.
Mǐn Huìzōng promoted him to be the Friend of the Prince of Fú,
as the Mǐn ruler Chǎng was initially enfeoffed as the Prince of Fú.
He provided much beneficial assistance,
and within the palace he was called
"the State Elder."
After Chǎng succeeded to the throne,
he became arrogant and unrestrained,
and no longer discussed state affairs with Qiào.
One day,
while Chǎng was attending to official matters,
Qiào, dressed in Daoist robes, hurried across the courtyard to leave.
Chǎng summoned him back,
bowed to him,
and said:
"Military and state affairs are pressing,
and I have not received you for a long time;
this is my fault."
Qiào kowtowed and said:
"This old minister has failed in his guidance and assistance,
resulting in Your Majesty having not a single good deed to be praised since ascending the throne.
I wish to beg for retirement."
Chǎng said:
"The late emperor entrusted me to you.
If government orders are not good,
you should speak out frankly.
How can you abandon me and leave!"
He bestowed generous gifts of gold and silk,
and comforted and instructed him to return to his post.
Chǎng's principal wife was Lady Lǐ of the State of Liáng,
daughter of the Tóngpíngzhāngshì Lǐ Mǐn.
Chǎng favored Lǐ Chūnyàn,
and sought Chūnyàn from Empress Chén,
as seen above in the sixth month.
Favor,
pronounced with the meaning of "lowly,"
also pronounced bójì.
Qiào remonstrated, saying:
"The Lady is the late emperor's niece,
married with proper rites.
How can you abandon her for a new favorite!"
Chǎng was displeased,
and from then on distanced himself from him.
Not long after,
Qiào again submitted a memorial discussing affairs.
Chǎng wrote at the end of the paper:
"A single leaf follows the wind into the imperial moat."
He then sent him away to return to Yǒngtài.
Lù Zhèn's *Jiǔguózhì* states: Yè Qiào was dismissed and returned to Yǒngchūn.
According to the *Jiǔyùzhì*,
Quánzhōu has a Yǒngchūn County,
and Fúzhōu has a Yǒngtài County.
It is unknown which is correct.
34 The Emperor commended Mǎ Quánjié's achievements,
for repelling the Shǔ army and securing Jīnzhōu.
Liú Yánlǎng sought a bribe,
but Quánjié had nothing to give him;
Yánlǎng wanted to appoint Quánjié as Prefect of Jiàngzhōu,
causing widespread discussion and discontent.
When the Emperor heard of this,
on the yǐmǎo day,
he appointed Quánjié as Liúhòu of Héng Hǎi.
Although the Emperor learned of it,
he did not punish Liú Yánlǎng;
rewarding the good and punishing the evil,
this is why the Guō perished.
35 In the twelfth month,
on the rénshēn day,
he appointed Zhōngshū Shìláng, Tóngpíngzhāngshì, and concurrently Shūmìshǐ Hán Zhāoyìn as Tóngpíngzhāngshì,
concurrently Jiedùshǐ of Hùguó.
36 On the yǐyǒu day,
he appointed the former Jiedùshǐ of Kuāngguó and Tóngpíngzhāngshì Féng Dào as Sīkōng.
At that time, there had long been no one formally appointed as one of the Three Dukes.
Since the chaos of the rebellions,
there had been those who concurrently held or were granted the titles of the Three Dukes through other offices,
but none were formally appointed.
Lú Wénjì wanted him to oversee sacrifices and sweeping,
according to Suí regulations: The Three Dukes participate in deliberating major state affairs,
in sacrifices, the Tàiwèi assists in the offerings,
the Sītú presents the sacrificial vessels,
and the Sīkōng performs the sweeping.
Lú Wénjì did not investigate deeply,
and thus considered it the duty of the Sīkōng.
Court,
pronounced zhí yáo fān.
"The Sīkōng's
duty is sweeping,
why should I fear it?"
Later, Wénjì himself realized it was not appropriate,
and stopped.
The history states that although Later Táng claimed to inherit the old domain of Táng,
its cultural heritage was insufficient.
37 The Mǐn ruler bestowed upon Dòngzhēn Xiānshēng Chén Shǒuyuán the title of Tiānshī,
trusted and valued him,
to the extent that even changes in generals and ministers,
punishments,
and selections
were all discussed with him;
Shǒuyuán accepted bribes and requests,
and whatever he said was followed,
his gate was like a marketplace.
Diàn Guǎngmíng punctuated, Niè Chóngqí proofread.
